articles.title: CABMEN'S MOVEMENT
articles.text:
THE CABMEN'S MOVEMENT

WITH the successful Aggregate Meeting of
Drivers, held at the Whittington Club, on the
evening of the 3rd inst., has.terminated the first
- phase of the 6abmen's Movement. The work
has been an uphill labour, but it has been
brought thus far to a successful conclusion.
Tougher and sterner work now lies before the
• delegates, but the pluck and patience' which
has carried them so far upon the road to their
emancipation from an odious, oppressive, and
one-sided law, will doubtless enable them to
overcome the many difficulties still standing in
the way. One of the most hopeful features of
the late meeting was the countenance and sup-
port it received from a large section of the
proprietors, many of whom were present, al-
though one only took any prominent part in
the proceedings, but they generally concurred
in all that had been done by the delegates. The
:above proprietor, Mr. Case, in the course of
• a very effective speech,. urged unity of action
'between proprietors and drivers as essential to
ultimate success ; and this view was endorsed
-by the large majority of the meeting when it
resolved to invite the proprietors to co-operate.
with the delegates'of the drivers. It is to be
• hoped this invitation will -be-cordially accepted
by the proprietors, and the task of obtaining
• that reform which will be alike beneficial to
both sections of the trade will then be more
easily accomplished. With or without the pro-
prietors, however, the work must proceed ; the
delegates have now gone too farto draw back
without covering themselves and their con-
stituents with ridicule. Their ineetlhg, with
the statement of their grievance and the re-
medies proposed, was fully and almost univer-
sally reported in the press; and having adopted
a petition praying for a Parliamentary Com-
mittee of Inqury into those grievances, and as
to the justice and neCessity of tile proposed
remedial measures, their next step must be to
pick out a few intelligent Men who, by clear
evidence, "ill be able:to substantiate the exist-
ence of the grievances of-which they complain;
and prove the justice of the proposed remedies:
On the selection of these witnesses willmainly
depend the successful issue of the movement. -If
-they are enabled to convince the committee
. that these grievances exist, it will ' no doubt
report to the House of Commons the necessity'
for measures being taken to remove, or modify
-them, if impossible altogether to be -ire-
moved. Whether the committee May adopt
the -whole or any of the proposed rremedial
clauses, and recommend their adoption into a'
new act; is:of course open to doubt, but they .are
generally so, moderate, and prepared with such
evident regard to the interests Of all
,parties
concerned—the proprietor, the driver, and-the
.publc—that they cannot fail of cominanding the
'attention of the committee. There are mem-
bers in both.HoUses of Parliament ,who take
much interest in the well-being of the drivers,
and these gentlemen will take care that justice
is done to them.. There is another favourable
'feature in the case. The statement of the griev-
ances under which cabmen labour, and the
clauses they desire to be worked into an act to
remove those grievances, have now been before
the public for some time, and there has been no
sign of opposition from that quarter.•
One thing, however, is quite certain, that if
the agitation is not further successful, it has
already, as far as it has gone, done cabnien a
Tast amount of good. It has obtained for them
a fair hearing in the pnblia press; it has dis-
armed public prejudice against them-to a large
extent; it has checked the arbitrary decisions of
police magistrates; it has curbed the insolence
of policemen; it has proved the falsity and
ignorance or thFt-.. --self ~uflicient newspaper
editcr who called them "indomitable beasts ;"
but, above all, it has taught cabmen
a lesson they are not likely soon to forget,—it
has taught them to rely upon themselves, and
has shown them the necessity- and advantages
Of union to obtain redress for wrong.
," Out
of evil cometh good." It is, after all, question.
able whether the editor of Lloyd's paper, by
his wibeastly" attack upon the whole body of
cabmen, has not proved himself their best
friend; having roused their feelings as men,
thus publicly to prove they were not brutes.
Even the best friends of the cabmen—those
who never joined in the cry with which they
were attempted to be hounded down—have
been astonished at the extent of intelligence
existing amongst them as a class, as evinced by
the good selection of men they have chosen to
represent them on the committee of delegates.
No body of working men ever had a better com-
mittee than the cabmens' delegates have
proved themselves to be; they are men of whom
their constituents may well be proud, and feel
satisfied that their interests are safe in such
hands. Temperate, but firm; moderate, but
just; cool, but decisive; they have, while
smarting under an amount of abuse and con-
tumely almost overwhelming, pursued the
"even tenor of their way," and in all their
deliberations, and in all their decisions, have
been animated with the desire to deal justly,
with all interests, and shown a remarkable apti-
tude for business. Such conduct cannot fail in
meeting its reward. It has already done so.
A few short months since to be known to be a
cabman was to be considered. a low, ignorant
blackguard, a man intent only on extortion and
the abuse of his customers. Now, it is generally,
acknowledged that, although there must neces-
sarily be a great many bad men amongst a body
of 10,000, as a class they- are as respectable, as
intelligent, as well-conducted, and as free from
drunkenness, crime, or • blackguardism, as any
other body of working men. Honour, then, to
the men who have rescued themselves and
'their class from the social degradation in which
they were supposed to exist. Such men, who
know their rights, and, knowing, dare publicly
to maintain them cannot long be kept under
the subjection of an unjust, vexatious, and
oppressive Act of Parliament.
Before closing these remarks, I may be per-
izitted to claim for the BEE-HIVE some small
Share in producing this healthful state of
Public feeling towards cabmen. At the first
commencement of their movement, it stood
almost alone amongst the press in upholding
and sustaining it. It has ever been found
willing to cheer on the good work; and its
columns have been freely opened for that pur-
pose. has It bprovided them a central place of
meeting, by the gratuitous use of its rooms, for
the delegates meetings, and it is owing to the
influence and exertions of one of its writers
that reports of their meetings obtained admis-
sion, into several of the daily papers. In. these
days of forgetfulness of services rendered, I
have felt bound to say so much for the BEE-
HIVE, and I have every confidence that the
cabmen themselves Will t
no_ overlook a paper
who has. thus upheld them. Be that as it
may, it will always be the pleasurable duty of
"the man in Bouverie-street,"—(to use the ex-
pression of Lloyd's editor),—to do all that
lies in his power, in the columns of this paper,
is to aid the just demands ef the cabmen,and to
apply, without any hesitation, when necessary,
to all their enemies, the
December 11th, 1862.

A WEEKLY NEWSPAPER OF GENERAL INTELLIGENCE, ;

THE . EAST LANCAS HI RE CEN VEAL 0 I 'ERA.-

The weekly meeting of the• Exebutive took place at
the Committee-rooms,'Speak Padilla-tn. Pre-
sent the Rev, E. A: Vdrity, B.D:, Rector of Haliefg-
ham, president. Deputies present, Messrs. James
Crompton, J. Pinder, L. Shackleton (Burnley), James
Heap, Henry Whitehead,'Geerge Hargreavo
ham), John Haworth, James Denbigh,,Wm. Wilkin'eon
(treasurer), and J. PeacOCk (hen: see.), Padiham: • The
, minutes of the last meeting were confirmed.
,The
secretary- delivered in his .report, which was highly
favourable. No grant had been received from London
since Mr. George Potter's fund had. "cerminated, and
the London trades had not yet had time to organise
and collect. .An appeal would be Sent to them so as
to 're,ach Wednesday's Council meeting. The tre'Fi-

of. Liverpciol had generously promised to send £lOO

(Cheers.)' A weekly giant was also expected from the
brethren in London. The best thanks of the cornmittee were awarded to each Of these gentlemen, and
to the trades of London and Liverpool. The 'trades of
Edinburgh are in "cotninunication with 'the Searetary on '
the same subject. The Chairman alluded to the letter
of Prefeeier Beesly,"and was reriuested to reily to it.
The depUtation to Liverpool gave in their repott. The
best thanks. of the Meeting were *given to the dePuta-
tion. After some discussion about the positioni of, CO:
operation in. the town and neighbourhood- of Burnley,
the,meeting, separated. Owing to the want of funds
no grants were made to the districts this week. ,

•The following letter has been received by the Rey.
Verity, from the Bristol Committee :
• PEAR. feel much
.pleasuEe, as 'requested by
the above conin-iittee, in forwarding you another Post;
office Order for:E10, which you will -please pay into
the East Lancashire Central Operative Relief Fund.'
Out deminittee iyet,e induced to forward what little we
have sent to this committee, because we thought that
they were likely to' appropriate it wisely and fairly—in
other words, we had confidence in their integrity in
the matter: Large nambers of men here, in. regular
employ, never subscribe a penny towards the relief' of
their suffering fellows in the cotton districts, but many
who do will send their subscriptions through any other
medium, rather than the one
.more immediately con-
nected with their own body. Our committee canhot,
help feeling that such conduct i not generous, while
they rejoice that help is afforded to those who are des-
titute through any other channel.—Yours,
Wm. BUTCHER, President.
Colston Hall, December 6.

THE TRADES' PROTECTION ASSOCIATION AND LANCA-
stuns DISTRESS.—On Friday the Liverpool Trades'
Association held a public meeting at Hope-hall in aid
of the distressed operatives. Mr. Lynch presided, and
said that he regretted that the use of St George's Hall
had been refused to a deputation that had asked for it.
for the purpose of that meeting. After some intro-
ductory remarks he introduced the Rev. E. A. Verity,
8.D., rector of Habergham, near Burnley, who deli-
vered a long address on the present cottom famine. He
complained of the Manchester committees, who, he
maintained, did not distribute the funds justly or
liberally, and advocated the formation of working
men's committees. He asserted that the Manchester
committees were chiefly composed of manufacturers,
who generally refused to relieve those operatives who
belonged to 60-operative societies and trades' unions;
and, therefore, that showed the necessity of work-
ing men's committees, and he urged the formation
'of- one in Liverpool.—Mr. Williams moved a reso-
lution expressive of sympathy towards the distressed
operatives, and •.urging that every effort should be
made by all classes towards obtaining continuous con-
tributions towards the funds. Mr. Winstanley
seconded the resolution. Mr. Brown, in an energetic
*peech, moved a resolution pledging the Liverpool
Trades' Association to do all in its power, either by
levies or voluntary contributions, as each society should
itself determine, to assist in as permanent and as
prompt a manner as possible their distressed brethren
in Manchester.—Dr. Daniel seconded the resolution.—
Mr. Lewin moved that the executive of the Trades'
Association resolve itself into a committee to collect
subscriptions, and that Liverpool be divided into dis-
tricts to act in concert with the central committee,
who shall be empowered to send a delegate to see that
their funds were equally and properly divided.—Mr.
Grenville seconded the resolution; a vote of thanks to
Mr. Verity and the chairman was then passed, and a
subscription having been made in the room, the pro-
ceedings terminated.

SYMPATHY WITH GREECE.—A meeting was held at
the London Tavern on Wednesday, to express sym-
pathy with the Greeks in respect of their late revolution.
Mr. Crawford, M.P., presided. Mr. }hillie Cochrane,
M.P., moved the first resolution, and Mr. H. Seymour,
M.P., the second. The first declared the gratification
of the meeting at the efforts made by tho Greeks for
the political regeneration of their counfry. The second
expressed the conviction that in the reorganisation of
their political affairs the Greeks will most scrupulously
respect the rights of other States. Interesting speeches
were made in support of these resolutions, which were
carried.

AFRICAN PRODUCTIONS.—The very interesting objects
contained in the Liberian Court of the Exhibition,
have been transferred to the offices of the West Africa
Company, at 41, Gresham House, with the sanction of
the Liberian Government. These productions have
attracted considerable public notice, especially the
samples of cotton, sugar, palm-oil, and the very beau-
tiful specimens of mahogany and otherhard timber. We
understand that it is the intention of the West Africa
Company to use these as the nucleus of an African
Museum], and as an illustration of the articles the
Company will import. It is satisfactory to know that
one of the agents of the Company has expressed his
belief that he will be able to ship 500,000 bales of
cotton from the Niger next year, and that a gentleman
has offered to invest £50,000 in cotton culture in
Liberia, upon an undertaking from the Company, that
he shall be guaranteed by the Company for his cleaned
cotton (Middling Orleans quality) three pence per
pound at the port of shipment.
HORRIBLE DEATH OF A SCHOOLBOT.—An inquiry was
held by Mr. Walthew, respecting the death of John
Barrett, eleven years of age, who was killed under
the following shocking circumstances :—The deceased
was the son of a widow, residing in Tooley-street,
Southwark, and he was in the habit of riding on the
coal waggons of Messrs. Rickett daily to school. Last
Saturday he got, as usual, on one of the waggons, and
rode to Hockington-road, Hackney. When there the
unevenness of the newly-gravelled road caused the
waggon to jerk; deceased was thrown off and one of
the large wheels literally cut off the upper half of his
skull. The poor boy, of course, was killed instan-
taneously. The coroner remarked on the melancholy
and horrible nature of the occurrence, and a subserip-
tion was got lip for the afflicted mother, who was in
indigent circumstances. A verdict of 'Death by mis-
fortune' vs,s returned,

AND TRADES', FRIENDLY SOCIETY, AND CO-OPERATIVE JOURNAL

No. 61.

PKOFESSOR, BEESLY AND MIDDLE-CLASS
~. RELIEF. COMMITTEES.
•TO THE EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."

Si,—ln the concluding remarks of Professor
Beesly's letter, in your last, impression, the following
words occur:—" In advocating a working. man's
relief fund for the Lancashire Distress, you. allege
that :relief. has been refosed to co-operators or
marked
,workmeo. Now, this is a serious charge to
.ma'ke,and I .hold that you ought either to give
names and circumstances, or say nothing about it."
. I
,admit with the Professor it is 'a—serious charge,
and, moreover, a very discreditable fact .if capable
of proof. But as lam in possession of such proofs,
and can substantiate such facts with names, dates,
and circumstances, I trust the Professor will no
longer withhold his belief.' I 'shall be glad to her
from him, or to conduct him to the victims' houses,
should he favour us with a visit • into Lancashire.
More than this, I have challenged the Central Com-
mittee's'Setretary; in Manchest6r, to attend a public
meeting in London, Birmingham, or Liverpool, and
will' undertake to prove, •

, 'l. That paupers are not relieved by Middle-class
Relief:Committees, and that the relief given by the
Poor-law Guardians is not sufficient.

That co-operators to the 'number of 2,000
have been refuled'relief. both by Guardians and Com-
mittees. •• •

3. That trades-unionists have in many instances
been refused relief by 'middle-class committees.—l
am, Sir, your obedient servant,

• . . E. A. VERITY, 8.D.,
President of the East Lancashire Operatives

Central Committee, Padiliam-.

articles.title: INGRATI2UDE OF WORKING
articles.text:
INGRATI2UDE OF WORKING

TO THE EDITOR OF THE ' BEE-HVIE.'

Sin,—The ingratitude of working men towards those
who labour for and in their interests is proverbial, and
instances, unfcrtunately, are constantly occurring to
prove the truth of the assertion. Many a man who
has started on his career of usefulness, with high and
eanguino hope, has ere long retired from-hio labours
dispirited and disgusted at the apathy and indifference
of those in whose interests he was working, and many
more are deterred from the same cause from entering
on the work at all. A glaring instance has lately
come under my notice in connection with the BEEHIVE
newspaper, calling for a few remarks.
At the commencement of this year the Journeymen
Garment Dyers were engaged in a struggle with their
employers for a reduction in their hours of labour.
Not only were the columns of the BEEHIVE placed
freely at the service of tlifir4arment Dyers' Committee
to report their proceedings, and gratuitous insertion of
their advertisements, and articles, written—conscien-
tiously written—by me in support of the movement,
but,:at great personal inconvenience, I attended a select
meeting of the employers, in the interest of the com-
mittee, and was thus enabled to afford them valuable
information which they could not otherwise have
obtained. I am not assuming too much for the
BEEHIVE when I say that it materially con-
tributed to the success which at last crowned
the efforts of the workmen's committee. Mark
the reward! A few weeks since the Journeymen
Garment Dyers' Trade Society, comprising the same
men who had been thus assisted in the above move-
ment, decided upon calling a meeting of the trade to
organise subscriptions for the relief of Lancashire
distress, and to advertise that meeting. They, of
course, gave the BEEmvz—their old friend—the bene-
fit, small though it might be, of their advertisement.
Oh, no! The existence of the BEEHIVE was ignored
by these grateful men, aid the advertisement sent to
a weekly paper that had never inserted or written a
line of its own on their behalf! What an encourage-
ment for newspapers to labour for and write for,
working men! The value of the advertisement—
about two shillings—is not the question. It is the
ungrateful action of which I complain. But
this is not all. Flaying collected upwards of £6
in subscriptions, although they know there was
a list open at the BEEHIVE Office, they must also send
that to the above paper, to be paid by its proprietor into
a committee, who, instead of sending it to feed starv-
ing operatives in Lancashire, invest it in consols in the
neighbourhood of • the Stock Exchange! Oh wise
garment dyers! Grateful garment dyers! Let other
bodies of working men copy your example, and you
will all soon be left to flounder as you may in the
slough of social slavery. R. HARTWELL.

SIGNOR GIUGLINI AND MRS. WINDIIAM.-011 Monday
evening Mdlle. Titiens and Signor Giuglini, accom-
panied by three operatic stars of less brilliancy, gave a
concert in the Music Hall, Aberdeen. The lady was
received with unqualified approbation; not so the
great tenor, his part in the last public act of the
Windham drama having created an unfavourable
feeling against him. The consequence was that the
signor, on making his first appearance, was greeted
with considerable hissing—a manifestation which not
a few evidently thought all the more deserved, that the
now notorious Mrs. Windham, nee Miss Rogers, occu-
pied a prominent place in the gallery, and was hearty
in applause of her favourite.

HANDEL FESTIVAL CHOIR.—The committee of the
Sacred Harmonic Society having come to the determi-
nation to keep together the 1,600 voices forming the
London amateur division of the above choir, have made
arrangements for a series of four rehearsals during the
present season, under the direction of M. Costa, the
first of which took place on Friday, the sth inst., when
the majority of the choruses from Mozart's Twelfth
Mass,' and the Dettingen To Deum,' were gone
through. From the freshness with which the various
pieces were executed it was evident that the choir has
lost none of its usual vigour, although a little more
briskness might have been desired in some of the tra-
vura passages. Altogether it was a very creditable
rehearsal, the most noteworthy pieces being the
Kyrie,' and the ' Gloria,' from the Mass, and To
Thee, Cherubim,' from the Te Deum, which, being
perhaps, the most popular of the pieces, may have
seemed to have been better sung than the others. The
alto opening of the chorus, 4 Lord, in Thee,' was re-
markably well dime,

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, 'DECEMBER 13, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, 'DECEMBER 13, 1862.

TILE L CASIIIR EiDISTRES

LONDON WORKING MEN'S CENTRAL RELIEF

COMMITTEE.

The second weekly meeting of the trades' delegates,
comprising this committee, was held on Wednesday
evening, at the office 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street.
Present :—Messrs. office,
carpenter; Odgers, shoe-
maker; Martin, cigar maker; Goddard, bookbinder;
Graham carpenter; Murray, bootcloser, with Mr. G.
Potter, the treasurer, and Mr. Hornsby, carpenter, the
honorary secretary. Messrs. Nieass and Page were in
attendance as a deputation from the 'workmen of
Notting-hill and Bayswater.
Mr. Jarvis having been called to the chair, said he
trusted after the present week, when the formation of
the committee had become generally known to working
men, their subscription list, would be widely extended,
as he had no doubt, but many working men in shops
and factories who were now sending their monies to
other channels, would send them to this committee.
Many reports had been made as .to the treatment
of trades unionists and co operators, by the
middle class , relief, committees in 'Lancashire,
and it had been thought desirahle,. before eny
monies 'were transmitted from this committee, that a
deputation should 'go to Lancashire and visit the
Padiham Committee and the operatives in various
districts, to ascertain the truth of these reports, and
as to how 'working men were really treated by these
relief committees, so that they might use a propeedis-
crimination as -to where and to •whom they should
transmit
.the subscriptions entrusted to them. Some
few objections had been made-to this course, but"thel
committee thought this deputation, who would only '
be absent for one week, and would cost but a few
pounds, would probably save some hundreds. At all
events, the committee would, by the information thuS
obtained, as •to the exact state of feeling of the
other
.operatives, be in a much better condition to
perform those duties than if they had trusted to written
correspondence or newspaper reports. (Cheers.)
- The Secretary then reported ' he had received the
following letter from Messrs. Cremer and 'Burn, the
deputation sent to Lancashire by the committee:l—
-' Padiham, Wednesday, Dec: 9, 1862:
'Dear Sir,—We have met the committee here, and
inquired into its constitution and character. We find
there are men on it of various creeds and occupations,
but seemingly all animated by one desire, viz., that of
relieving the distress, and so of doing good. The
operations of the committee extend to Habergham,
Burnley, and Padiham districts, in which there are
many thousands out of employment; and we find
from inquiries that those who are in employment are
-earning but 6s. or 6s. per week at the most. We are '
just going with Mr. Verity to see for ourselves some
of the recipients of the funds you have sent, and also
to judge for ourselves of the distress. To-night we go
to Oldham, to meet there a working-man's committee.
To-morrow to Bacup, to ascertain from the co-
operators there whether they have been refused relief
on account of their being so. We believe the com-
mittee here to be of the right sort—some union and
others non-union men—and we believe from their
accounts, which have been and are now open to us,
that the money they have received has been honestly
expendal.—W. R. CREME; WM. BURN.'
The Secretary reported he had received applications
for relief from the Padiham Committee, and from the
following bodies of working rr.en :—Manchester Calen-
derers and Makers-up, Blackburn Cotton Spinners,
Blackburn Power Loom Weavers, Preston Spinners,
and the Manchester and Stockport Overlookers. The
following are extracts from the letters :---
MANCHESTER CALENDERERS.—The Calenderers and
Makers-up Society was established in 1824, and now
comprises 190 members, 60 only of whom are in regular
employment, 20 on short time, and 110 idle. These
latter are being relieved out of our sick and funeral
fund mcney, which is nearly exhausted. During the
Ilast twelve months our income has been £lO4, and our
expenditure £1,170. Our present loss is'£2s weekly.
I I brought our case before the Manchester Central
Relief Committee, but can get no decided answer; but
I have ascertained from several of the members indi-
vidually that we cannot be relieved as a body, and our
members would not like individually to apply for
relief.—Tuomas S. CONNOR, President, 71, Hall-street,
Green Hays, Manchester.
PRESTON SPINNERS AND MINDERS.—We are 1,267 in
number. Our funds have been completely exhausted
in supporting our members, and also £lOO we borrowed
from the Amalgamated Engineers. We shall be com-
pelled to give up our institute and meeting-room, for
want of funds. We have applied to the relief com-
mittee, but they turn a deaf ear to us. Many of the
parties on those committees would like nothing snore
than to see us broken up and dispersed.—THomms Burixs.

BLACKBURN POWER- LOOM WAVERS.—You must be
made acquainted with the manner in which the com-
mittee here distribute the money entrusted to them;
there is an unjustifiable degree of favouritism towards
the adherents of different churches and chapels, and
there are numbers who cannot get admission into any
of the denominational schools. The present affords an
opportunity for oppressing those men of the different
trades who have formerly taken a leading part in the
protection of labours' rights, and such opportunity is
not being lost sight of by the employers and their
agents in these towns. The employers in this town
have commenced upon a very large scale to break
through their engagements as to the prices paid. For
many years we have worked under a standard list of
prices for weaving fabrics, but they are now taking ad-
vantage of the pressure of the times to break through that
list, ofering a reduction 0/at least 25 per cent.—Wuxuar
CROSSLEY, Secretary.
Accompanying this letter were several printed
documents, naming many employers who are acting as
above, the most prominent on the list being Mr. It H.
Hutchinson, the late mayor of the town.
A letter was also read from the workmen in the
employ of Messrs. Palmer, iron ship yard, Jarrow, near
Gateshead, enclosing £9 75., and stating it to be their
intention of raffling a mule in a few days, the proceeds
from which it was expected would be about £l5.
The following grants were then made :—To Padiham
Committee, £l5; to Preston Spinners, ;to Black-
burn Cotton Spinners, £10; to Blackburn Power-loom
Weavers, £10; and to Manchester Calenderers, £5;
with an intimation that grants would be extended after
the reports of the deputation.
It was then resolved that the secretary write to the
deputation who left town last Monday that their mis-
sion would terminate on Saturday (this day).
It was also resolved that deputations wait upon
those London trades not represented on the committee.
It was then moved" that a special meeting of the
General Committee be held at the office, 2, Bouverie-
street, Fleet-street, on Wednesday evening next, at
eight o'clock, when the deputation to Lancashire will
make their report. It is hoped that every delegate
present at the Bell inn, Old Bailey, on the night of the
formation of the committee, will make a point of at-.
tending this meeting. Delegates from societies not
represented, or from shops, factories, or any body of
working men who subscribe to the funds, are invited
to attend and aid in the good cause.
*** Subscriptions to be sent to . Mr. G. Potter, the
treasurer, at the office of the committee Z, Bouverie-
street, Fleet-street, London; and all letters and appli-
cations for relief to. Mr. Horniby,, tke honorary
secretarh at thQ 4c4) as above.

articles.title: AN ADDRESS .TO THE HEN OF LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
AN ADDRESS
.TO THE HEN OF
LANCASHIRE.

Men'of Lancashire,---I appeal to you in your distress
with the ardent deMre cf beina useful to, you, not by
praising your Caithness. and resignation—no! let the
lords de that, they who live by the misfortunes of
others; they who alwr.ys enjoy all the comforts an 4
superfluities of life, while you are starving;—let those
Praise you for Suffering
.meekly and dying with want
in the midst of plenty.
The appeall make to you is to inquire seriously into
the causes of your present Misery. It is time that you
'should knot that though you prcklube the wealth of
the land, there is no possibility, of your ever being free,
from,poverty and starvation under the present form Of
Government.

" Issit right that in a wealthy cOuntry like England,
those who, produce that wealth by their toil should
always have•the least 'of it? Is' it right that those
who, produce nothing should, enjoy everything, that
they should spend treasures by thousands while those
`who produce them by overtoil and at the risk of their
life are deprived ,of everything? " It is of immense
iMportanCe that you shake off your apathy, that you
examine and study these questions seriously. Hitherto,
you have allowed the privileged classes to make laws
for you, but
.what is the result? The laws are made
in their favour, and against you. Do they ever suffer
from diStress and want? 'Do their children die like
yours, at the rate of 55 per cent., before they are five
years of age? Are they reduced, when old age
_comes,
to go to the workhouse, or to perish with hunger and
Cold? , No, they take good care of that; they make the
laws! Then why not you have a voice in making
them? While there is in this country, or in any other
a class, calling itself superior by birth, who possesses
the soil, whose influence gets for its families and crea-
tures all the fat livings and lucrative appointments,
who directs education and combines all its forces to
prevent your being rightly educated or fairly repre-
sented—while such a class exists, you will always be
treated worse than slaves; you may 'exist in times of
industrial prosperity, but the least accident, the least
blunder Of your rulers, or even the constant recurrence
of natural causes of slackness in trade, will again con-
demn you to starve by thousands. But these lords,
spiritual and secular, so arrange matters that they
never starve. They never even deprive themselves of
their su perfluiti es. Is that j ust ? Is it right ? Is it manly to
allow it? Will you leave to your children the same
prospects through life I leave those questions for
you to answer; but that you cannot do unless you at
once form yourselves into a league, and let all the
sufferers join with you throaghtna-the Mull, -to inquire
into the causes of such unnatural misery caused by the
manifest injustice, or evident incapacity, of your
rulers.

A WELL-WISHER TO THOSE WHO lIELi.
THEMSELVES.

A WORD TO THE INDUSTRIOUS CLASSES.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sirn,—The merry bells of England will soon sound
in the welcome ears of the inhabitants of this favoured
Isle on the Christmas festive day, thus calling to
memory past events and suggesting future prospects.
It is the season for interchange of thought and
friendly greeting around the social board. At this
time of joy , and pleasure, we lose all sympathy with
sorrow, but no one knows but he who gives, the plea-
sure there is in lending a helping hand to those who
are in need, and more especially those who are brought
to the door of want, and the cause cannot be attributed
to their carelessness or improvidence. Such is the
case with the industrous classes of Lancashire. A
bloody and uncalled for war is raging in a country to
which they look for the material on which their
labour depends, and to sustain our national position,
and our love of neutrality, the wants of Lancashire are
sacrificed to that end.

Can we then, as Englishmen, hear the cry of
distress, without feeling for, and being called upon to
do our utmost to its alleviation. Thousands have
for some time given a trifle weekly to assist
their fellow-workmen. Allow me to suggest that on
the week prior to Christmas they double their sub-
scription, and thus help to cause a feeling of joy in the
heart of a starving brother, and thereby enable him
to meet his wife and little ones around the social
board.

Your eyes may not look upon the scene, or your
ears hear a word, but you may depend you will have
the thanks of an honest English heart, and the con-
sciousness will give you more pleasure than that you
give can do. I. will not attempt to picture the distress,
for that has been done through the medium of your
powerful journal, or mention the noble sacrifice that
has been made by the men of Lancashire, for that is
patent to us all, for every working man knows the
amount of sacrifice he will make before he will become
a recipient of another's bounty.
Trusting this appeal will not be made in vain, but
will help to wish in a tangible form our brethren in
Lancashire the old English greeting, 'A merry
Christmas to you.' WILLIAM GLOVER.
Kentish -town.

THE PEABODY FUND.
TO THE EDITOR OF THB BEEHIVE.

SlR,—Early in the year Mr. G. Peabody, the Ame-
rican merchant, made a munificent gift to the poor of
London, the amount being invested in the hands of
certain trustees. The Registrar-General's returns
lately show deaths resulting from want of sufficient
food and starvation. May I ask, what has become of
the Peabody Fund? Is the present generation of poor
to be benefitted, or only their successors? Has any
decision been arrived at as to the most advisable course
to adopt in order to carry out the benevolent wishes of
the donor? Or has there yet been a meeting of the
trustees upon the snbject ?
These questions should elicit some explicit answer,
if you think well to give them publicity.—l am, &c.
Islington, Dec. 10. EAGLE EYB.

THE WORKMEN OF NORTHFLEET DOCK-
YARD.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sin,—Having read in a local paper that ihe inhabi-
tants of Nortlafleet complain of the want of police, I
also notice an unjust remark made by Sir Joshua
Jebb, stating the cause to be owing to the workmen of
the Northfleet dockyard. He states that there are
many ticket-of-leave men employed here. Let me tell
him that he will find as many respectable mechanics at
this dockyard as at any factory in England. Among
so many men, it is impossible for all to be patterns
of virtue, but there are none of the sort he mentions.
I am of opinion that Sir Joshua Jebb knows very
little of the working classes or he would be more
mild in his remarks; and, if he can point out to us any
way to better our present position in society, let him
step forward and do so, and not try to stir up strife
between us and the inhabitants of Northfleet. I am
at a loss to know what Northfleet or any other place
would be without the working class; and I hope the
day is not far distant when they may feel the want of
us, and have to acknowledge the same in milder terms
than at the present.
A WORKING BOILER. MAKER,
Northfleet Dockyard, Kent, Dee, 9, 1862.

articles.title: LItEIIATTIRE.
articles.text:
LItEIIATTIRE.

A Memoir of Thomas Martin Wheeler, Founder of the
Friend-In-Need Life and Sick Assurance Society,
Domestic, Political and Industrial. With extracts
from tis Letters, Speeches - and Wzitines. By
William Stevens. London: John Bedford' Leno,
159, Dury-lane. Price One Shilling.
In writing the life of any individual Cc, e great fault
of the biographer generally lies in a too partial view
of the life of the Man whose history he records. The
stand poiet generally selected is one from which is
seen only the best part of the character of the de-
ceased. The good' qualities, the best actions, and the
brightest examples are always set forth; but the faults,
the shortcomings, and cleric spots are seldom shown, or,
when mentioned, are done so in a very meagre form.
If a biography has for its object the inducement of
others to follow the example, walk in the steps and
imitate the good actions set forth in the life of the
man, then we contend that the faults' errors, and bad
qualities should also be recorded in rder to act as a
"warning to be avoided and guarded against. We wish
that biographers 'would see this evil, and in future
biographies avoid it. Much evil is wrought by these
one-sided histories, and great opportunities for doing
good are lost.. We hope the day is not far distant when
we shall be able not only to read of the good and
noble qualities of our greatimen, whose histories are to
be recorded, but also their failures and defects.
Mr. William Stevens deserves credit . for the able,
although somewhat partial, manner in which he has
put the life of the founder of the Friend-in-Need
Society before the public'. Our space will not permit
us to give many extracts from Mr. Stevens's excellent
Memoir of the Life of Thomas Martin Wheeler, but
"we avail ourselves of the opportunity of giving a few,
and at the same time express our hope that Mr.
Stevens's little work may have a wide circulation,
be read with-profit by a large number of the working
classes, and that enany such men as Thomas Martin
Wheeler may come forth from amongst them and take
part in the efforts now being mado to ameliorate their
social condition' and obtain for them that• political
power which. has been so long and so unjustly kept
from them. •
•
Thomas• Martin Wheeler was .born -on • the 23rd of
November; .1611; at Weiworth. 'When .he attained his
seventh year lie was sent for instruction-to a.celebrated
academy at 'Walton-le-Dale, near Preston; from thence
he was sent to a school at Stoke Newington, where he
remained- until he was fourteen.. • his life seems to
have been a busy one, and Mr. Stevens has divided it
into three parts—Domestic, Political, and Industrial.
We shall give an extract from each :
Shortly after leaving Mr. Clements, he as apprenticed
to his
‘uncle. Mr. Pebbles, at Banbury, to learn the wool-
Combing and haberdashery business; a good trade at that
time, but since destroyed by the introduction of machinery.
His uncle being infirm, our apprenticethadeto attend more
to the business of the shop than to the mysteries of the
craft.. His stay at Banbury was short, through some mis-
understanding with his aunt. She had taunted him with
submiting to her own harsh treatment, aritihad said that
if he had the blood of a Wheeler' in him he would not
put up with it. Taking the old lady at her word, young
Thomas packed up his luggage, threw it across his back,
and started for London, walking some ninety miles to reach
his home. Wheeler did not forget this worthy pair in after
life; for, in his story of Sunshine and Shadow,' he
sketches them to the life: He says that the hero's
master was a demure, hypocritical pretender to sanctity.
His yoUth had been passed, in excesses, from which his
constitution was now suffering, and, unable to enjoy
pleasure himself, he detested even the semblance of enjoy-
ment in others. His wife was -a thin, wiry woman, wrapped
up in her own merits, and' jealously alive to the demerits
of all around her, not fOrgetting those of her demure
spouse.' He was ;hen apptenticed to Mr. R. Payne, of
Reading, Berks., to learn the hiking busk ess. With Mr.
Payne he did not remain the full period of his apprentice-
ship, though long enough to- get 'an insight into the busi-
ness. He left Reading and found his way to London.
The difficulty our embryo •bal!er had in procuring work,
Wheeler well describes as having befallen his hero, in the
story I have already quoted. '7Dayafter day did Arthur
wander from street to street seeking employment, but in
vain; trade was unusually dull,' and the country appren-
tice was not sufficiently initiated into the mysteries of
London trade societies, to be a "successful competitor with
older hands acquainted with the eways of town.' At
last Wheeler obtained employment of a Mr. Shepherd,
whose shop was at the corner of Charles-street, Soho-
square; but his stay was brief. On leaving Mr. Shep-
herd's, in imitation of the German students, he made a
tour on foot through Kent and the southern counties,
visiting Canterbury, Chichester, Dover, and •other towns
on the south Coast. His journeying being 'at an end, he
settled down to work on Henley-on-Thomes, and here he
formed the acquaintance of the lady who subsequently
became his wife,—Ann Allder, a young widow of respect-
able family, about his own age--twenty-four—and a
native of Marcham, in Berkshire. .
The political part of the memoir is very interesting.
It treats largely of Wheeler's connection with the
Northern Star, and also of his delegations to political
meetings. We give an extract :--
In September, 1843, he was returned by the Chartists
of London and Readins ab Delegate to a Conference held
at Birmingham. At this Conference it was moved and
carried that Wheeler be the General Secretary in the room
of J. Campbell, who, air we have already seen, had been
arrested. Mr. O'Connor said, 'lf Mr. Wheeler took the
office of Secretary, he must give up his post as correspon-
dent to the Northern Star; he should, however, be sorry
to lose so valuable a servant.' Here I may be allowed to
quote similar testimony respecting the ability with which
Wheeler discharged his duties as correspondent from Mr.
W. Rider, a gentleman who was connected with the
Northern Star from its commencement to the time it was
sold by Feargus O'Connor. Mr. Rider says: •As our
London correspondent he never introduced any objection-
able matter into his reports, nor was there any necessity
for curtailment in his explicit communications.' The
office of General Secretary to the Chartist body was not a
sinecure; independently of the labours involved in ap-
pointing and paying the lecturers for upwards of forty
districts of the metropolis, Wheeler had to answer the
whole of the correspondence which came in from all parts
of the kingdom to his office, 243 f, Temple Bar. In all
matters in which advice was needed by his country
friends, to him they appealed; and when any of them
came to London respecting strikes or other trade matters,
they at once made their way to Wheeler's residence; in
fact, his office was a club-room to the politicians of the
working classes.
The industrial part gives Wheeler's connection with
the Friend-in-Need, to which he was appointed
manager and secretary, and which office he held up to
the time of his death. We give an extract
In the early part of the same year some disputes arose
among the members respecting the management of the
Friend-in-Need, an old Burial Institution in the neigh..
bourhood of Whitechapel, which had been instituted in
October, 1831, certified and enrolled ae.cording to the Act
of Parliament in March, 1836, and revised under the
sanction of J. T. Pratt, Esq., in October, 1839. These
disputes caused a split, and in May, 1853, the revised rules
were again submitted to J. T. Pratt, Esq., and certified
by him. Mr. John Shaw the founder, was at this time
one of the Trustees, and President of the original Friend-
in-Need, and Wheeler one of the Committee, Wheeler
soon saw that the errors which his friend Shaw had battled
against in the old management of the Friend-in-Need
would occur again under the new, from no fault of the
Managers but simply from the nature and constitution of
the body itself. While it sought an extended support its
objects were purely local. He urged his views upon those
interested in the welfare of the Friend-in-Need, but for a
long time to little purpose. He pointed out to the Mem-
bers and Managers that in order to insure success they
must take a wide area for their operations; how else could
they obtain a fair average of the lives of those they
assured? After awhile Shaw fell in with the views •
Wheeler had propounded with such force, and it was
agreed between them that a meeting should be called to
take the matter into consideration. Mr. George William
Wheeler was written to, end requested to join them at
their first meeting on November 16th, 1853. He did so.
The whole bearings of the question having been discussed,
it was agreed to start the Society on the basis proposed by
Wheeler. Mr. John Shaw was appointed Metropolitan
Manager, Wheeler Acting Manager and Secretary, and his,
brother Mr. George William Wheeler, Provincial Mana-
ger. The new modification of the Society was put in
motion on November the 28th, and Mr. Stammers, one of
the Members, and an Auditor of the old Society, joinea
the new body on the same day.
The first regular policy was issued on the sth of Decem-
ber, 1853. Mr. George William Wheeler began his
agency at Reading with 34 Members, and the temporary
offices of the new institution were at 24, Gloucester-street,
Commercial-road East. The one fact of the adhesion of
the old Members to this young and now gigantic !nstitte-
tion, in December, 1860, would be sufficient proof, if none
else were at hand, that Wheeler was right, and those who
did not then join him were wrong. • In March, 1854, the
Sick branch of the Friend-in-Need was enrolled, and thus
commenced an industrial institution which at the present
time is one of the largest of its kind in the British
Empire.

articles.title: COTTON FAMINE IN F.RANCE.
articles.text:
THE COTTON FAMINE IN F.RANCE.

The industrial crisis produced by the scarcity of
cotton in the European markets,' says the Moniteur,
began to make itself felt in France towards the middle
of this year. At that period the public works in the
country still occupied a large number of hands in every
part of the empire. But at the commencement of the:
bad season, the sufferings of the spinners becoming mores
severe occupied the earnest solicitude of the Emperor,
who requested the Minister of the Interior and the
Minister of Public Works to take without delay the
necessary measures for assisting the populations of the
manufacturing.districts.

Although —the cotton trade is carried on ia forty
different departments of the empire, there are only four-
teen or fifteen in which it is really important. Among
the latter that of the Seine laferieure takes the first rank,
containing as it does more than a fourth of the looms
now employed in cotton spinning.
In that department, the Minister of Agriculture,
Commerce, and Public Works, in conformity with the
intentions expressed by his Majesty, ordered, at the end
of the mewl' of October last, the opening of workshops
for the rectification of the levels of imnertal rnaan.'

articles.title: HURDER NEAR vrcrakm
articles.text:
THE HURDER NEAR vrcrakm

DOCKS.

On the 6th, two men, George Mitchell and Thomas
Hewitt, were brought up on remand at the Ilford Petty
Sessions, adjoining Ilford Gaol, Essex, on the charge
of causing the death of Arthur Melton, aged 21 years,
a porter lately in the service of the Great Eastern Rail-
way Company, under circumstances which have already
appeared in this journal.
Matthew Scott deposed that he lived at Greenwich,
and was chief mate of the James Dixon, at present
lying in the Victoria Docks. The prisoner Mitchell
was second mate and Hewitt was cook on the same
vessel. He recollected the night of Monday,
the 24th ultimo. On that evening he went into the
Robert Stephenson beer-shop, near the Dock-
house. He remained with the first.mate of the John
Bowes steam-ship until 11 o'clock, mhen they left
together. The two prisoners were in the same house
when-he left. The two prisoners, with two other men,
followed. Upon reaching the Dock-house he saw three
men standing outside, and two of them he recognised as
porters belonging to the Tidal Basin station. He walked
about nine yards past them, when he heard a disturbance.
Mitchell was standing in a fighting attitude, and witness
saw a little man whom he ran at and dealt him a severe
blow, exclaiming, You are one of the -.' The man
he struck was the deceased, and the blow was on the
forehead. The deceased fell backwards, with his head
towards the Victoria Docks. Witness saw Mitchell
with his left foot raised, and witness exclaimed, My
God! what has that poor man done to you?' Mitchell
made no answer, and deceased was lying on the ground.
William Brown, the chief mate of the John Bowes,
said that.he lived at No. 12, Nixon-street, Jarrow,
South Shields, and gave confirmatory testimony to the
last witness.

The learned Chairman then cautioned the prisoners in
the usual way, when
The prisoner Mitchell said: When I left the Robert
Stephenson it was about ten minutes after the two mates
(Scott and Brown) had left, and when I came out of the
beershop I heard a noise. I had my coat off at the time,
and when I reached the lamp-post by the Dock-house I
saw the three men, the tallest of whom was in a fighting
attitude. One of them made a hit at me, when I struck
bim and knocked him down. He got up again and I
ran. after him. He shouted 'Police!' when I came
down and stood near the lamp-post, and I then saw the
young man lying down. He (Hopper) then came up
and gave me into custody for striking the deceased. I
said that it was not me, and one of our men said that I
was innocent. That is all I have to say.
Hewitt was also cautioned by the bench, and said
nothing but, I was too drunk, and I do not recollect any-
thing about the affair.
The depositions were read over by the clerk, and
having been duly signed, the prisoners were fully com-
mitted to Newgate to take their trial for the murder of
Arthur Melton.

articles.title: MR, DISRAELI AND THE LAIV CA SHIRE
articles.text:
MR, DISRAELI AND THE LAIV CA SHIRE

DISTRESS.

Mr. Disraeli, M.P., has addressed the following letter
to the editor of the Aylesbury News :
Sir,—There is a subscription now taking place through-
out the country in aid of our suffering fellow subjects in
Lancashire, and I heartily hope that its amount may be
worthy of the community and adequate to the critical oc-
casion. There is, however, in reference to this subject,
one special point, which I am anxious to bring under your
consideration. In our dark period of 1835-6 many of our
people, with the encouragement, and the instigation, of
the local authorities, emigrated to Lancashire. Their
sufferings and struggles were at first severe. Some
returned. home; some sank before small-pox and fever:
but some remained and prospered. In one town of
Lancashire, at this moment, is a little Buckinghamshire
colony of 33 persons. They have sustained themselves
for nearly a year on the property which they had realised
by their industry, but that is now exhausted. In their
dire necessity they have appealed to their ancient home,
I hope not in vain. The local sentiment is the strongest
that influences man, and is the foundation of many vir-
tues. A fund his been formed here to afford them
immediate relief; but it is mokit desirable that they
should be supported for the next twenty weeks. Any
contributions, with this object, addressed to myself, or
the vicar of Hughenden, will be acknowledged in your
columns.—l have the honour to remain, Sir, your faith-
ful
,servant, B. DISRAELI.
Hughenden Manor, Dec. 2, 1862.'

articles.title: CASE OF ROSALIE DOISE.
articles.text:
THE CASE OF ROSALIE DOISE.

The French paper the Temps, having opened a sub-
scription on behalf of Rosalie Doise, the late victim of
an Imperial court ofjustice, M. Victor Hugo has written
the following letter to the editor of that journal:—
TO THE E.AITOR OF LE TEMPS.
Sir,—Have the goodness to put down nay name for
100 francs in the subscription Gardin. But we must
not confine ourselves to money. Something worse
perhaps than the affair of Lesurques, the re-
establishuaent of torture in France in the 19th
century, confession extorted by suffocation, strait
waistcoat put on a pregnant woman, the pr;soner
urged to madness—l know not what frightful legal
infanticide the child murdered by torture in its
mother's womb—tlfe conduct of the examining magis-
trate, of the judges and two procureurs-generau—
x
innocence condemn td, and when afterwards acknow-
ledged insulted in open court in the name of that justice
which should have fallen on its knees before her: all
this is not an affair of money.
No doubt the subscription is well, useful, and praise-
worthy, but a higher indemity is called for. Society is
more deeply wounded than Rosalie noise. The outrage
to civilisation is profound. In this matter the greatest
insult is offered to Justice herself.
• Subscribe—he it so--but it appears to me that the
ex-kee; ers of the seals, and ex-leaders of the bar, have
something more to do, and, as for myself, I have a
duty, and I will notshrink from it.—l have, &c.,
