articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1862,

also the £2O silver eup for the best short-wool sheep.
If the perfect symmetry and exquisite finish of the
South Downs are astonishing, so also are the great size
and weight attained by the Hampshire Downs, by
the Shropshire and noble Oxfordshire sheep. Of the
latter breed
,Mr. °Caries Howard, of Bedford, is the
ch ,mpion, and his sheep are certainly most extraor-
dinary for frame' weight, quality, and wool. But in
this class, in the Hampshire and Wiltshire Down class,
and in the an,s-breed class, we observe prizes and
commendations awarded to animsls that still show by
the light colour on their backs where the shears have
shaped the fleece into deceptive symmetry—some sheep
are so clipped flat and broad that, when lying down,
their smooth level backs display almost the pe ri ect
curve of a plough mould-board. If the mountain sheep
are interesting, with their hems and picturesque
appearance, the grand &ass of cross-breeds is interest-
ing from the great value of the sheep in wool and
mutton. Consumers of meat and wearers of woollen
can desire no better animals than the Sussex and Cots-
wold wethers of Mr. Stilgoe, of Banbury, which win
the £2O silver cup, as the best in the other' classes.
The pigs make an average show. Mr. Lynn's white
pigs under four months old, are marvels of early
maturity; Mr. Cattle's Lincolnshires' are exceedingly
fine, and Mr. Baker's black Hampshires,' 16 months
old, winning the gold medal as the best pigs, are un-
commonly well formed and splendidly fel. Mr. Crisp's
black sow in the extra stock class is also an amazingly
good specimen of Suffolk pork.
If it be impossible to give more than a general glance
at the numerous classes of live stock in a rapid walk
past the long line of stalls and pens after eight o'clock in
the evening, it cant, ot be expected that we should smul-
taneously find out the novelties in a vast assortment of
machines and implements almost equalling that in the
late Exhipition. All the leading firms are there.
Steam culture, the great fact of the day, is repre-
sented by something more telling and important than
mere models or sketches of apparatus; the machines
themselves are exhibited, and the several inventors are
furnished with the irresistibly-persuasive argument of
testimonials by the hundred, detailing the practical
experience or hearty approval of customers. The con-
tents of these steam cultivation catalogues' whether
published by John Fowler, of Leeds; by Howarcls,
of Bedford; Smith, of Woolston, or other inventors
and manufacturers, are truly astonishing. One
maker offers to do most and best work for the
money; another can deal more readily with small
angular inclosures ; a third grubs up a seed-
bed and plants the seed in a single operation;
and the very extensive evidence in favour of the various
machines, alike on the churlish clays' and on the more
easy-tempered medium or light soils,' completely
establishes every essential point in the question of steam-
power tillage. The saving of one-third the farmer's
teams on a large occupation repays the prime cost of a
steam plough in a few years, while two small farmers
can join in the purchase of an apparatus too costly for
one. The experience of several hundreds of machines,
breaking up many thousands of acres in a single season,
has demonstrated that the work is profitable in point
of excellence and efficiency, and more profitable still
in point of augmented produce of cropping; and
recent improvements in carrying the wire traction-
rope clearly off the ground have reduced the wear
and t‘ar to a minimum. The notabilities of the show,
however, are not solely among machinery of a
massive character; one great curiosity is the cow-
milking machine (from the Lacteal Works,' Birming-
ham)—an American 'notion' for obviating the immense
loss suffered by farmers the whole world over from
spoiled udders in the hands of careless or fraudulent
milkmaids and-men. It is said that a fortune is being
realised by the invention, and so simple is the movement
producing the requisite suction and squeezing' that,
when slightly altered in detail to suit the varying dimen-
sions of bovine wet nurses, this milk-pail with pump-
handles will probably supersede the one now replenished
by the ruddy palms of the milkmaid. Another
Yankee labour-saver is on up-and-down saw (shown
by Childs of Oxford-street, London), worked from a
rotary motion by means of a cross-shaped slide, which
enables the instrument to operate at any angle, as in
sawing through or ripping up logs, and secures many
other advantages with the least possible number of
working parts and the utmost simplicity and efficiency.
The display in the galleries is not confined to me-
chanics; vegetables also receive due place and at-
tention.

articles.title: SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE-SHOW:
articles.text:
SMITHFIELD CLUB CATTLE-SHOW:

corn, down horn,' may be a wise market maxim; I
and of late years the,converse has undoubtedly proved
true. Low quotations in Mark-lane have been counter-
balanced by good figures in the emporiums of animal
produce, and the demand for boiling and reasting pit ces,
- • d frys and all manner of meaty luxuries,—
ie $ c hunger for cheese and butter, and its thirst
for the sweet beverage which the strong man no more
than the babe and weakling can relinquish,—almost
defy the fecundity of flocks and herds and the resources
of fattening provender in the hands of our breeders and
graziers. No matter, then, that the scientific detum of
a cool summer and a light weight in the bushel' has
been this year demonstrated by a wheat-yie:d below the
average. John Bull is ready as ever with his prodigies
in flesh and blood for the Christmas shows and
market& And more than this, he is no longer
a grunihler against politics and Providence; was
never 'before so jubilant in all his provinces
with grateful harvest thanksgivings;' and (to
his lasting credit) is now gracefully opening
that capacious pocket of his, and with generous
hand ministering to the distresses of the very interest
which he considers deprived him of his profit on taxed
bread loaves. We find him, of course, in his glory at
the great annual Cattle Show. Not in Baker-street, for
we have no longer to pay our shilling between the glass
cases of bright bits and stirrups, and march past the
spectral horse in glistening harness which guarded the
entrance to the carriage bazaar; but on foot, or by cab,
or by omnibuses, making some two thoueand journeys
to and from the new locale, agriculturists from the rail-
way termini and sight-seers from all corners of the me-
tropolis will this year visit an Agricultural Hall'
specially erected for their welcome and gratification.
The new farmers' palace rears its handsome front hard
by that ancient hostelry and focus of modern traffic—the
Angel, Islington.
The hall may be approached from Islington-green,
near the new fountain and statue of Sir Hugh Myddel-
ton but the principal entrance is in the Liverpool-road.
Arranged along this front are the pay boxes, free tickets
entry, catalogue stand, bookstall, parcel and cloak room,
and telegraph, inquiry, and police offices; so that, with-
out passing through any antechamber' you at once enter
the main hall at its western end. This noble apart-
ment, 384 feet in length by 217 feet in breadth, is
surrounded by deep galleries, the spaces below these
being lighted by windows in the external walls, while
the central area is illuminated from the skylight roof,—
an arch of trussed iron framework of 144 feet span,
resting upon 56 iron columns, 33 feet in height, the
crown of this roof being 76 feet from the floor. In the
evening an artificial day is created by some 5,000 flames
of gas. The ventilation is effected by means
of two longitudinal chambers, each six feet in
breadth, perforated underneath, supported by the iron
oolumns, and communicating with the towers, which
are designed to maintain a draught on the principle
of tall chimneys. At the western end of the building,
where is the entrance from Islington-green, is a minor
hall of 100 ft, square and, to give some idea of the
magnitude of the whole, it is said that the roof
comprises twe acres of slates and one acre of
glass, while the space afforded by the galleries alone (to
which there are five staircases) considerably exceeds an
acre.

The arrangement of the different kinds of live stock
and of the implements is discovered at a glance. Light
implements, stalls, &c., occupy the glleries ; heavy ma-
chinery is placed underneath, close to the walls; the
sheep-pens (of wrought-iron tubing) stand next, down
both sides of the hail; and the cattle occupy the central
portion of the ground-floor, in four ranks the beasts
being all separately haltered to four lines of iron fence.
Each animal has a space of 6ft. breadth, in which to
stretch his limbs or lie down, and the public can walk
in front of the handsome heads and horns, as well as
behind the long rows of tails and heels, the central
avenue forming quite a spacious promenade. The
swine hold an odorous levee by themselves, in their
100 ft. square drawing-room, at the eastern end of the
main hall.
The Club has hanselled its new residence with an
additional £6OO in the prize sheet—the money prizes,
silver medals, and handsome silver cups which are now
substituted for the gold medals, amounting to the total
value of £2,066: and the entries of animals are 418,
against 349 lalt year, the sheep in particular having
been furnished with several new or expanded classes.
The 180 cattle, as a whole, may be characterised as
equalling, though certainly not surpassing, the standard
excellence of former occasions. But visitors should be
aware at the outset of the illusion produced by the mere
spaciousness and loftiness of the Hall in diminishing the
apparent size of the animals. There is a larger pro-
portion of simply good butcher's beef, and there are
fewer specimens of rare development and early maturity
than a year of progress might Ifave expected. Breeding
has become a refined art, andleeding is conducted witi
wonderful judgment and skill; but while, in combination,
they are improving the entire herds of Great Britain,
and pushig particular races into pre-eminence, the
fact still remains that we are beholden to volun-
tary feats of nature for those individual animals which
now and then anstonish us with their perfections. Calves
that will grow into noblest proportions and rarest beauty
are not dropped every day, and, unfortunately, the pre-
sent year has given us no steer of ox of superlative
merit; while Mr. Eastwood's 'Rosette' (out of Mr.
Wetherell's herd), good as she is forms a poor substitute
for that exquisitely beautiful milk-white heifer ofCdlonel
Towneley which delighted us as Beauty's Butterfly.'
This year lathe triumph of the cross-breds. The £4O silver
cup for the best steer or ox in the Hall is carried off,
not by a short-horn or Hereford, as usual, :int by the
produce of a Devon bull and shorthorn cow, bred and
fed by Mr. John Overman, of Burnham-market, in
Norfolk. And the reserve number' or the judges
was that of the cross-bred shorthorn and polled
Scot, which won the highest honour at Birmingham.
In appearance, Mr. Overman's steer is like a ruddy
Devon, of very great size and substance, but without
the defective hindquarters of that breed. The girth is
Oft. or 91n. less than that of Mr. Stewart's heavier
polled cross-bred; but in several points, as the round and
neck-vein, in general beauty and in touch, the winner
of the cup is clearly superior; and then Mr. Stewart's
great but plain ox, now apparently suffering from long
journeys, and gone off in touch since the Birmingham
show, is one year and four months older. Bearing in
mind that the judges are instructed to keep strictly in
view the oDject of supplying the markets with the
cheapest and best meat,' we are disposed to acquiesce in
their decision; especially as the places of distinction
here awarded to two first cross animals are the truest
compliment to the vaiue and perfection of the parent
breeds. The £4O silver cup, for the best heifer or cow
In the Hall, is given, not to Mr. Eastwood's cow
Rosette,' but to a heifer of Mr. Tennant, of Leeds
(thus reversing the Birmingham judgment). Her sire
was the Sixth Duke of Oxford,' but first-rate blood
has not conferred upon her any special beauty; her
head is not very handsome, she is not good before the
shoulder, and though girthing Bft. I lin., one inch more
than the cow, hardly shows evidence in her own person
why she should have borne off the piece of plate.
Glancing now at the shorthorns in general, we find
a rather ordinary collection of steers and oxen. Mr.
Frost's roan steer is level, of good frame, but has a
girth of only 7t. Sin.; it is fair Christmas beef, a little
loose in hind, but not a splendid show animal
such as some former year. 3 have brought us. And
the Duke of Beaufort's steer, which is here first in
the class because the Birmingham first has not come, is
by no means first-rate, defective in the flank, and girth-
ing Bft. sin. Earl Howe's prize ox, second at Birming-
ham, is first in his class here, as Mr. Sunimertun's ox
could not be admitted to double the conquest of last
year, when it ought properly to 'have been slaughtered
and eaten long ago. Neither Mr. Woitley's roan, Earl
Spencer's big strawberry, Mr. Stratton's ox, Mr. Walter's
heavy beast, nor Mr. Harradine's commended' animal,
letrieve the want of quality in. this large class. The
heifers are certainly much better; in fact, they make
a very fine class, and the cows are little less mcrito-
,ious.

The Herefords are unusually good; Major-General
Hood wins with a steer from the Flemish Farm, Windsor
Park. In the still better class of older animals Mr.
Ald worth, of Abingdon, takes first prize with a big heavy
ox that many people will consider out of place. Mr.
Hatcher's ox, of the same age and six inches greater girth,
is the truer type of a Hereford, very wide and deep in
frame, with better rounds of beef, but has gone off in
condition since the Birmingham show. Mr. Shaw's steer
of superb quality comes in for the second prize. The
Hereford heifers and cows make two classes of rare mcrit;
Mr. Turner's cow, especially, having splendid iledi and
a beautiful curly coat.
Of the Devons there is an average show, the older
steers or oxen exhibiting considerable size with their
wonderful quality of flesh; and the cow class comprises
some prime specimens of this beautiful breed.

We- find a lam show of the useful ied Sussex cattle;
only a couple of the dairy polled breed of Norfolk, and
three of the Longhorns, Mr. Burberry's cow being fat,
#44.4114,ti0,g more beauty and quality than is generally
present in the classes of the antique breed. The Duke
of Beaufort's yellow West Highland is a very superior
animal; and in the capital classes of polled Scots, Mr.
M'Combie's black ox and Mr. Stewart's brindled ox
vet y properly change their Birmingham places in favour
of the former.
We can say but a word or two on the very numerous
and well filled sheep classes. It can hardy be in ac-
cordance with the Club's desire of distinguishing the
cheapest and best meat that the nO silver cup for the
best long wools has gone to Mr. Foljambe's splendid
little Leieesters, instead of to Mr. Mills's Cotswolds, of
about the same age, but half as heavy again, with
as prime mutton. Among the grand pens of South
Downs, Lord Wolsingham and the Duke of Rich-
mond are here only second to Mr. Rigden, who takes

articles.title: AN INCIDENT OF THE PRINC.E'S
articles.text:
AN INCIDENT OF THE PRINC.E'S

VISIT TO BOXE.

A letter from Rome describes the following painful
incident which took place during the stay of the Prince
of Wales and the Prince and Princess of Prussia at the
Caffarelli Palace:—

The Prussian Minister, Baron de Kanitz, either from
mental predispo,ition, or from the excitement caused by
the presence in his residence of so numerous and distin-
guished a train of guests, began some days ago to show
signs of insanity, although not to such an extent as to
cause alarm amongst his friends. But whilst taking
exercise on horseback, as recommended to him, he un-
fortunately sustained a fall Which injured his head, and
probably accelerated the development of his lamentable
malady. On Monday evening, the Prince of Wales
having left Rome for Civita Veechia that morning, whilst
the Prince and Princess of Prussia were at dinner with
their usual circle, and the Duke and Duchess of Monte-
bello, to the surprise and horror of everybody, in stalked
the baron, as pale as a ghost, and looking very like one,
in his night-shirt and dressing-gown, and demanded in
an imperious tone what all the persons he beheld were
collected for in his palace, and whether they or he were
to be considered as masters of the house. The evening
was stormy, and great was the :dismay of the company
at the apparition of the unfortunate baron, and at the
very strong language which he proceeded to make use
of towards them which found a fitting accompaniment
in the thunder and lightning which burst over the Capitol
at that precise moment.

The Princess' although of course much alarmed, be-
haved admirably on the occasion, and his Royal Highness
also addressed soothing expressions to the baron, who
finally allowed himself to be conducted back to his room,
whence on the following day he was removed to the
residence of his brother-in-law, the Duke of Sermoneta.
I regret to say that the condition of the sufferer con-
tinued to get worse, and being a very powerful man and
getting violent, four keepers were placed in his room
yesterday. This morning it became necessary to put on
him a strait-waistcoat, as his paroxyms of delirium as-
sumed a dangerous form. The event has caused great
regret and sympathy amongst the present inmates of the
Caffarelli Palace, as well as the diplomatic circle as the
baron had the reputation of being a very straightforward,
hoaourable man, and was generally esteemed.

The new Montgolfier balloon, invented by M. Godard,
the aeronaut, has a capacity of 4,300 metres. The car
is provided with an apparatus which enables the aeronaut
to ascend without either gas or ballast, and to descend
or go higher up at pleasure. This apparatus consiAs of
a kind of stove-formed by three cylinders, separated from
each other by insulating substances, whereby all danger
of fire is averted. The flame is completely under the
control of the aerial traveller, and is prevented from
rising too high by a cap of wire gauze. M. Godard
asserts that he can inflate his balloon in thirty minutes,
and load it with from 600 to 800 kilogrammes over and
above the weight of his person and his accessories, and,
moreover, that his balloon may he piPreed with a bomb-
shell without endangering the aeronaut, who can him-
self cast projectiles of any kind with impunity. Should
his new invent:on succeed, this balloon may be of con-
siderable service in time of war.

DIOCESS OP LONDON.—The Bishop of London has
appended to his charge, which he has just published, an
elaborate statement in reference to the r arochial districts
under his episcopal jurisdiction, with the number of
clergy to each. He divides them into four classes. In
all tbe fparishes of class A, each containing more than
30,000 people, there is a population of 100,000 persons,
with 11 clergymen, or one to every 9,100 persons. In
this class there are only three parishes—namely, S.
Peter's, Walworth; St. Dunstan's, Stepney; and St.
Mary's, Hagger,tone. In all the parishes of class B,
containing between 20,000 and 30,000 people, there is a
population of 309,9.55, with 53 clergy, or one to every
5,850 persons. In class C, containing parishes havin
between 15,000 and 20,000 people, there is a population
of 224,000, with 39 clergy., or one to every 5,760 per-
sons. In class D, containing parishes with between
10,000 and 15,000 people, there is a population of
710,582, with 198 clergy, or one to every 3,590 persons.
These are exclusive of four country paridtes (Perivale,
Littleton. Cowley, and Ickenham), havinz a population
under 400, and of 31 city parishes with populations
under 600.

SHIP ON moat melancholy accident oc-
curred in the outer harbour of the Hartlepool Docks
early on th) morning of the sth inst., and which might
have caused a fearful disaster among shipping if it had
not been discovered in time. A considerable number of
vessels were lying in the outer harbour, when some
people, who were astir, observed smoke coming up the
'companion' of the schooner Mary, of Hartlepool, and
were further attracted to the ship by the barking of a
dog in a neighbouring vessel. They found that the
cabin was on fire, and having given the alarm, buckets
of water were poured down the companion, and, as soon
as the fire was got under, Mr. Peck, a ship captain,
went down into the cabin amid a dense smoke, and found
Ralph Day, the mate of the vessel, lying dead upon the
cabin floor, with one of his feet nearly burnt off, and
both his legs severely charred. The body was brought
up, but life was extinct. The cabin was completely
gutted. The cause of the fire wa,s not known.

articles.title: AIETROPOLITAN RAILTFAY:
articles.text:
THE AIETROPOLITAN RAILTFAY:

The date of the opening of this railway remains still
undecided, and the only reply to inquiries on the subject
is, that it will shortly De open. This a promise which
has been made repeatedly for the last six months; but
a variety of causes seems to have operated to prevent
its fulfilment. This much is certain, that no official
inspection has yet taken place; and that until this
has b-en made, and the certificate of the Railway
Department has been grated, the line cannot be
opened for traffic. The station at the Great Western
Railway, at Paddington, is at last completed, and thus
one assigned cause of delay has been removed. The
system for working the signals is still incomplete, but
a hope is expressed that all difficulties upon this
head will shortly he overcome. The plan adopted for
making the engines consume theit• own smoke, and con-
dense their steam answers perfectly, and though engines
are now constandy running along the line, no inconve-
nience is experienced in the tunnel from the smoke or
waste steam. The supply of the water required for the
condensers of the engines has been provided at the ter-
minal stations. As the water in which the steam is
condensed will of course quickly become heated, and
unfit for condensing, a liberal supply of cold water will
be necessary at the terminal stations, and this will be
supplied by some very ingenious mechanical arrange-
ments. In the open cuttings the en,ines will blow off
the steam in the usual manner, and in the tunnelled por-
tions only wril the condensing apparatus be used. The ob-
ject of making the carriages to run on the line wider:than
those in ordinary use on the Great Western Railway was
to economise as much as possible of the platform space at
the stations. The length of the platform in the tunnel
is, of course, rather more limited than where the railway
runs on the open ground, and by reducing the length of
a train, and giving the carriages increased width, the
station space would be available for a larger amount of
traffic. In giving this increased width to the carriages,
however, the doors will-not open the whole way back in
the tunoel, but may be opened sufficiently wide, how-
ever, to admit of the egress of passengers. At the stations
this difficulty does not occur, and there they open to the
usual extent. The Great W.estern Railway Company
have long completed all their arrangements, and are pre-
pared to commence the working of the•line immediately
that the necessary sanction has been given by the govern-
ment inspector.

A Warsaw letter states that acts of vengeance against
the secret police still continue. One of these agents
has recently been poisoned at a cafe, but medical aid
was procured in time to prevent a fatal remit.
At a recent sitting of the Belgian Chamber of Repre-
sentatives a petition from the communal council of
Marchiennes, relative to the employment of children in
factories was discussed, but no decision come to, and
the head's of manufactories remain at liberty to act as
hitherto in the matter.
NEW RAILWAY ROUTE IN IRELAND.—On Wednes-
day a railway line from Longford to Sligo, completing
the communication between Dublin and the west of
Ireland was formally opened. Among the stltions on
the line are Carrick-on-Shannon, the chief town in the
county of Leitrim; Boyle, one of the principal towns in
the county of Roscommon; and Ballysadore, where
there are large flour mills; and from the character of the
whole district traversed a remunerative traffic is antici-
pated. Near Drumsna the line crosses the Shannon by
a splendid bridge, and the scenery through which the
line passes, especially approaching Sligo, is exceedingly
picturesque.
The following is given by the Athens journals as the
text of the speech addressed by the Jim. Mr. Searlett,
the British Minister at the Court of Greece, to the
chiefs of the demonstration in favour of Prince Alfred:
Athenians, I am flattered by the honour you do me
by this manifestation in favour of Prince Alfred and of
the English nation. As far as regards the choice of
Prince Alfred, I must maintain the same reserve that I
have hitherto shown. It is a question depending on the
highest considerations, and on which it is not in my power
to determine. Whatever may occur, you may be sure
of the deep interest which England takes in the welfare
of Greece. I recommend to you calmness and mode-
ration in your proceedings, and to wait for the meeting
of your National Assembly.'
EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF MANSLAUGHTER.—At the
Liverpool Assizes on Saturday, Patrick Cain was
charged with causing the death of Mr. Henry Raw-
cliffe, of the Swan-inn, Kirkham, on the night of the
28th of September. On the evening of the day in
question it appeared that the prisoner and some of his
friends were forcibly ejected from the house of Raw-
cliffe for creating a disturbance; ultimately, one of the
party, named Garnty, was taken into custody by the
police. This fact so greatly enraged the prisoner, that,
in spite of the remonstrances of his friends, he armed
himself with a poker, uttering violent threats against the
police and Rawelifle. At this time Rawcliffe, being at-
tracted by a noise created by the prisoner, unfortunately
opened one of his windows and looked out. The prisoner
at this juncture threw the poker at him, and so surely
and so swiftly was it thrown, that it entered one of the
eyes of Rawcliffe, and penetrated the skull. Strange to
say, in spite of this fearful blow, Rawcliffe lived two
hours.—Cain was found guilty, but the judge deferred
passing sentence.
THE PICTURES IN THE INTERNATIONAL EXHIBITION.—
Redgrave has made ' the following satisfactory
report to her Majesty's Commissioners for the Inter-
national Exhibition of 1862 My Lords and Gentle-
men, The British pictures in the International
Exhibition being now removed from the walls, and
the greater part of them already returned to their
owners, I think it my duty, as having been specially
intrusted by you with their collection and arrangement,
to report on their condition and safety. My duties
terminated with the opening of the galleries to the
public, and Mr. Sketchley was charged with the
superintendence of them during the Exhibition, and
with the removal and return of the pictures. But I
have, in company with him, from time to time ex-
amined the collection, and given especial attention to
those works whose condition, prior to their reception
was unsound or doubtful, and have also been present
from day to day at the removal of the pictures from
'he walls; and it is with great satisfaction I am en-
abled to say that the precautions taken for the safe
keeping of the works committed to your care have
been so successful, that, with hardly an exception, the
pictures are uninjured by damp or otherwise. I have
also every reason to hope that, from the careful atten-
tion which is given to their packing, and the arrange-
ments for their transit, the whole will reach their
owners in perfect safety.' R. F. Sketchley, the super-
intendent of the Fine Art Department, concurs in the
above report.
AUSTRIAN GUNNERY EXPERIMENTS.—The Austrians
have been steadily pursuing a systematic course of ex-
periments with gun-cotton, and not only have they per-
fected this material, so as to use it in field guns, but
have also been led to investigate the properties of metals
with the view of finding an alloy which would impart
hardness to copper' and enable them to obtain a perfect,
safe, strong, and durable gun. This they have now
effected, and it is said that their gun-metal, by the ad-
dition of a small quantity of iron, has been made very
hard, and also exceedingly tough and elastic. One great
advantage possessed by this gun-metal is, that it can be
recast at small cost if the guns become damaged, or the
rifling prove unsatisfactory. The field-pieces have been
rifled
_with grooves, which help to support the projectile
in centering upon a rounded bearing. The projectile is
of iron only, indeed nothing else would withstand the
force of the gun-cotton, which is more instantaneous in
its explosion than gunpowder, and therefore a higher
velocity can be obtained with a much shorter gun. The
Austrian government is now about to cast large ordnance,
and if the reports given to us be correct, they have cer-
tainly hit upon the right metal, as it withstands the
blows of shot fired at it much better than any material
which we have yet used in England.—Army and Navy
Gazette,

I The theatrical company at Compiegne is very nume-
rous, and its members are so hospitably treated as were at
Versailles the comedians who performed Moliere's plays
before Louis Quatorze. They all travelled from Paris in
a special train, consisting of first class carriages, no
matter whether they were scene shifters, stage carpenters,
mutes, or piompters. As they set out at about three in
the afternoon they reached their destination about four,
when a dinner, served on two tables, awaited them in an
immense Around one table were placed the
itat major of the company, such as the director, stage
manager, actors, actresses, author or authors of the pieces
they were to act in the course of the evening, and the
principal members of the orchestra. The rest dined at
the second table. But all were given the same dishes,
the same wines, and served with equally fine linen,
porcelain, and silver, as well as provided with the same
number of attendants. Cigars and coffee were handed
round after the cloth was removed in two salons, where,
after they had dined, the two sets retired for half an
hour, at the end of which they proceeded along a
seemingly interminable passage to the theatre, where the
play appointed for the same evening was rehearsed till
half-past 7. At half-past 8 the Emperor and Empress
made their appearance, which was the signal for the per-
formance to commence. When it was finished the
theatrical company were again conducted to the salle a
manger in which they dined, where a champagne supper
awaited them.

THE MURDER BY A. TINKER IN LIVERPOOL.—On
Saturday the coroner held an inquest on the body of
Ann Read, who was so brutally murdered by her
husband on Thursday morning last, in Lower Myrtle.
street, Liverpool. One witness swore to having seen
the husband of the deceased pull her violently about the
kitchen by the hair of the head, while another deposed
to seeing him with a knife in his hand, and which he
dropped through a grating. The coroner's jury returned
a verdict of Wilful murder against Read,' who up to
Saturday evening had eluded the vigilance of the police.

articles.title: 'FALSE IMPORTS OF GAROTTIITG
articles.text:
'FALSE IMPORTS OF GAROTTIITG

CASES.

" A strict inquiry into the reports of several alleged
deaths by garotting, which have been published, has
led to the discovery that they, as well as some of the
reports of garotting cases, are unfounded.
One of the victims was a gentleman who was alleged
to have been struck down and robbed in St. Paul's-
churchyard, and subsequently died from his injuries.
The following are the authentic facts :---A gentleman,'
employed in an office in the City, absented himself
from duty. Upon his return he said that he had been
set upon in a court in St. Paul's-churchyard, rendered
senseless by a blow on the head, and robbed, and
that he was conveyed, covered with blood, to the
hospital. He showed his forehead bound up with
alhesive plaster, and he added, that the ruffians who
assaulted him had been taken to the police-station after a
terrible encounter. The police instituted inquiries, and
when he was at the station informed him that they had
learned at the hospital that he had not been admitted, as
he alleged. He said that he had been taken to the Eye
Hospital—inquiries, however, proving that he had been
to the Eye Hospital for a lotion, and not for a garotte
attack. A policeman, with some audacity, pulled off the
adhesive plaster, and disclosed to view—nothing, no scar,
no trace of the wound which had covered him with blood.
This closed the interview, and the police heard nothing
more of him until his decease, from his injuries, was
announced. They had no terrific fight with a uarotter
under the shadow of St. Paul's.
The murder and robbery of a woman named Jane
Stokes was announced to have taken place in Stamford-
street, Lambeth. Neither Mr. Carter, nor the other
local coroner, nor the'police' have received the slightest
information of the fact, and the origin of the story seems
to be as follows :—A few nights since a man presented
himself at the police-station and stated that a woman
had been garotted and robbed at the corner of Thomas-
street; that he ran for the police, and then when he
came back the body was gone. The body of a woman,
however, having been just brought in on a stretcher
by some officers who had discovered her in a beastly
state of intoxication at the corner of the street indicated,
the police were not much distressed about the matter.
The woman in question, however, was not named Stokes,
and she had certainly lost money, either by dropping it
or having her pocket picked.
The murder and robbery of Michael Garretty, of
Webber-street, in the St, George's-road, on Saturday
night week, is equally unknown to coroners and police,
but the latter, by way of compensation, received infor-
mation which has not been published as yet—of the
murder by the garotte of a baked potato vendor well
known in Lambeth-walk. The inquiries instituted
resulted in its being ascertained that the unhappy man
had been garotted sedundenz artem, and rifled of his little
all, and that he had just died from the injuries he re-
ceived. While searching for eye witnesses, however, the
police found the man himself selling his potatoes.
While publishing the above results of inquiries made,
we need not add that they do not affect the truth of the
Let that garotting is prevalent. The cases in the
police-courts are evidence sufficient, and if some fictitious
stories have been mgde public, there are, on the other ,
hand, many cases known of privately which have not
been published.

articles.title: TEE PRIZE RING.
articles.text:
TEE PRIZE RING.

(From an article by Mr. Thomas Hughes lathe Spectator.)
The Saturday _Reviewer cannot help thinking that
where there is room for experiment with rifled guns and
iron-plated targets, a few yards of turf may well be spared
for testing the powers of penetration and resistance of
the human fist and cheek. Surely the police have plenty
to do in looking after garotters, and might venture to leave
the prize-fighters to themselves. It is rather hard upon
the patrons of this sport that they must sit up all night,
and steal like malefactors amid the fog of early morning
to an out-of-the way spot, where it is only just possible
that the police may be an hour or two behind them.' Can
this be meant for a joke? If it be fooling, it is about the
heaviest we have ever met with. But we fear, after
reading the whole article through more than once, that it
is all meant in sober seriousness. A man who writes thus,
and counsels us to legalise prize fighting, should, at least,
know something of what he is talking about. This
article carries its own evidence that the writer knows
nothing of boxing, for he blunders as to the meaning of
so well known a term as a counter.' Is he competent
to speak on any ground? Has he ever seen a prize
fight? Has he ever set eyes on that inner ring of
privileged spectators who have paid their guinea or two
apiece to be protected during the fight, and sit on soft
wrappers, cigar in mouth, and betting,book in hand—a
strange mixture of young exquisites, bill discounters,
and other aristocratic and Middle class rowdyism—on
that broken nosed band who stand round to protect
their patrons in consideration of the guineas,
against the oetpr circa. et bowling and blaspheming
lower class rowdyism, which frets and strains
round the privileged inner ring? Has he seen the
fierce lust of blood flush up in all faces, as after the first
few rounds the men begin to get home, and tremendous
blows are exchanged, and the very likeness of humanity
is smashed out of the faces of the fighters? Has he seen
the sickening struggle of the weaker man when the
fight is lost in all but name, as he totters up round after
round in answer to the goading of his backers? If he
has seen all this, does he really mean that we should
relax the law, and give facilities to the patrons of this
sport' to indulge in their cowardly taste for brutality?
If not—if he is simply ignorant of what he has taken
upon himself to write about—how dare ha come forward,
even anonymously, and pleads n the columns of the
most popular of our high-class weekly papers for the
most utterly demoralising and blackguard custom, which
is still allowed to drag on a hole-and-corner existence
in our country?
Let us speak out plainly about the prize ring. There
is not a redeeming feature about it. Fighting men are
r a peculiar class. If left to themselves, after a turbu-
lent youth, they might become decent members of
society. They are laid hold of by the patrons of this
sport,' begin sparring at ben-fits, are backed for a pound
or two to fight in cold blood for the amusement and
profit of the said patrons. Then comes the starring at
fighting houses, when the stakes are deposited, the
training, the fight, and the subsequent orgies, after
which not one in fifty of them ever turns to honest
industry again. A flash house in Whitechapel or ' St.
Martin's-lane, the resort of prostitutes, card-sharpers,
dog-fanciers, and bullies, is almost always .the
end of the successful ones. The unsuccessful
drink themselves into the workhouse, the prisons,
or an early grave, and meantime haunt and
skulk about the flash houses, and form the outer
circle at prize fights. As to the character of the
regular prizefighters, there is nothing whatever of the
heroic about them. Their object of worship is mere
brute strength and cunning, and so they fall more and
away from all true manliness. They are pampered and
humoured till they become as vain and frivolous and
fanciful as spoilt mistresses, and when a turn in luck
comes, are cast off as lightly as these by the patrons of
this sport.' They are far better, no doubt, than the
regular parasites, who live with and prey on them, and
are not fighting men, better than most of their aristo-
cratic and middle-class patrons; but, as a rule, a young
fellow whs once takes to the ring in England is utterly
ruined in character, and almost as certainly in worldly
prospects.

COLLECTORS OF INCOME AND ASSESSED TAXES —ln
reply to a memorial from the Bristol Chamber of Com-
merce to the Board of Inland Revenue, praying that
they would make arrangements whereby the collection
of the income and assessed taxes in the city and borough
of Bristol might be placed in the hands of officers ap-
pointed by the Crown, the following reply has been
received from the authorities at Somerset-house:
am directed to acquaint you that the collectors for the
several parishes in the city of Bristol have been ap-
pointed for the current year 1862-3, and consequently
that the Board are unable to take any steps at present
in order to a compliance with this application. I am,
however, to add that when the time shall arrive for
making the appointment of collectors for the year 1863-4
the Board will take care that the necessary communica-
tion shall be made to the district Commissioners, with a
view to carrying out the arrangement desired.'
LANCASMIRE RELIEF FUND,---The musical profession
seems resolved not to be surpassed in generosity by any
other section of the community. In addition to the
performances already announced in aid of the Relief
Fund, a morning concert will be given at Messrs.
Collard and Collard's Pianoforte and Concert!rooms,
Lower Grosvenor- street, on "hursday, the 18th inst., at
' 1 o'clock. It will take place under the patronage of the
Duchess of Roxburghe, the Duchess of Wellington, the
Marchioness of Carmarthen, the Marchioness of T weed-
dale, the Countesses of Albemarle, Fife Wemyss,
Kinnoul, Home, Paulett, Hardwicke, Harewood, and
Zetland, the Viscountesses Elcho and Nevin, Ladies
Lindsay, Henniker, Alvanley, and Augusta Milbank,
the Hon. Mrs. C. Bruce, the Hon • Mrs. Austrnther, Ladies
Anstruther of Balcaskie, Howard, Rothschild, and
Wallace, and Mrs. Frederick Milbank. The following
eminent artistes have generously given their services:—
Vocalists—Mesdames Louisa Pyne and Laura Baxter,
Steele, Florence Lairia,
Messrs. Harrison, Ciabatta Lansand Sainton Dolby;
mere, and Fortuna.
Instrumentalists—Pianoforte, Herr Pauer ; violin, Herr
Molique ; violoncello, Herr Lidel ; guitar and concer-
tina, Signor Regonch ; clarinet, Mr. Lazarus. Messrs.
Benedict and Frank Mori will preside at the pianoforte.
Tickets may be had of Mes;rs. Collard and Collard, 16,
Grosvenor-street; of Mr. Robert W. 011ivier, 19, Old
Bond-street, and of the lady patronesses. The proceeds
will be handed to the Relief Fund in aid of the suffer=
lug operatives.

Uarittitg,

Mrs. Swinfen, the chief witness in the famous 'Swin-
fen case,' so excited herself during the trial, that she
has been seriously ill.
An English lady resident in Hamburg has just sent
over to the Lord Mayor a very large supply of clothing
for the distressed in Lancashire, entirely made by the
poor of Hambisrg.
There were never known so many golden Plovers,
are no* in our marshes. By some persons this is con-
sidered indicative of a severe winter.
It has been stated that the Marquis of Hertford has
intimated his intention of leaving his splendid collection.
of pictures to the nation. May he be long spared to
enjoy them as a reward for the generous thought!
The wretched anonymous horsewoman is coming back
from America, being disgusted with the American
people. This is the handsomest thing that has been said
in their favour for many a day.
A certain West-end house has received orders for
several suits of chain armour, to wear under the clothes.
They are of different degrees of btrength, according to
the place where they are to be worn. The strongest
will turn a Minis bullet.
We understand that all the members of the Royal
Family will continue to wear mourning after Christmas,
but it will be of a slight character. Her Majesty will
wear deep mourning for another year.
A distinguished physician in Paris, Dr. Robert De
Lambelle, announces that a shock of electricity given a
patient dying from the effects of chloroform immediately
counteracts its influence, and restores the suffera to
life.
Mr. Mayall, who had the honour of taking photo-
graphs of the Princess Alexandra last week, in different
positions, has been allowed to publish eight of them,
since which time, we understand, he has received orders
for one hundred thousand.
The 'blockade-breakers' which leave Liverpool appear
to make no secret of their intentions. The names of
four have been reported, which had left the Mersey all
laden with valuable stores, intended to aid and comfort'
the Confederates. Their names are the Thistle, Severn
Monmouth, and Nicolai First.
A distinguished artillery officer in the French service,.
gives the following very decided judgment on the Whit-
worth system It 'appears to me now that Mr. Whit-
worth will beat all his rivals, and that his guns will
effect another modification in the construction of ships,
of war.'

It is a remarkable fact thlt, during the month of
November, four M.P.'s of the Lower House died, and
all of them suddenly. Mr. Willcox died from the fall-
ing of a tree upon him. Mr. Mills died instantaneously in
the hunting field. Mr. Coles and Mr. Deedes both died.
after a few hours' illness.
It is reported that the Duke of Modena has given
orders to the commander of his brigade not to engage
any fresh men, and not to increase the present effective,
or even to fill up the vacancies made by decease. This
may be considered an additional indication that the dis-
solution of the corps is near at hand.
An indignant contributor tends the Dundee Courier
40. as his quata of the Relief Fund, accompanied
by the following poetical epistle, in which he asserts
that his mite is equal to that of the great 13uccleuch
The widow's mite I've long admired,
So this I send to you,
The tenth part of mylaily wage,
To be upsides with4Succleuch.'
Theodore Hook, who had a large fleshy nose, once,
entering his club during a dOussion upon some inte-
restin- topic, one of the members, observing him
coming, pointed to him, and exclaimed, Oh, Hook
knews." No,' was ti o reply- he instantly made,‘
Bottle nose.'
The French are gettina a subscription to present
Dr. Nelaton with a gold snuff-box, in token of their
admiration of his unpaid and successful opinion of Gari-
baldi. Would it not be as graceful an act were we to
do something of the same kind to our physician who
attended Garibaldi?
While our valiant sparrow clubs are killing the far-
mers' friend other countries are asking for them. A
letter from Leipsic states that M. Webber, of that city,
who has recently returned home after a long residence
in Australia, has been charged by the Aeclimatisation,
Society of Melbourne to send out to the colony as many
German sparrows as he can possibly procure. Cater-
pillars and other insects commit such ravages in Aus-
tralia, particularly in Victoria, that those birds would be
the most effectual means of destroying them. A great
number will be shipped off in March next.
Sir Richard Mayne has submitted a plan to the-
Ministers for the prevention of garotting. Its basis is
said to be the application of the lash freely and fre-
quently ; the dose to be repeated, in fact, as often as the
patient's health will permit. Certainly, the publie
unanimously say, 'Use the lash;' and the argument in
its favour is simply that for the discipline of the rascal
the law need not be more tender than it is in the dis-
ciplining of the seaman and the soldier.
Within a few days of Lord _Breadalbazie's
Lausanne, a telegram reached him from her 11.1ajrsl y,
with her usual kind inquiries as to the state of ills
health. The enfeebled Marquis with difficultptaised,
himself up in his bed, and, asking for matelials, wrote
his farewell message to his Sovereign. The closing
words of the brief telegram ran as follows Loyal and.
faithful to his Queen to the last.'
The Duke of Cambridge, in the course of an after
dinner speech recently, expressed his conviction—a con-
viction which was strengthened by the recent experi-
ments—that, in the contest between armour plated ships

AMERICA.

EW YORI, Nov. 25 (Eveuing).—The Federal Govern-
ment has issued an order for the release of all prisoners
held in military charge for discouraging the enlistments
and opposing the draught. All persons arri sted in the
rebel States for hostility to the Federal Government will
be discharged on parole, or allowed to leave the country.
This does not refer to persons who have been in arms
against the Government. The expedition for opening
the Mississippi will consist of 40,000 men and 40 gunboats.
The Confederates have created very extensive fortifi-
cations at Port klud,on on the Mississippi, 150 miles
above New Orleans, commanding the entrance to Red
River from below. Federal reconnaissances have been
made from Fortress Monroe up the Peninsula as far
as the Chickahominy River. President Jefferson Davis
has ordered the Conf derate General commyading the
Mississippi department to demand the surrender of Fe-
deral General M'Neil for murdering 10 Confederate
citizens of Missouri. If this is refused, and the charges
are proveato be true, the Confederate General is instructed
to execute the first 10 Federal officers that are captured.
President Lincoln has ordered the Attorney-General to
take measures for carrying out the Confiscation Act.
Mr. G. Brown, the newly-elected Abolition Member to
Congress from Missouri, has issued a proposal urgino. the
Northern States to agitate the question of a gradual
emancipation of the slaves in Missouri. The British
steamer Kelsie is reported to have been sunk by a
collision 50 miles from Nassau. It is reported from
Peru that the loan effected in England would cause
some uneasiness, the President requiring the money and
Congress refusing to touch it.
NEW YORK, Nov. 25 (Evening).--The futsire finan-
cial policy of the Government continues to be discussed.
It is supposed that more legal tender currency will
be issued, _ The Ftderals have extended the time for

- the inhabitants of Fredericksburg to remove their
women and children until the morning of the 23d. No
news has been yet received of any bombardment, all
being reported quiet. Confederate General Lee
is at Fredericksburg, and, it is supposed, will
resist the passage of the Rappahannock by the
Federals. The Confederates remain in the im-
mediate front of the Fed.erals at Harper's Ferry.
The reports of Stone wall Jackson's m9vements are
Very conflicting. All sorts of rumours are current con-
curling the desdnation of the large Federal expefition
under General Banks. One report states that the expe-
dition will proceed to the Peninsula, and will co-operate
with the gunboats in the attack on Richmond by way of
James River. Earl Russell's refusal to co-operate with
France in mediation is seriously interpreted, many re-
garding the question of mediation as only postponed.
The New York Times thinks that the official announce-
ment of proposed mediation will give a definitcness to
American policy, which will leave European Govern-
ments no room to doubt what will be the result when
they shape and indicate their own course. General
11‘Clellan has refused a public reception in New York.
NEw YORK, Nov. 26 (Evening).—Rumours are cur-
rent that General Burnside's threatened attack on Fre-
dericksburg is merely a feint to cover the transportation
of his army from Acquia Creek to the Peninsula. It is
impossible to ascertain if the rumours are well-founded.
The general impression is that an advance on Richmond
by way of Fredericksburg is impracticable. A force of
sixty Confederate cavalry have made a dash into P ooles-
vine, Maryland, capturing the telegraph operators,
whom. they permitted to telegraph their capture to
Washington. The Federal Congress assembles on Mon-
day next (December Ist). To-morrow being Thanks-
giving-day, no business will be transacted in New York.
NOvEmnna 27 (Morning).—The Confederates are
.3trengthening their position at Fredericksburg, the
condition of the roads rendering any movement of he
Federal army impracticable. The New York press
generally criticises the official corre.,ponience on the
subject of the proposed mediation in an unfavourable
tone towards England and France; to both of whom
kaerested motives are attributed. The policy of Russia
favourably criticised. The New York Times thinks
that the threat of Jefferson Davis to execute the first
ten Federal officers captured in Missouri will be carried
out, and will form the most frightful incident in the
present war, demanding instant serious consideration ofthe
people. To-day being Thanksgiving-day contributions
. .

are received in Church-for the L-ancarhire- operatives.
NEW YOB.K, Nov. 28 (Evening).—The bombardment
of Fredericksburg is postponed. President Lincoln.
left Washington on the 27th and had an important in-
teryiew with General Burnside at Belle Plain. New
• Orleans correspondents of Northern journals assert that
the specie which the Federal Government ordered
General Butler to return to the French consul, was
afterwards sent to an agent at Havannah of the Confede-
rates, for the purchase of food and clothing. Numbers
'apolitical prisoners have been unconditionally released
from Fort Warren, Pierre Soule has been discharged
from Fort Lafayette. The Legislature of Georgia has
voted 600,000 dols. fbr obstructions to be placed in all
the navigable streams in Georgia. The New York
journals urge the Givernment to offer mediation be-
tween France and Mexico. President Lincoln's. Mes-
sage will probably be transmitted to Congress upon the
first day of the session.

TEE WORLD Is SUST.—It has been said that 'the
great soul of the world is just.' The manner in which
ether nations view this American. struggle seems to
demonstrate that in a certain sense the great head of the
world is clear. Man is, after all, a creature of principle.
When not diverted by self-interest or inflamed by
• passion, he is not to be blinded by profession without
principle, or deluded by a substitution of names for
things. America has set great store upon her size and
her material greatness for drawing upon her the admiring
eye of the 'world; but the mere vastness of her armies
and the enormity of their slaughter have failedto prevent
that eye from being but idly bent upon a straggle in
which the head could discern no great principles
Avowedly at issue, and with which the heart was for-
bidden, by the deepest instincts of humanity, to

A MAN BOILED ALIVE.—An inquiry was held at
:rat
Bishop's Stortford, Herts, on Friday afternoon, into the
circumstances of the death of Samuel Curtis, 37 years
of age, who had been in the employment of Messrs.
Hawkes and Co., brewers, Stortford. On Tue.iday
last deceased was engaged in cleaning the 'vats in
which boiling water had been placed. He was mop-
ping out one of these vessels, and instead of doing so
from the outside, he improperly got within it, and

-
stood over the vat on some cross pieces of woos that
'were only used for the purpose of removing the yeast
from off the beer, when by some means the poor fellow
slipped, and fell into the boiling liquor beneath. His
companion, whose back was turned at the time, heard
the splash and also screams, and upon looking round he
Perceived the uplifted hands of Curtis issuing from the
vat. Ile, of course, ran to his assistance, and, with
the aid of another man, extricated him. Medical at-
tendance was procured instantly, but the poor man died
the following mornini after a period of great agony.
Verdict of Accidental death.'

THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, _OECKAIBER 13,- 1862.

THE BOULEV4II?..D DU PRINCE
EUOENE.

Like the Boulevard Sebastopol, it will present a
straight line of white stone houses, a wide road, and
so icious pathways planted with trees, and provided
with seats for the public. Here and there open spaces
occur in this long cut, beginning where stood that nest
of small theatres of the Boulevard du Temple, and end-
ing at the Place du Trone, a distance little short of a
mile. The present aspect of the Boulevard Prince
Eugene is curious and not uninteresting; the houses
cut away have left others standing which appeared
to be placed in the most odd positions, presenting
most meaningless angles and fronts. Here and
there a street is pierced by the new road, and
it may be half a house presenting empty rooms
and broken staircases. All along the line are
boards telling you where the ground can be bought,
On ordinary days droves of workmen are moving about,
and idle people are gaping at the walls of the houses
which will back the new buildings. As this boulevard
runs through a more humble quarter of Paris than
others, one would suppose a more humble class of
houses would be erected for the industrial classes; but
the few that have already begun to rise are of white
stone, and indicate that costly construction which cha-
racterises the Parisian architecture of our day. The
visitor to Paris will understand the site of the new
building by being reminded that it begins near
the old Theatre Lyrique, and in its progress
the new boulevard of Prince Eugene cuts the
angle of the street de la Tour, passes the streets
Jeu de Boules, d'Angouleme and Menilmontant, then
through the street of the Grande Prieuse, and reaches
the canal at the corner of the passage Saint Pierre. Im-
mense have been the difficulties which have attended the
tunnelling that was required for piercing under the
canal to unite the two extremities of a boulevard now
transformed into a picturesque promenade for the people,
which bears the name of La Rein.e Hortense. Garden
plots, accompanied by fountains richly ornamented, are
interspersed at intervals along the whole line until the
Bastille is reached. This boulevard joins at its angle the
street Bt. Sebastien. The new road passes the street of
S. Amboise, having at its right hand the church of that
name, and ends in a square forming a parallelogram,
where the mairie of the 11th arrondissement is now con-
structing, and where also a statue of Prince Eugene is
erected.

The new boulevard, then passing along a wide ex-
panse and reaching the streets of Charonne,.of Boulets,
and Montreuil arrives at the angle of the Faubourg St.
Antoine at the Place du Trone. The Emperor, who
has taken the deepest interest in all that could gra-Lily
the humbler class of society, which forms the piincipal
portion of the inhabitants of this quarter, has determined
on rendering the neighbourhood as strikingly beautiful
as that which terminates the Champs Elysees. The
designs for tha public monuments have been accurately
examined, an are now executed in plaster and other
temporary materials, with a view of exhibiting what
the effect will be when the whole is completely termi-
nated. When this great work is completed it will be one
of theimost striking features of imperial Paris.
A letter from Paris, in the third edition of the Morn-
ing Post, describes the ceremony of opening the new
Boulevard. The writer says :
It was a dull day for the ceremony of the opening of
the Boulevard Prince Eugene, sunless, and a damp,
warm atmosphere. The Moniteur told us that the Em-
peror would leave the Tuileries at half-past one o'clock
on horseback. Long before that hour fife and drum and
military bands animated the streets as they preceded the
troops, which took up positions all along the line through
which the Emperor and staff, with the Empress folio w-
ing, passed. The cavalry was posted round the triumphal
arch and the tent erected for the inauguration cere-
mony, and thus occupied the whole Place du Trone, the
picturesque uniform of the Guides and Lancers giving
a gay aspect to this central point of the ceremony.
Behind the troops the black-looking civilan crowd of
spectators was seen, fringed by the coloured line of
military who prevented carriages from occupying the
road. The windows of the lofty hotels of the old
boulevards were crowded with ladies and gentlemen in
holiday toilettes, and along the line, here and there,
you saw flags protruding from the balconies into
the streets. But there was no great amount of
outward signs of a fete. The Emperor proceeded
by the way of the Rue di Rivoli and up the Boulevard
de. Sebastopol, then turning towards the Boulevard
Prince Eugene. His Majesty was accompanied by his
Imperial Highness Prince Napoleon and several gene-
rals. The Empress rode in a state carriage,
and saluted the crowd frequently. As far as I could
observe, there was little enthusiasm on the part of the
people, either for the Emperor or the Empress: all went
off coldly. The Prefect of the Seine and the municipal
bodies met their Majesties at the Place du Trone, and
conducted them to platforms, where all the Cabinet
Ministers awaited his Majesty. There at' address was
read, and the Emperor made a reply, the nature of
which I could not hear a word.; but no doubt it was of
the ordinary character, and suitable to the occasion.
The Emperor and Empress must have reached the
Tuileries by half-past three. Thus this day of anxiety
for many closed without any unpleasant associations, or
without any display of enthusiasm on the part of the
people in the streets.
'M. Dumas having addressed the' Emperor in the
name of the municipal commission, his Imperial Majesty
replied in terms which we would not presume to sini-
marise. It is sufficient to state that the speech of 'the
Emperor was enthusiastically received. Two portions,
however, of the address attracted the attention of the
audience.

The Emperor touched upon the question of the
baking trade of Paris as regards its bearing upon the
interests of the population, and. then continued,
"It. was at first intended to bestow upon the
transverse boulevard the name of Queen Hor-
tense, but I have no desire to monopolise for my family
the tribute of popular homage, which ought to be re-
served for our national glories." The Emperor stated
that he should give a new boulevard the name of
Richard Lenoir, who, from a simple workman, became
one of the most eminent manufacturers in Europe, and
who, after having given his workmen food in times of
distress, transformed them into soldiers and marched at
their head at a period when the country was in danger.
His Imperial Majesty, in conclusion, dwelt upon the in-
stitution by Lenoir of" loans to labour," and said that
his proceedings falsified. the proverb that it is only the
rich who are able to borrow (" on ne prete qu' aux
riches"). Numerous cries of "Long live the Emperor
and Empress" followed the speech of his Majesty.'

CHILD MURDERS IN THE PROVlNCES.—lnformation
was received on Saturday at the various police-
stations in the metropolis of two cases of child murder
ocaurring in the provinces. The first is that of a fine
female child, whose body was found in a drain at Bos-
ton, West Lincolnshire. It was quite naked at the
time of being discovered, ana its skull was very much
fractured at the back of the head. An inquest has
been held on the body, and stands adjourned until
Friday next, the 12th instant. The second case is that
of a fine male child, about four months old, whose
body was found in Westaston pool, near Nantwich,
Cheshire, with only a small cotton shirt on, in a new
calico bag, pinned at the top. The child appears to
have been in good health, and to have been placed in
the water whilst alive, a sleeping potion having been
previously given to it. The coroner's jury in this
case have returned a verdict of Wilful Murder against
some person or persons unknown.' Previous to inter-
ment photographs were taken of the unfortunate child,
which, it is to hoped, may be the means of bringing
the guilty party to justice..
A RAILWAY SQUADELE.—The West Midland Rail-
way Company have been endeavouring to recover
forcible possession of the refreshment-rooms at the
Worcester station of their line, which have been held
adversely by the tenant, Mr. Walton. The company
and their tenant have been for some time at.loggerheads
on this account, and the company have repeatedly given.
Mr. Walton notice to leave, but he refused; and there
being an uncertainty about the terms of his tenancy, the
company or their officers (acting with or without autho-
rity from the Board of Directors) proceeded to take
forcible possession of the refreshment-rooms. Accord-
ingly on Saturday night last, after all Mr. Walton's
servants had left the railway, a party of railway work-
men nailed up the doors and windows of the refresh-
ment-rooms, and barricaded them with boards. Next
morning (Sunday) Mr. Walton, accompanied by a party
of friends, made an attempt forcibly to regain possession
of the rooms. They were met by a body of railway
workmen, armed with staves, and on Mr. Walton
attempting to get in at a window one of the men, named
Jarrett, felled him to the ground by a blow on the head.
Mr. Walton was carried away insensible, and a mob
having collected and taken the part of Mr. Walton, a
serious riot would have been the result, but for the
opportune arrival of the police, who took Jarrett into
custody. He is to be examined on Monday next. The
manager of the railway, Mr. A. C. Sherriff, is the
Mayor of Worcester, and he has addressed a letter to
the Town Council, stating that in consequence of
aspersions cast upon his character in connection with
the affair he can take no part in business of any kind
connected with the city until the charges now sub
ludice are investigated and decided on by the proper
tribunal.' _

ROYAL CoLosszum.—The Barrett Minstrels, whose
first appearance we noticed some weeks since continue
to increase in popularity, the refinement of their enter-
tainment justly entitling them to the applause they
nightly receive from this usually undemonstrative audi-
ence. The very agreeable hour presented by these
13entlemen mist, in addition to the very varied attractions
of this popular institution draw large numbers of our
collar), cousins who will flock this week to the great
Cattle Show.

towards the Relief Fund. In addition to the £2,500
sent to the Lord Mayor from the city of Toronto and
neighbouring places, 100 barrels of flour, a contribution
from the village of Elord, have been consigned to the
Central Relief Committeein Manchester. Of the receipt
of the money an acknowledgment was requested in the
Times.

articles.title: CENTAL RELIEF FUND
articles.text:
THE CENTAL RELIEF FUND

On the 3rd of December the total receipts of the day
were £21,000; on the 4th of December, £10,490 ; and
on Friday, £10,590.
The following letter has also been received from Lord
Shaftesbury :
London, Dec 5.

' Sir —I have the pleasure to send you a dr. aught for
.El 2 as. 4d., of which a 7s. 6d. are to be regarded as
donations—the rest, DI Bs. 10d. as the amount of a con-
tribution to be continued for ten weeks. I am very
anxious to show in this statement what can be done
and without real inconvenience to any on, by small
weekly payments over larger surfaces. The parish in
Dorsetshire whence it comes consists of about 450
inhabitants, entirely agricultural labourers, with the
exception of the rector, three principal farmers, a
steward, two small tradesmen, and the landed propriezor.
The people were called togetner after the,r day's work,
a statement was made to them, and the following
resolutions were unanimously and most heartily
adopted :
'l. That a weekly subscription be instituted and
maintained for 10 weeks.

'2. That the subscription of a lai:ouring man or
woman do not exceed 2d. a week, or the farmers,
steward, rector, and landed proprietor ss.
3. That the subscriptions be collected every week by
persons whom the rector shall appoint.
4. That they be sent weekly to the Central Com-
mittee in Manchester.

N.B.—The above regulation is not meant to super-
sede any donation tlrit the richer might give apart from
this weekly subscription.'
Had the appeal been made for a single payment, it
would not have been possible to have collected a
fifth part of what the aggregate sum will have reached
at the end of 10 weeks. Now, if such a plan were set
on foot in all the great and small, rich and poor, parishes
of England, above £lOO,OOO might be easily collected
every week to meet tha present exigency in Lanca-
shire. _

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
11AFTESBURY.

Mr. J. W. Maclure, Secretary,
Central Relief Committee, &c.
The Bishop of Chichester has issued a letter (dated
Dec. 2) to the clergy of the diocess, recomalenciing
them to have collections made in their churches in aid
of the Central Relief Fund. The following are ex-
tracts from the letter :—"lhe distress of the people in
the cotton manufacturing districts of the kingdom
demands the sympathy of the country at large. That
sympathy has from many quarters been manifested to-
wards them in a christianly, praiseworthy manner. It
has come to be generally felt that we must not pause to
inquire whether the landowners, employers, and nearest
neighbours of those who are suffering have done, or are
doing, for the relief of the sufferers all which one may
fancy their relation to them requires at their hands.
. . . I leave it to yourself to determine in
what way the collections in your church shall be made,
—whether as at an offertory, or in what other way, and
whether you will address to your people only one ex-
hortation to contribute, or more than one. But Ido
recommend that several, I would say weekly opportu-
nities be presented to them for making their offerings
for their brethren as unto God. This will be especially
acceptable to our industrial classes. Almost univer-
sally they take a deep interest for those of their own
rank in life now suffering in the cotton distDicts.'

articles.title: BLACKBURN.
articles.text:
BLACKBURN.

At the guardians' meeting held on Saturday, Mr.
Richard Eccles in chair, a deputation of a small trades-
men and cottage owners attended to ask the board, in
conjunction with other authorities of the town, to join
us in applying for a loan of £50,000 from the Consoli-
dated Fund, the repayment to be spread over a number
of years.' The memorial which the deputation presented
to the board sets forth that many of the small trades-
men and cottage owners are in that financial strait that
they know not how to obtain food. Some of them have
paid rates and extended aid in goods to their unem-
ployed customers until their own credit and stocks are
exhausted; while those among them who, after a life of
struggling, had succeeded in obtaining an interest in a
few cottages, in hopes of preventing Gependence on cha-
rity when old, find that the value of their little proper-
ties is almost consumed through the loss of rents, claims
for mortgage interests, and the payment of excessive
rates.' The deputation intimated that they had seen
the mayor, and that he was willing to co-operate with
them with the view of having a town's meeting on
the subject. The memorial was signed by nearly 900
persons, and a considerably larger number could have
been obtained had they desired Government to make
them a grant from the Treasury. This they did not
wish; they merely asked that they might be allowed
time—say one or two years—after the distress times had
terminated. They had no wish to shirk any liability,
but as they could not get rents they could not be ex-
pected to be in a position to pay rates, and they begged
that the guardians would not levy any additional rates
f®r a few months.

The Chairman intimated that the matter had been
mentioned to the district auditor, and he had expressed
his readiness to allow the rates now due from distressed
ratepayers to be paid at some future time, and to be car-
ried forward from one rate to another. He (the chair-
man) thought that circumstance would meet the wishes
of the deputation.
He was answered in the affirmative.

With, regard to the levying of rates, the Chairman said
the overseers and not the guardians, were the persons
whom the deputation would have to see on the subject.
The deputation replied that they did not wish to escape
any legal claims. They considered it cruel, unwise, and
impolitic either to force payment of present rates or to
levy new ones.
The Chairman replied that the guardians had nothing
to do with that subject; it was clearly the duty of the
overseers.

The deputation then withdrew.
The returns of out-relief showed that during the
week the relieving officers of the union had applied
£1,436 Bs. 7d. to the relief of 23,673 persons, of whom
9,836 were described as able, bodied, against, 4,411 per-
sons relieved with £2Ol Bs. 11d, in the corresponding
week of 1861, two months after the distress had been
severely felt. The chief constable's return, made up to
Friday, shows that an improved trade is operating for
good in the diminished numbers of the unemployed. He
says 16,601 are still out of work, 4,706 working short
time, and 5,967 full time. This (Monday) morning the
of Mr. Joseph Bolton, Nova Scotia, will resume
operations at the rattt of five days per week. This will
be a great assistance to the operatives of that district.
Trade is improving, and the manufacturers believe that
they will shortly be all enabled to run their manufac-
tories from three to four days per week.
A sick kitchen =fleeted with the Established Church
has been opened in the Town-hall, and is of consider-
able service. The infirmary now being completed has to
be opened as a general sick kitchen, but means are still
wanted to complete the work.

articles.title: BURNLEY.
articles.text:
BURNLEY.

The Mayor, Mr. Moor, presided at the weekly meeting
of the Lo?,al Relief Coramitte, held on Thursday. The
committee granted the sum of £4BL Is. for the relief of
6,844 persons for the week, £43 ss. 6d. to the industrial
schools, £lB 2s. 6d. tor the adult tehools, £l4 Bs. 2d. fol.
the school pence of children, and a 4s. for expenses
attendant On the sewing department. It was reported
that 291 girls attended the industrial school, and 12
monitors and 141 young men the adult schools. The
committee acknowledged the receipt of £l,OOO from the
Manchester Committee for general relief, and a further
sum of £5OO for clothing ; also a check for £lOO from
the Baroness de Rothschild. This money 'will be in-
vested in coals. A fulther sum of £l,OOO from the
Mansion House Committee was also acknowledged. The
committee also agreed to grant £l,OOO to be expended in
clothing to •persons not in receipt of relief from any

are below 3s. per head.

articles.title: CLITHEROE.
articles.text:
CLITHEROE.

The destitution of the operatives is gradually and
surelyincreasing. At the meeting of the Relief Com-
mittee on Wednesday they passed accounts of £3lO 19s.
Bd., including £213 2s. for groceries, &c., £5B ss. 3d. for
blankets, £lO to the overlookers' fund, and £l6 to the
sewing schools, &c. The. committee agreed to purchase
additional blankets, and £l5O was granted for that pur
pose. It was also decided that the clothing to be dis-

every article stamped with the die of the committee.
Several minor detailed amagements for the better
management of toe sewing schools were ordered. The
committee determined to get material made up in thise

which earnings are not to be accounted as relief.

Tun SCANDALS.—We understand that his Royal
Highness the Duke of Cambridge has referred back to
the court of inquiry upon the Burnaby.scandal, the re-
port which, as we 6t ,ted last week, it had laid before
him in his capacity as Colonel of the Grenadier Guards.
We have already characterised the report as incomplete
and unsatisfactory, and his Royal Highness would ap-
pear to share this view, from the fact of his seeking
further information upon this very delicate subject.-

articles.title: CITY T.RAFFIC-PAST AND PRESENT.
articles.text:
CITY T.RAFFIC-PAST AND PRESENT.

The City traffic has always been a subject of
interest to citizens, and those who use the City; as
the first have to pay for its partial regulation, and the
second are daily annoyed by its bulk and complications.
Though, in company with a large and influ ntial majo-
rity of the Common Council, we may not approve of the
Traffic Regulation Bill lately drAwn up to order by the
City Remembrancer, we are quite ready to admit the
pressing nature ot the difficulty. Martial law is not a
thing to look forwal d to with rapture, nor to cure
the evil—if evil it be ; and we believe that the cost
of delays and blocks acting upon the sensitive frame of
commerce will eventually do more to regulate the cir-
culation of vehicles within the City than any unpopular
law. The labour which the City traffic now throws
upon the City police is undochtedly very harassirlg and
costly. We shalt prcbably be within the mark if we say
that the police management of London-bridge absorbs
twenty constabb s, who represent an annual charge of a
thousand pounds a year. Half the work of the six
hundred well-selected and well-officered constables who
form the City police consists of a daily struggle with the
traffic, and may be put down as not being paid for
with less than fifteen thousand pounds a year.
The City traffic, of course, has grown with the
population, and without ref,rring to official records,
it would be as easy to calculate the number of carts and
people flowing in and out of the city during twenty-
four hours as it would be to reckon how many coats a
certain mass of people is likely to wear, or how many
loaves an army is likely to consume in a day. As
records exist, however, which give us precise figures
concerning the City traffic at different periods during
the last fifty years, it may not be uninteresting to pre-
sent a few of these facts at the present time. Black-
friars -bridge seems to have been regarded with interest
in 1808, and men were placed there to gauge the daily
traffic for six weeks in the summer and winter of that
year. They reported that 48,000 persons passed over
the bridge every 24 hours, but that, on a fine Sunday
morning in August, this number was increased to up-
wards of 70,000 persons. Holiday-making must have
been very popular then in St. George's Fields.'

In 18f1 -a

London bridges on the same day, to ascertain the
average number of passengers and vehicles that daily
