The waggons and carts alone which now pass daily
over this bridge, as we showed the other day, at a time
when our London population is about 2,800,000, must
be at least 12,000, while the journeys to and fro swell
this number to 24,000.

Cheapside is more blocked up than London-bridge,
because of the side streams of traffic, and the stoppages
at shops and warehouses. Thirteen thousand vehicles
flow through it every afternoon from east to west and
west to east between four and five o'clock. This only
shows the state of one channel for traffic, and there are
many other streets—amongst which we may reckon
Ludgate-hill—in the same condition.

LIFEBOAT FOR NEW ZEALAND.—OR Monday Some
interesting and satisfactory trials were made at the
Regent's-canal Dock with a new lifeboat, on the plan of
those of the National Lifeboat Institution, for New
Zealand. The boat is 35 feet long and six feet wide,
and seems to be admirably adapted for the special pur-
pose for which she is required—namely, to land passen-
gers at Auckland from ships when the surf would be too
heavy for ordinary boats to venture off. Her self-
righting properties answered extremely well; and when
full of water, the boat self-ejected it in fifteen seconds.
She possesses all the qualities of the single banked boats
of the Lifeboat Institution. She will be shipped on
board the emigrant ship Huntress, which leaves in a
day or so for New Zealand with 200 or 300 emigrants.
The boat has been built by the Messrs. Forrestt, of
Limehouse, under the directions of Mr. John Marshall,
the intelligent emigration agent for the colony of New
Zealand in this country.
SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—A serious accident took
place on Monday morning a little after eight o'clock on
trio Great Eastern Railway, by which considerable da-
mage has been inflicted on the permanent way and
rolling stock; but, as on all such 'occasions, it is im-
possible to ascertain from the officials the amount of
injury. The train which leaves Hertford at 8 a.m., and
is due at Shoreditch at 9.30 a.m., had scarcely got upon
the main line when the engine left the rails, carrying
with it the tender and several of the carriages. The
extent of the injury done to the line may be estimated
from the fact that all the up-traffic has been interrupted
for a long time. To prevent any collision between the
disabled train and the expre:s train from Norwich, which
was due in about half an hour or twenty minutes, men
were sent forward with danger signals, at the sight of
which the driver of the express promptly brought his
train to a standstill.
MEMORIAL OF QUEENELIZABETH.-7A remarkable article
occurred at the sale of the late Canon Tierney's library,
which has just been dispersed, under the hammer of
Messrs. Sotheby and Wilkinson. It was thus described:
—Elizabeth (Queen). A Declaration of the Sentence
and Deposition. of Elizabeth the usurper and pretended
Queue of Englande, broadside excessively rare (1588).
This scurrilous broadside exconimanication issued with
the name of Sextus V., was intended to have been posted
on the walls throughout England if the Armada had
been successful, and must have been a most offensive
libel to the Queen, as it described her as an Heretike,'
a bastard,
.conceyved and borne by incentuous adul-
tery,'an unjust usurper," a perjurer," a murtherer '
and with other similar epithets. On the failure of the
expedition this broad-ide was so studiously suppressed
and destroyed, that its very existence has been doubted
and denied. It is supposed to have been printed at
Antwerp, and, although attributed to Cardinal Allen, is
considered to have been really penned by Father Robert
Persons. Purchased by Mr. Toovey at £3l.—Athlnanon.

CONVICTIONS UNDEE THE Fislnnic AcT.—Some of
the fishermen on the river Severn, having been in the
practice of using nets on that river during the fence
time, ostensibly for the purpose of taking small fish,
though there can be no doubt unseasonable salmon are
frequently taken by this means, the conservator of that
river, acting under the directions of the officers of the
Severn Fisheries Protection Association, has just prose-
cuted two men, named William Owen, sen., and William
Owen, jun., for using a net in the night time, on the
9th of November, contrary to the statute. The facts
were clearly proved by a number of witnesses, who saw
the defendants on the river' and who received a quantity
of small fish, which they had taken in nets of small
mesh. The elder Owen, having been convicted on
former occasions, was now fined £5, including costs, or
two months' imprisonment, and the younger £3, or one
month's hard labour. A third defendant, named
Thomas Owen, was summoned, but did not appear, and
a warrant was issued for his apprehension.
A MODEL LANDLORD.--411 the course of, the re-
joicing at Eglinton Castle last week a letter by the Earl
of Eglinton to his commissioner was read, in which the
earl Raid: I shall feel obliged to you informing my
tenants, at such a time and in such a manner as you
may consider most expedient, that at next May term it
is my intention to make them a present of 10 per cent.
off their rent for this year's crop. lam well aware
that the last four years have been anything but re-
munerative to the farmers of this part of Scotland; but
I wish you distinctly to explain to my tenants that the
above gift is in no case to be considered as a solatium
for bypast losses. I beg that those who may have
suffered so seriously as to injure their prospects of
managing their farms successfully will candidly make
their position known to my factor, and I shall be only
too glad to give my attentive consideration to each case
that is brought under my notice.'
It is estimated that in Illinois there have been raised
from 50,000 to 75,000 acres of sorghum this season.
The value of the product by syrup is estimated at one
million dollars.
SIMPLICITY or GENIDS.—When. Bewick was asked to
what he owed his marvellous success in portraying
beasts and birds, his answer is said to have been that
he supposed he looked harder at thin' than most men
did. So Mrs. Siddons, when questioned as to the art
with which she produced such electrifying effects on
the stage, said she simply did the best she could.'

Dzss=res.—They gave me a bed-room there;. a very
neat room on the first floor looking into the pretty
garden. The hotel must look pretty much as it did a
hundred years ago when he visited it. I wonder
whether he paid his bill? Yes: his journey was just
begun. He had borrowed or got the money somehow.
Such a man would spend it liberally enough when he
had it, give generously—nay, drop a tear over the fate
of. the poor fellow whom he relieved. I don't believe a
word he says, but I never accused him of stinginess
about money. That is a fault of much more virtuous
people than he. Mr. Laurence is ready enough with his
purse when there are anybody's guineas in it. Still,
when I went to bed in the room, in his room; when I
think how I admire, dislike, and have abused him, a
certain dim feeling of apprehension filled my mind at
the midnight hour. What if I should see his lean figure
in the black satin breeches, his sinister smile, his long
thin finger pointing to me in the moonlight (for I am
in bed, and have popped my candle out), and he should
say, You mistrust me, you hate me, do you? And
you, don't you know how Jack, Tom, and Harry, your
brother authors, hate you 1' I grin and laugh in the
moonlight, in the midnight, in the silence. '0 yon
ghost in black satin breeches and a wig! I like to be
hated by some men,' I say. I know men whose lives
are a scheme, whose laughter is a conspiracy, whose
smile means something else, whose hatred is a cloak,
and I had rather these men should hate me than not.'—
A Roundabout Paper in the Cornhill Magazine.
WHO, of the present generation, knows anything of
Count Rumford? At the mention of his name every-
body thinks of stoves. In most people's minds there is
a sort of wonder whether he could be a real Count if his
business in life was—stoves. Some of us elders of our
day had fathers who knew Count Rumford, and who
remembered and talked of him, not in connection with
stoves, but as a nebleman of great knowledge of an
active inquiring spirit, of great administrative faculty,
and the most indefatigable resolute, vigilant, and enter-
prising benevolence. 'Whenever society needs the
largest amount of ccmfort at the smallest cost, the name
and memory of Count Rumford come up again. In
times of ordinary prosperity, when our workpeople are
well employed and paid, and our gentry gather new
luxuries about them, and entertain their minds with
study and speculation, the man is forgotten, or spoken
of only for this or that invention. When we have a
particularly bad harvest, or any commercial adversity
which throws millions of destitute people on our hands
to be fed and cheered, Count Rumford's name is heard
where old people are talking together of the black years
of their lives. There may be less and less of this as the
old folks pass away; but it will be a good while yet
before there is nobody left to quote the sayings and
doings of the large-hearted and practical-minded man
who fed the hungry in four countries in Christendom,
and showed how the greatest number could be nourished
and cheered at the smallest cost.—Once a Week.
It is recorded of the Rabbi Chananiah that when he
undertook to write a commentary upon part of the
Prophet Ezekiel, he required the Jews to supply him
with three hundred tons of oil for the use of his lamp,
while he should be engaged in it. —Southey.
ORIGIN OF OLD NICK:—The application of this
term to the swarthy father of all evil has never yet been
satisfactorily accounted for; it is doubtful whether it
ever will. Some authors are for carrying the origin up
to the celebrated Nicholas Machiavel, whose cunning
policy in the 16th century was noted and proverbial.
He is as cunning as Old Nick,' was then a common
saying; but how it ever came, to be transferred to his
Satanic Majesty is left in mystery. Possibly the fol-
lowing conjecture respecting the origin of this term
may be considered not ill-founded. The Danes and
Germans, according to Keysler, wbrshipped a diety by
name Nocca, or Nicken, which name he derives from the
German nugen, synonymous with the Latin necare, to
kill. When the Danes invaded England, they brought
with them their language and peculiarities. What
more probable, then, than that this appellation is
handed down to us, like many other of their words, and
that as Christianity dispelled the absurdities of super-
stition, it was at length applied to the monarch of the
infernal regions.
TURBOT.—The fishing season for this fish commences
in March, and terminates in August. The Dutch are
supposed to have drawn not less than 80,000/. a-year
for the supply of this fish to the London market alone.
The English fishermen purchase largely at sea of the
Dutch; nevertheless, the Dutch send boats laden with
turbot up the Thames, each boat bringing about 150
fish. The Danes also are said to derive from 12,000/. to
15,000/. a-year for sauce to this luxury of the table, ex-
tracted from a million of lobsters, taken on the rocky
shores of Norway, though our own shores are in many
parts plentifully supplied with this creature, equal in
goodness to those of Norway. The finest turbot are
taken on the Flemish banks, and the banks called Broad
Forties. Excellent fish are also taken by the French
fishermen on the two large sandbanks called the Verne
and the Ridge, stretching towards the French coast in
the Channel, not many miles from Dover. These they
sell to the English out at sea, or send into Dover. The
average size of turbot is from three to ten pounds
weight; but some of large size have been occasionally
taken, which have weighed from 50 to 70 pounds, and
one was caught in 1832, near Whitby, which weighed
190 pounds.—Cassas Natural History.

CELTIC REMAINS IN NORTHUMBERLAND.—It is well
known that the different tribes of Celtic Britain lived in
a continual state of hostility with each other, but there
is a circumstance apparent in the connexion of those
towns with that on the opposite hill of Ritta, which
would indicate an intended combination to resist a
threatened assault or invasion; and if this connection
can be traced to exist in common with other fortifica-
tions on these hills, there might appear grounds for the
supposition that those settlements may have been
strengthen-A and united into one common lino of
defence on the extension of .tha Roman occupation of
Britain in a northern direction; and that, in fact, we
have on the wild Chevoit hills a sort of counter-part to
the great work of the Roman wall erected with a kindred
view of limiting the incursions of a common enemy.—
Once a Week.

GOETHE'S BELIEF i IMMORTALITY.—One evening,
in his old age, returning with his secretary from a
drive through the wooded valley of Rudolstadt, he
caused the carriage to stop at a place where four roads
met, to enjoy the prospects of the red sun sinking over
the river and distant hills, and shedding its tranquil
light through the splendid avenue of black Italian
poplars. After viewing the descending orb for some
time, turning to Eckerman, he said, cheerfully, When
one is 70 years old one cannot fail at times to think of
death. The subject I contemplate in the most perfect
peace, for I have a firm conviction that the soul is an
existence of an indestructible nature, whose working is
from eternity to eternity. It is like yonder sun which,
to our eyes, indeed, seems to set, but properly speaking
never sets—shining in unchangeable splendour ; ' add-
ing that to him the idea of the soul's immortality
flowed from that of its activity, 'for if I progress in
intellectual activity in the same proportion as my bodily
tenement weakens, nature thereby seems to pledge her-
self to bring me into a state of existence more suitable
to the ripe state of my inward man.'—Dublin University
Magazine

THE PARISLM—The Parisian is to the Frenchman
what the Athenian is to the Greek; no one sleeps
sounder than he ; no one is more frankly frivolous and
idle than he; no one can pretend to forget so well as he,
but he must not be trusted; he is suited for every
species of nonchalance, but when there is a glory as the
result, he is admirable for every sort of fury. Give
him a pike, and he will make August 10th; give him a
musk at, and you will have Austerlitz. He is the support
of Napoleon, and the resource of Danton. If the country
is in danger, he enlists; if liberty is imperilled he tears
up the pavement. His hair, full of wrath, is epical,
his blouse assumes the folds of a chlamys. Take care;
for of the first Rue Grenetal he comes to, he will make
Caudine forks. If the hour strikes, this Faubourien
grows, the little man. 'looks in a terrible manner, his
breath becomes a tempest, and from his weak chest
issues a blast strong enough to uproot the Alps. It was
through the Parisian Faubourion that the Revolution,
joined with armies, conquered Europe. He sings, and
that forms his delight; proportion his song to his
nature, and you shall see! so long as he has no burden
but the Carmagnole, he will merely overthrow Louis
XVI. ; but make him sing the 'lllarseillaise,' and he
will deliver the world:— Victor Hugo's Les 3liscrables.

Prince Alfred on boatd, put in at Algiers on the 30th
ult., but the hour at which she arrived being after

ing morning. During the day Marshal the Duke de

LONG AND toMoRT .rROJECTILEs. Since the Ord-
nance stores have been filled with long lead-coated shot
sufficient to last for several years—if they can be made
to keep without deterioration from galvanic action—it
is said to have been discovered that short shot are the

METROPOLITAN CATTLE MARKET.
DECEMBER B,—The total imports of foreign stock into
London last week amounted to 5,033 head. In the ern-
responding week in 1861 we received 4,951; in 1860,
6,103; in 1859, 4,311; in 1858, 4,322; in 1857, 1,773;
and in 1856, 1,622 head.
The show of each kind of foreign stock here to-day was
only moderate. There were some good Dutch sheep
amongst it; but, generally speaking, the quality of the
supply was inferior. Buyers operated cautiously; never-
theless, prices were supported. With home-fed beasts we
were seasonably well supplied, both as to number and
quality. The arrival of meat up to Newgate and Leadenhall
Markets being extensive, the beef trade was by no means
active. However, the bulk of the supply was disposed of,
at prices equal to Monday last. The general top price for
beef was 55. per 81bs. ; but a few very superior Scots and

900 various breeds ; • from Scotland, 200 Scots and Crosses;
and from Ireland, 600 oxen and heifers. With sheep the
market was scantily supplied, and we observed very little
improvement in their quality. Prime Downs and half-
breds moved off steadily, at full prices, the top figure
being ss. 56. per Blbs. ; but long- woolled sheep were a
slow inquiry, at abut last week's currency. The supply
of calves was moderate, and the veal trade ruled heavy, at
previous quotations. The top price was 4s. 6d. per albs.

NOVEL SHIP ',Atm-ex.—A brigantine of about 200 'GIs
has been launched from the yard of Mr. J. Robinson,
Duke's Dock. The launch excited some interest among
nautical men, inasmuch as it exemplified some new prin-
ciples both in the art of shipbuilding and in the mode of
launching. The length of the vessel in question is 103 ft.,
breadth 22ft. Sin., and depth of hold 12ft. 3in. She
will carry upwards of 400 tons at lift, draught. She is
built in a manner that insures great strength, being
diagonally planked both inside and out. The launch
was effected with per:ect success, notwithstanding that
no bilge logs, packing, poppets, or wedging-up were
used. The vessel glided beautifully down, her bottom
resting on the ways' and although the water was five
feet from the pier-head and entirely one-half the vessel
at the moment of launching was without support, yet
she overcame this extremely severe test without a strain
—a fact that speaks volumes for her strength. She was
christened the Richmond. The chief peculiarity of the
vessel is light draught, which adapts her to the naviga-
tion of shallow ports and harbours. She has also a novel
arrangement of sails and is intended chiefly for the
conveyance of machinery, having a very large hatch.
Who can wonder at the intensity of a mother's love,
when even strangers hardened by a struggle with the
world are often affected by the engaging ways of
children? There is not a more interesting sight in
nature than the sudden smile which they sometimes call
up in a countenance rendered habitually grave by the
cares of business or ambition. I remember entering a
well-known mercantile house in London, just as some
unfavourable intelligence had been received. The head
of the arm, with his hard but honest features, looked at
once stern and anxious. A small hand twitched his
coat behind. He turned slowly, round, with a sullen and
almost savage brow. His eye fell upon the prettiest little
human face that ever gleamed upon the earth. But the
child's merry laughter was scarcely more delightful than
the bland and beautiful smile that kindled on the
merchant's care-worn cheek. His aspect underwent
such an instantaneous and entire change, that he looked
as if he had changed his nature also. Had a painter
stamped his portrait on the canvas at that happy mo-
ment, it would have presented an exquisite illustration
of amenity and love. Few, hewever, of his mercantile
friends would have recognised the man of business. Ho
was single and childless; but the fondest parent could
not have greeted his own offspring with a sweeter wel•
come..—. Essay an Children, by D_,L. Richardson.

SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1862.

SUMMARY.

The Greeks proceed in their election of
Prince Alfred with remarkable unanimity,
although" the three Powers" agree in barring
his appointment, and in nominating Ferdinand
of Portugal to the vacant throne. The choice
of the three Powers may be termed the
"Dowager" King of Portugal, still a young man,
although one of his sons was King of Portugal,
and died last year; and another of his sons,
now King of Portugal, is married. The ex-
King Ferdinand may answer; and if
Princ Alfred be unattainable by the Greeks,
they may be contented with his cousin. He is
recommended to them by the consideration that
be would marry again, and bring up
his children in the Greek religion.
He is a Protestant, who promised, when he
married the Queen of Portugal, to allow the
education of their family in the Roman Ca-
tholic religion; and he has kept his promise.
If the Greeks accept him, and he marry , again,
he will have no difficulty respecting their form
of worship. And he will keep that promise
also respecting a second family. Prince Alfred

could not accommodate parties in that-lianner,
having in view his' possible sueetssibn to the
British throne. The advice of King Leopold
is now intelligible. He urged our Govern-
ment to refuse the Greek Crown on the part
of Prince Alfred, in order to maintain good
relations with France and Russia, and make
provision for a nearer relative, now unem-
ployed._

- he Emperor .of Russia has gone to Moscow,
and met there a deputation of seven chiefs from
the peasantry. He advised these chiefs to coun-
sel the peasantry to pay up the money clue for
their freedom with punctuality, and not to
indulge dreams of additional liberty in the pre-
sent condition of affairs—meaning thereby the
present generation. The Emperor is honest
in declining to promise reforms that he has no
intention to concede, or no power to effect.
One of our statesmen would have promised to
bring in a bill and lay it on the table, there to
continue under discussion and dust for half a
century.

A new Italian ministry has not yet been
clearly carried into business through the crisis;
although the leaders are named. Garibaldi's
health improves, and he proposes to revisit
Caprera. Disturbances continue in Naples
and other departments of the Southern terri-
tory. The Emperor of the French passed
safely through the ceremony of opening the
new street on last Sunday; and no infernal
machine was visible. From Mexico accounts
have been published, stating that the health of
the army is improved, and that the march on
the Mexican metropolis would commence with
December. The King of Prussia proposes the
inauguration of a new fete in March next, to
celebrate peace and war. March of 1863 will
complete a hundred years from the termination
of the seven years war; and fifty years from
the commencement of the war of emancipation
or independence against France. The Hano-
verian ministry have been changed, but it is
difficult to say ii" for better or for worse."
No change had occurred to the 28th ult.,
in the position of the armies in the States.
The Confederates looked across the Rapahan-
nock, from the South, at the Federals, who
looked over the river, from the North, on the
Confederates. Great rains had fallen, and
placed the river •in an eight dais flood, bind-
ing those enemies to keep the peace. The
correspondence between the British and the
French Governments concerning intervention,
or mediation, had been published, and had
caused more umbrage with Great Britain,
which is threatened by all parties, or nearly all,
for doing something, or not doing something;
but the deeds consecutive to these angry words
are postponed until after the restoration of
the Union as it was.

The remittances to Bombay, per this weeks
mail are again nearly a half million. The ex-
portation of cotton from that port for the year
commencing in 1861, ending in 1862, exceeds
one million of bales, and brought on the spot
over twenty millions sterling. A steamer with
the homeward mails from Australia, and part
of the Indian, has been lost, with part of the
mail, but all the lives are saved.

The West Indian Mail contains no political
information, although statements appear in
the papers regarding small patches of cotton
which promise to be productive.
A report appears in our papers on Western
Africa, with a statement that 500,000 bales of
cotton may be expected from the Niger next
year. They may be expected—that, at least,
is a truth undeniable—but they will not be
received,—nor 50,000, perhaps 5,000, could be
scraped together.

E-mploy-ment in many departments is re-
ported dull. The wages earned by "the em-
ployed," in some of the cotton works, are only
nominal. In Blackburn one man had tzvopenee
and his cottage rent for a week's work. One
overlooker, who has to support eight children,
managed to make eight shillings. Another had
seven, but he has a family of only five persons.
Employment in some of these towns is becom-
ing less productive than idleness.

he times, in noticing Captain Mangles
defeat at Southampton, says that he had no
avowed purpose, except vote by ballot and ex-
tension of the suffrage; measures deferred to
the next century. It is a long prediction, but
the apathy and indifference of the people
endow it with the appearance of truth.
• Cotton is a penny per pound dearer, and in
demand this week. Consols have fallen to 1,
and are 92-4. without the dividend. Wheat has
receded by one shilling per quarter. The
grocery markets are generally lower, and pro—
visions are slightly higher.
The garrotting agitation continues to frighten
London. One policeman advises as a remedy
all parties to keep early hours, and go straight
home. The outcry, like many historical
novels, is founded on few facts, and much
fiction. It may lead to a re-consideration of
our relations with the criminal class, who are
at present better clothed, fed, and lodged than
many of the honest class.

THE. EDMUND'S MAIN CATASTROPHE.

Another great mining accident, second only
in the destructi,,on of life to the calamity at
the Hartley Colliery, occurred at Edmund's
Main, near Barnsley, on Monday last. This
colliery belongs to Messrs. Mitchell, Bartho-
lomew, and Tyas, and is very extensive. The
workings extend for more than a mile, and the
mines must, therefore, be in some places at a
great distance from the shaft. The Barnsley
seam produces large quantities of gas, and is
dangerous only for that reason. At Edmund's
Main all the common precautions against
accident had been adopted, and the proprietors
were engaged in connecting the workings to
the south with a new shaft, when the explosion
occurred. An investigation of the circumstances
before the coroner's jury is adjourned to
Monday, but all the facts are, perhaps, already
known.

The explosion originated in the operations
necessary to connect the pit with the new
shaft, and not by any accumulation of fqul
air from neglected ventilation. The men em-
ployed to cut a passage from the workings to
the shaft pursued their labours on Monday
morning, by blasting. As the coal gives out
a large amount of gas, blasting is extremely
perilous. No doubt, whatever, exists that all
the men who died at Barnsley, on Monday,
perished because the persons engaged in cut-
ting this connection decided on blowing down
some of the obstructions, and it may be a
question whether this plan, although economi-
cal and effective, should be allowed in any posi-
tions where an accumulation of gas maybe ex-
pected, with indifferent or restricted ventilation.
In making use of this catastrophe for future
guidance we have a clear explanation of its
origin; and blasting should not have been per-
mitted in the locality; for it was not absolutely
necessary. The miners did not require gun-
powder to clear their way which they
could have accomplished with a little
more labour and time by their ordinary
tools. This fact requires to be fixed in
and on the public mind. The lives lost in this
mine are squandered, to save money. Economy
is more valuable than life in the business

management, because the miners are freemen.
Strong men sell in'the Sonthern 'States even at
present for £2OO to £250 each; and more than
sixty men andboys were destroy-ea. at Edmund's
Main on Monday, but there were boys among
them, and instead of 5.200,,we reckon .£l5O or
.£9,000, and if that sum had been risked by the
proprietors, from the use of gunpowder; they
would have irdered their men to "pick" their
way.

We are delivered from the atrocity, the
shame, and the superlative wrong of slave-
holding; bat we .are also entitled to deliverance
from a reckless and scandalous waste of life.
These fifty men were, doubtless, "free," yet
their lives Should have been, and really were,
valuable to the state. A free man must be
of more value to the nation than a slave to his
owner. Discharging from consideration for a
moment the higher interests of humanity and
of life, on the lowest possible ground of money,
and therefore of political economy, the state is
interested in conserving life, and preventing
all needless risks.

The proprietors of Edmund's Main are
doubtless humane men; more distressed by
this calamity in their mine than any other
men; and we do not impute any moral culpa-
bility to them in the business, for they folio wed
the common system, pursued around them
without any dread of results. This is the best
interpretation that can be placed on their
position, and it leaves clear the necessity for
legislative precautions in mining, more strin-
gent than those in common use. We are
perpetually reminded that the Government
must not interfere between employed and
employers; but as the perpetual danger of
slaughter exists, the Government for econo-
mical and humane reasons is bound to re-
move the risk.

The " blast " occurred between seven and
eight, on Monday morning, and ignited a
" blower "of gas. The overseer on the spot
was said to:be a very intelligent man, and he ex-
pected to conquer the flame without alarming
the miners in other branches• of the workings.
Along with the few men engaged in cutting
the ,new passage, he made strenuous exertions
for this purpose, but they were unsuccessful,
although continued up to eleven o'clock, when
from the accumulation of foul air, the first
explosion occurred. Nearly 260 men and
boys were engaged during these three to four
hours in the mine. _ They might all have been
safely removed, except for the overseer's daring
efforts to save a little money to the owners. -
As the proprietors. had..their mines under
excellent ventilation, and were engaged at the
moment in providing- a new shaft,- and as no
blame attaches to them' respecting the shafts,
it is possible that' the employment of gun-
powder, in blasting at the spot, was inconsist-
ent with their instructions. On that and other
matters, information may be hereafter obtained;
but we need no farther inquiries to know that
the employment of gunpowder, in blasting,.
ignited the gas and that the loss of three
hours, or more than three, in attempting to
overcome the flame, destroyed the men. The
overseer is dead; he has given life in attempt-
ing to subdue a subtle foe; .but that strife
risked and lost many lives.
The explosion at eleven o'clock was the first
alarm that more than 250 men and boys,
scattered over underground workings, ex-
tending for more than a mile, received of a
danger that had been impending over them for
nearly four hours. They all then endeavoured
to find safety at the shafts, but the fire spread
rapidly in the pit, and more rapidly still sped
the foul air from the explosion, through the
workings. No time was lost in taking the
men up the shaft, but two dangers
gained fast upon them in the anxious
moments occupied in drawing up drafts of the
miners, until only a few yards around the foot
of the shaft were safe from the "hot air," and
the "after damp."• Beyond these few yards,
the air was poison, and each breath was fire.

The remainder of the story is the sad and
sickening statement of sorrow, helpless and
unavailing, carried at once to nearly all the
homes of a neighbourhood, with its gloom
broken by honest sympathy, and lightened by
the efforts of true-hearted courage, not less
devoted than the courage that leads men ever
to hazard life by field or flood. At Edmund's
Main, several of the miners who had been
drawn out of the terrible scene, so far down
in the gloom beneath them; at once volunteered
to descend again in search of their mates.
They may not have taken time to look

"On sun and sky ar.d plain
As things they ne'er might see again."
but no warrior ever exhibited courage greater
than the devotedness of the mdli who breathed
freely once, to plunge again into the chasm
where life struggled with death in a conflict
almost hopeless; in circumstances most terrible.

Men from the neighbouring collieries, and
others acquainted with mining, volunteered
their assistance, and among the dead are several
of these persons who went down to rescue
others, until the first explosion was followed
by a second; and the Government In-
spector declined to permit the risk of more
lives when he deemed that all hope of life in the
pit was past. The miners and viewers of the
district apparently share the opinion that none
of the men could have survived to a late hour
of Monday afternoon, but a proposal to extin-
guish the fire, which is supposed to exist, by
turning a stream down the shaft had been
delayed up to Wednesday night. The stream
wouldhave extinguished the fire, the any linger-
ing hope that a single life might be added to
those already saved out of the working. Any
of that nature must soon be en-
tirely lost, and all that will remain is the desire
of neighbours and friends to recover the re-
mains of their acquaintances and friends.
Edmund's Main is an illustration' added to
that of Hartley Colliery, of the dangers of
mining. A large district is overwhelmed in
gloom. More than a hundred and twenty-
widows and orphans are left helpless. Sixty-
labouring men are taken from their hard
toil; some of them by a painful death, without
a hand they loved to close eyes that grew dim
amid a darkness lighted here and there
only by the fires of death. Some of
the miners who penetrated farthest to help
the scorched men, came to places where
their passage was barred by poisoned air,
' although they could hear the men suffering
beyond this invisible barrier, more secure and
invulnerable than any dungeon walls, in the
anguish of their departure, when "flesh and
heart" had "fainted and failed," committing
all to the author of their spirits—seeking from
him strength for the moment, forgiveness and
hope for the eternity, linking the names of
theirs with the great name that all may use.
Genius never had a more heart-searching
subject than these narrow subterranean ways
where the miners creep; with the praying and
dying men beyond the invisible wall of air that
painters find no colour for; and the eager
helpers, in health and strength, watching on
the edge of this breath of destruction, unable
to penetrate the space where fire and miasma
fought together against life.
Sorrow for the dead, sympathy for the living,
MIME

all will feel, aad many will convert the feeling
into substantial means of relief; but the deaihs
are from preventible causes. The agony could
all have been avoided. The original cause is
a blunder, or a mistake, or anything so far as
the name goes, but something that should not
have occurred, something that in future should
be prevented; a policy that always makes
light of life ; and now has led to many deaths;
and the public must not forget that truth
in the present duty of assisting the ruined
mourners.

articles.title: COTTON SPINNER'S FUND.
articles.text:
THE COTTON SPINNER'S FUND.

WE refer to the report of the Committee of
the London Working Men on this subject. They
have received more applications for assistance
from Lancashire already than they can meet
with their present funds. Many of these ap-
plications are extremely urgent. The co-opera-
tive spinners and minders of Preston say that
their society has been associated for many years,
and has 1267 members, of whom 860 are idle,
and the remainder have only two or three days
employment in each week. They have paid away
all their fund which was "a good one" at thu
commencement of the panic, and they are likely
to lose their hall, for which they pay a rent
of £26 per annum, and have a 10s. of poor
rates to meet. The loss of the hall would be,
in several respects injurious, as it supplies
some shelter to idle men in the winter time.

The distress in Blackburn is extremely
severe, and one person writes that difficulty
exists in procuring admission to some of the
" denominational " schools—a great mistake,
unless the schools be full; and the matter
should be examined into by their supporters. At
Blackburn the table of prices has been in some
instances reduced by twenty-five per cent., so
that on account of bad material, the :earn-
ings_ of the employed are very low at the
current rate of wages.
The Overlookers Society of Stockport repre-
sents 2,300 persons, the families of 450 mem-
bers, who urgently appeal for some issiitance
from the trades, in order that they may escape
the necessity of accepting parochial relief.
The efforts of this society to work through
the difficulty without applying for parochial
payments deserve acknowledgement, when a
labour test is offered that might be necessary
in common times, and is extremely wrong in
existing circumstances.

The 'society of Calenderers and Makers-up
in Manchester say, that since its establishment
in 1824 they have always supported their own
members; allowing 10s. per week to persons
out of employment, and 6s. per week during
sickness; and they name six disabled members
who have been paid £395 6s. from the fund.
The society numbers 190 members, of whom
60 only are now employed, and they contribute
4s. weekly to the fund: 20 are on short time;
and 110 are entirely out of, work. The exist-
ing payment to the members is now taken from
the sick and funeral money, which must be
soon exhausted. During the last twelvemonths
the receipts of the fund have
been £7o4 9s. 4d.
And the expenditure has

been

1,170 14 5

Loss £466 5 1
The expenditure at present exceeds the in-
coine by £25 per week.
These men have not yet either accepted or
received assistance from any fund, for the
110 members out of employment. The sub-
scriptions sent by the working classes to the
Central Fund, at Manchester, or the Mansion
House Committee here, are useless to them.
They are not counted among the 430,000
recipients of general 0/ parochial relief, but
they invite their fellow workmen to assist
them, feeling that they can receive such aid
without destroying their independence. The
circumstances of this society are those of
many more. We have repeatedly mentioned
the fact that the members of trades' societies
are making large contributions from their owu
accumulated funds, and taking nothing from
the general and parochial funds; but it is
absolutely necessary to support these societies,
or submit to their destruction. For that
reason we feel that the working classes who
are members of similar societies should aid
their fellow labourers, so far as they can con-
tribute in maintaining their independence
through this emergency unimpaired; and that
is one object of the special fund, now being
raised by the Working Mens' Committee, in
London.

articles.title: AMERICAN CONTEST.
articles.text:
THE AMERICAN CONTEST.

An opinion is prevalent in some quarters,
although it has not yet found expression in the
journals, or in the proceedings of cotton-specu-
lators; that the result of the elections and the
correspondence between the British and
French Governments, respecting intervention,
have induced the Cabinet at Washington to
ponder the possibility of a compromise. This
idea is fostered by another idea, namely-, that
the steamer which carried out the last-named
correspondence had also another and important
batch of letters.

The second parcel consisted, according to
this impression, of earnest entreaties from
some of our leading statesmen to the President
and his advisers for a reconsideration of their
policy, in order that the initiative of any move-
ment towards peace might be taken by them.
We remark that, although these
,statements
may be true, yet they are uot shared by the
cotton-dealers of Liverpool, who have pur-
chased at enhanced prices in large quantities
during the week.

articles.title: SHIPPING FATALITIES.
articles.text:
SHIPPING FATALITIES.

A dolorous old ballad begins with the line,
"There was a ship sailed on the sea." The
ship could not have sailed on the land; but it
might have taken a lake or river voyage. The
character of ballad is overmuch associated with
sailings on the sea and unnecessarily so. It
is a serious fact that there never was a good
cause for one-half of all shipwrecks.
We noticed in a recent number the loss of
one ship out of Liverpool two days, with thirty
men drowned; but the ship according to the
law should have carried more than forty men,
although no steps have been taken to vindicate
this law. The cargo was doubtless insured, and
so was the ship. Everything was safe except
thirty lives, and they were lost, but seamen
are very cheap!
The barque, Eliza, sailed from Liverpool
for Monte Video fourteen days ago, and is
heard from by the return of two persons saved
from a crew, including officers, of twenty-six
men. Twenty-four lives are lost, with the
cargo and the ship. The material loss will be
probably compensated or over compensated by
insurance; but the lives are lost. No insurance
issues on them. The Eliza foundered at sea,
but how the ship was "found" or "manned"
will ever remain unknown. Twenty-four men
go down to the depths of the sea—a weekly
tragedy—save by destitute relatives unheard
of or unheeded.

articles.title: STEAM BOILERS.
articles.text:
STEAM BOILERS.

We noticed last week the death of five
persons, and injury to many others, by the
explosion of a steam boiler, in a N orthumbrian
farm yard. The boiler burst, obviously, from
old age, and the want of water. On Wednes-
day week a similar accident occurred at the
Midland Iron Works, Masborough, resulting
in the death of seven men, and severe injuries
to twenty-five. The exploded boiler was on the
high-pressure principle, being the only one of
the kind in the establishment, and likely, on
that account, to be neglected.

The public, and especially workmen, need to
recognise the fact that accidental explosions
seldom occur. An accident is extremely im-
probable.

Explosions proceed from careless supervision
or inadequate material. Not a single boiler is
in operation to day without gradually becoming
inadequate. Iron wears like all other created
things. Its wears rapidly under the steady
action of fire and water, and with degrees of
rapidity depending on the nature of the water.
An explosion is far more 'expensive than ade-
quate supervision, but unless some general
law be adopted on the subject we shall go on,
as labour is cheap, sacrificing to economy in
raising steam several hundred live in each
year.

CLOTHING FOR LANCASHIRE.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."

SlR,—The effort made to redeem the day and
night clothes of the Lancashire male and female
operatives, has been already productive of good
results. What are the facts of the case, as they
must be known to every female? The day and
night clothing cannot be worn away by the idleness
of three, of six, or twelve-months. I am referring
to clothing, and especially under clothing, absolutely
essential to comfort and health. Renewals are
frequently required, if people wish to be neat and
nice, and fashionable; but for the mere purpose of
life, clothes are not like quartern loaves, and do not
disappear at once from the earth. They may become
mended and patched, shabby, thin, and torn, but
they arc in existence in some shape. I therefore,'
the female Lancashire operatives have no winter
clothing, they must have parted with them for
purposes very creditable to themselves, but not
altogether so creditable to the nation, which left
industrious persons the alternative of selling their
clothes or starving, from a reason entirely out of their
control. Night clothing, if it be missing, has still
more evidently been put aside to supply pressing
wants. Families require a renewal of blankets and
sheets, and such like things, now and then, but all
know that the bedding of a county would not wear
out simultaneously in a summer, and certainly no
night clothes are ever so thin and worn that they
would not be better than none. Every woman
knows that such things are used after, long after,
the owner thought they were done with, and should
have been renewed; and it is absurd to suppose
that families require a renewal of these necessaries
once a year, or once in seven years. Blankets are
not like coals, or any other commodity, that wastes
rapidly in using, but if they were in use during
1861, they would be of some service in 1862.
I gather from these facts that wherever a defi-
ciency of clothing exists, the stock has been
transferred to obtain ready money at a high rate of
interest. The Lancashire operatives were well
employed, and well paid, up to the latter part of
1861. During the present year, to the present date,
they have had exactly half the work among them
that they had in 1861, but it has not been equally
divided; for, while a number have made full time,
and suffer nothing, except by exertions to assist their
neighbours or relatives, many more have made
inconveniently short time, and a vast multitude have
no work. It Would be a reflection on the habits of
that population to suppose that during their pros-
perity they were not fairly supplied with all absolute
necessaries; and the latter, although less valuable
now than they were in 1861, are probably much
more suitable to their owners than any old clothing
for night or day that could be supplied to them.
Proposals have been made to buy cloth and make
new*clothing, and a considerable expenditure has
been already incurred in that respect.

Dorcas—like many of our ladies and school girls,
are sewing and stitching resolutely to clothe the
poor in Lancashire, who could be easily supplied
for less money than new cloth costs with their own
old goods redeemed. Besides this fact, we have
a certain charitable power in this country—and
especially in this metropolis—which may be over-
strained. Ever since my memory serves me we
have had Dorcas associations in connexion with
nearly all the congregations of London. Of course
they serve two purposes, in doing good to many
deserving orphans, widows, and often to di stressed
sick families; and in bringing womankind together
for a good hard bout of stitching, a little talk—
which we do dearly love—and then tea and toast.
You business people know nothing of all tfie pleasant
ongoings at these nice meetings, where you are
discussed in every possible way, except an
improper way. We are all very proper,
very prudent, anti-scandaldealers, and have no
garrotters of private characters among us—not one
would admit any such person. Farther than this
negative quality, these meetings are, to a certain
extent, religious. "Essays and Reviews," have been
very severely cut up, I assure you, and deserved it
no doubt, while I have been cutting out flannels and
shirtings, and supplying buttons and thread, and
such-like odds and ends, to an industrious circle.
We talk of the Zambesi, and Dr. Livingston, and
Bishop Mc'Kenzie and his conflicts, the slaves and
the Southerners, and Mr. Newman Hall's opinions
of them; also of late, concerning one Dr. Colenso,
a semi-Zulu, converted backwards, I hear, and of
whom the general opinion seems to be that he is a
"Wolf in sheep's clothing ;" but, Miss M. P—.
"Miss P. is above a certain age, and a little strict—
whispered me, on Monday evening,—yes, it was
surely Monday evening,— exnetly last Monday
evening,—and Miss P. whispered,—" An Ass, my
dear." I looked astonished, wondering what the
lady meant, and she repeated it, with additions,
"An Ass,„ my dear Miss Lee, he is, in sheep's
clothing." My friend is not generally censorious,
but is an active benevolent person, (though we
sometimes speak without the book), running here
and there, always doing good; and these societies
are really good institutions, having enough to do
with local wants, which may be neglected in the
pressure of mis-directed efforts for Lancashire.
A clergyman who paid out £172 to redeem the
pledged clothes in his district, writes that they were
good value for £320, so that by this means money
goes farther in helping the operatives to face the
winter than by buying cloth and making
new clothes,
while London needs all the old clothes it can pro-
duce and spare in the relief of its own depressed

articles.text:
classes.

Could not the working men's committees employ
part of their funds in the redemption of the day
and night clothing, now lying useless in the neigh-
bourhood of the Lancashire operativFsF The

question may deserve consideration., for the-re i-b7a--
great want near home ;and If the common and

Ordinary sources of relief are all directed on an
extraordinary calamity, what, please, will come of
our chronic and regular Wants? What will be
done with our own poor people if we be all employed
in the relief of this northern and terrible army of
sufferers? As in no winter is too much done for

London, so in this winter its necessitks are likely
to be entirely overlooked.

EVELYN L.
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

articles.title: ITHIRD EDITION.- SATURDAY EVENING.
articles.text:
ITHIRD EDITION.- SATURDAY EVENING.

ITALY.

TuRIN, Df.e. IL
The following is the list of the new ministry as
published in the Official Gazette :
Signor Farini, President of the Council; Pasolini,
Minister for Foreign Affairs. Peruzzi, Minister of the
Interior; Pisanelli, Justice; Minghetti, Finance;
Della Revere, War ; .Menabrea, Public Works;.
Armari, Public Instruction; Manna, Agriculture ;
Ricci, Marine.
Viscount Venosti, a Milanese, has been appointed
St..cretary-General of Foreign Affairs.
Trunc, Dec. 1.1.
The Italian Parliament reassembled to-day. All
the new Ministers were present. Signor Parini
officially announced the formation of the Cabinet and
its programme, which was received with great marks
of approval.

The following is a summary of the speech delivered
by Signor Farini :--c We shall find in the assistance of
Parliament the necessary authority for accomplishing
the interior organisation of the country, and for
worthily representing Italy abroad. The administra-
tive reforms will be based upon a system of decen-
tralisation and the development ot constitutional
liberties. The first condition of liberty is the mainte-
nance of public order. With unshaken confidence in
the accomplishment of Italian unity, we abstain from
making promises which might not be followed by
immediate effects, and await the course of events,
without illusions and without discouragement. We
shall be careful to maintain alliances whilst preserving
the independence of the country.' Signor Farini con-
cluded by making an appeal for Italian concord, which,
he said, was personified in the King.

articles.title: GREECE.
articles.text:
GREECE.

ATIIRNS, Dec, 10.
The election of representatives to the Greek Cham-
bers has terminated tranquilly. The national suffrage
continues almost everywhere favourable to Prince
Alfred, who, in the capital :and provinces, has now
received 70,000 votes. Perfect order is maintained.
PARIS, Dec. 10.
The three great Powers, England, France, and
Russia, have agreed to recommend King Ferdinand of
Portugal, the husband of the late Queen Donna Maria
Gloria, to the Grecian people, for their future King.

RUSSIA.
Sr. PETERSBURG, Dec. 10.
The Journal de St _Petersburg of to-day says The
Emperor has received at Moscow many chiefs of the
peasantry. In reply to the chiefs, his Majesty asked
them to be obedient to the authorities, to pay the taxes.
punctually, and to effect their redemption from their
position as serfs as speedily as possible. The peasants
promised obedience on all points. The Emperor said,
in conclusion, that the peasantry must not expect more
liberties than had been already granted them.'

articles.title: AMERICA.
articles.text:
AMERICA.

THE MASSACRE AT PAL3IYRA.—NEW YORK, Nov.
29.—1 n reference to the retaliatory order recently
issued by President Davis, the New York Herald says:
General M‘Neil, utider whose order the ten bush-
whackers were shot at Palmyra, is only a 111ilitia
general, commanding a portion of the Home Guard of
Missouri. Not being a regular United States' officer,
of course the general Government is not responsible
for his acts, and the recent threat of retaliation, made
by Jeff. Davis, will probably be withdrawn when this
fact becomes known at Richmond.'

TRADES' GARIBALDI DEMOXSTRA-
TION COMVITTEE.

I A meeting of this committee was held last evening
at the BEFIIIVE OFFICE, Mr. R. W. Grey in the chair.
Mr. Hartwell, the secretary, reported, from communi-
cations with Garibaldi, the General stated his health
I had much improved, and the exact time at which he
would visit England would shortly be made known.
His offer from Mr. Richardson, Ihe common councilman,
to give a lecture at the Whittington Club, on the
'Life of Garibaldi,' in aid of the demonstration fund,
was accepted, and Messrs. Grey, Castle and Butler
appointed to attend to the details. Full particulari
will be announced. After the transaction of some
business details respecting the demonstration, the com-
mittee adjourned until Tuesday evening, Jan. 1, when
as some important business will come forward, it is
hoped every member of the committee, and as many
delegates as possible, will be present.

CABMAN'S SI7NDAY REST ASSOCIATION.—The fourth
annual meeting of this society was held last evening in
the hall of the Reformatory, Euston-road, Mr. Arthur
Kinnaird, M.P., in the chair. Mr. Charles read the
, report, which stated that at the present time there
were 5,662 licenced cabs in London, of whom 1,863
worked with six-day plates, and 3,797 with seven-day
plates. All cabs with numbers under 10,000 were
seven-day plates, and above that number, six-day
plates. There were 1,300 licensed omnibuses, of whom
only 108 ceased moving on the Sunday. The report-
considered the movement successful. The report was
adopted. About 500 were present, having, previously
to the meeting, been supplied with tea and cake.
THE BARNSLEY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—The trench-
for flooding the mine was completed on Thursday.
The engineers had no doubt whatever but that portion
of the pit where the explosion commenced was com-
pletely inundated; there were, however, evidences of•
fire yet existing in a portion of the upper workings.
Several additions have been made to the list of men in
the pit, which brings the number of dead up to fifty-
nine or sixty. The additional names are—John Lister,
Worsborough, wife just confined, and three children;
James Tonge, hurrier for James Ratcliffe, has left a
wife and two children; —Eastwood, of Jump, a harrier
Phillips, alias Leech, wife and six children.
VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER AGAINST A CAB DRIVER.
—Yesterday evening, Mr. Bedford held an inquest at
Westminster Hospital, on the body of a child named.
Adams, who was killed by a collision between two
cabs in Parliament-street, on Monday last. Edward
Freeman, cab driver, deposed :that OR Monday last, be.
was driving his cab along Parliament-street, having a
fare of three persons inside. The deceased child and its
mother were riding on the box with him. A Hansom.
cab came right in front of him and ran against his cab,
turning it over, throwing witness and the woman and.
child into the road. The cab fell on the woman and
the child. The driver of the hansom cab was drunk._
His name was Edward Hope. He had been taken be-
fore the magistrate and remanded. The jury returned
a verdict of manslaughter against Edward 'lope, the
driver of the Hansom cab.
ANTI-SLAVERY MEETING.—A public meeting was,
held last evening at the Lambeth Baths, Westminster
-
road, under the auspices of the newly formed Emanci- ,
pation Society. The Rev. Newman .Hall, in the chair..
The meeting was addressed by Mr. G. Thompson and
other gentlemen, and resolutions adopted condemnatoty
of the slave system of the Southern States. Andrew
Jackson, the coloured coachman of the Confederate
President, Jeff Davis, was present, having lately made
his escape from his master. The meeting was largely
attended by working men.
FIRE AT CLAPHAM.—A destructive fire took place
yesterday morning on the premises of Mr. Diggles,
13, High-street, Clapham. The premises, with the
furniture, pictures, &c., were destroyed.
TnE PERMISSIVE BILL.—A meeting in advocacy o
the Permissive Bill of the United Kingdom Alliance
was held at Taylor's Repository, near the Elephant
and Castle, on Tuesday evening. Mr. Dibley pre-
sided. Several gentlemen afterwards spoke and re-
solutions in favour of the Permissive Bill were
adopted.

Two FRIGHTFUL DEATHS FROM FIRE.—An inquiry
was held by Mr. Walthew, at the London Hospital,
respecting two deaths by fire which occurred under
the following circumstances :---The first case was that
of Mrs. Mary Burt, who resided at Poplar. She was
sitting up last Sunday night to get everything ready
for the departure by the first train of a lodger for Bir-
mingham. While settling the fire her handkerchief
blazed up, and she placed it unfortunately next her
dress while she crumpled it up in her hands. Her clothes.
were instantly set on fire, and her screams were dread-
ful. Her husband and the lodger rushed downstairs to
her' assistance and cut her clothes off and threw them
into a ditch outside the house, but the injuries received
were dreadful, the poor womans chest and neck in par-
ticular being so burned that the flesh peeled away-
She was removed to the hospital, where she died. The
other case was that of a girl named Rhoda Tinicae,
aged 7 years. She was left in a room with a sister and
a little brother. The latter lighted a cane in the fire,
and set his sister's frock into a blaze. Verdicts of
Accidental death' were returned.

articles.title: 'TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
'TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

'TEE LONDON BOOKBINDERS' STRIKE.
In our late edition last week we noticed the serious
dispute that had broken out between Mr. Bone, the
binder, of Fleet-street, and his workmen, 37 in number.
We then stated that Mr. Bone had for some time
past been making innovations in his shop on the
customs and privileges of the trade, pluming himself
on his expressed intention of turning his establishment
from a binders' stop' into a binding factory ! '
There is a proverb which says, 'That those whom God
desires to destroy he first makes mad.' Mr. Bone, in
his recent conduct, somewhat exemplifies this proverb.
Here is a tradesman, employed by some of the first
houses in the business, on good and remunerative pay,
and surrounded by a staff of about forty skilled
workmen, for the sake of effecting a paltry saving
of a few shillings per week in wages, resorting to
Practices so opposed to the best interests of the trade,
and so repugnant to his workmen, as to drive them ,
out of his establishment, many of them having been
employed there for fifteen or twenty years. On Mon-
day last, after vainly remonstrating with Mr. Bone,
in the hope of inducing him to retrace his steps, 37
skilled workmen left the employ, only one out of the
whole body of men remaining. The places of these
skilled workmen have been filled, to the number of
about a dozen, by the usual tag-rag-and-bob-tail
always in every trade on the alert to supplant their
more honest and reputable fellow-workmen. Two
of these fellows have already suffered imprisonment
for robbing their former employers; and the whole of
them would be dear at any price. Of the 37 men who
left 32 belonged to the London Consolidated Lodge,
four to the West End Society, and one to the Con-
solidated Society; and of the former number thirteen
have already obtained employment in shops' not
'factories.
The Bookbinders' Society are also sending out
circulars to the committee and other influential
gentlemen connected with the Society for the Promotion
of Christian Knowledge, remonstrating with them on
the conduct of their manager in continually beating
down the prices paid for the work done for the society,
which, if persisted in, must eventually tend in a
reduction of the journeymen's wages. In this circular
the society says On various pretences fresh estimates
are continually being required, with the fullest
intention of getting the lowest possible price, without
the least regard whether skilled and experienced
workmen are superseded by boys, or whether, as the
only possible alternative, they are obliged to work for
reduced wages.' It is to be hoped the remonstrance
will have the desired effect.—R. H

TO THE ZINC WORKERS OF LONDON.
GENTLEMEN,—.If you are not already aware of the
fact, then I most respectfully beg to inform you that
there is now, and has been since Nov. 25th last, a com-
mittee formed entirely from or amongst the various
trades of London, to obtain funds for the relief of the
distressed ones in Lancashire. This committee, of
which notice appeared in the Times, Nov. 26th, and
BEEHIVE newspaper, on and since Nov. 29th, is known
as the London working Men's Central Committee,
chief offices, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, and every
other particular relating thereto may be obtained
through the trades' newspaper every Saturday.
My principal reason for addressing you is because I
have heard that many have sent contributions through
Lloyd's to the London Lord Mayor, and those great
ones (by position) will, no doubt, gladly obtain, as
heretofore, not only the praise for receiving, but also
(from many) the paying away in their select way the
working classes' cash; and, also, because I would
urge every working man to contribute through the
Working Men's Committee in preference to any other
medium, whether newspaper proprietors, parsons, or
even Lord Mayors; and, more especially, as I believe
by that plan only will it be certainly known the
precise sum total subscribed by each of the London
trades, and that such is carefully paid away, irrespective
of creed or calling, in the most impartial manner, to the
most needy fellow workmen. Society and non-society
men, let us all unite in this, perhaps, unparalleled
case; and the small sums that each may give un-
grudgingly will, no doubt, prove a great help to those
who, without our little aid, may die—starved in a land
of plenty• moreover, may produce within ourselves
individually a conscientious conviction that we, a
least, have done our 'duty. I would add here, also,
that I believe, under good feeling, and without much
exertion, we, as a trade, may contribute weekly a sum
equally large in proportion to any other trade in Eng-
land.

The total sum collected weekly will be sent through
the Central Committee, and as regularly acknowledged
in the BEEHIVE newspaper. From the zinc workers of
London, to avoid expense, the committee which I refer
to will act gratuitously. The chief office is free of
expense, and, of course, every collector, myself in-
cluded,. will feel a pleasure to collect front every one
belonging to his own trade especially.
Postage stamps will be received by me if forwarded
to 64, Upper Seymour-street, Euston-square; or, I
may be seen to receive even the smallest sums every-
Saturday evening from nine till ten, at 18, Denmark-
street, Soho. I will also, if required, call upon any
zinc worker to receive weekly that which he may have
collected amongst his shopmates. I. am very anxious
to see zinc workers equal to any other body joining
this general desire to show how working men can
render assistance to each other in time of adversity.—
Your's truly, W. FAST.

articles.title: BOLTON JOINERS.
articles.text:
THE BOLTON JOINERS.

The following is the balance-sheet and report of the
Bolton Joiners' Strike, for the week ending November
29th :—Fellow-workmen, —ln presenting this, our
twenty-fourth balance sheet, we are still obliged to
urge upon you the necessity of continuing your kind
and generous support, as the employers are advertising
for men in Ireland to come over to Bolton they being
in want of hands, at 285. per week. This, you will
see, is another piece of delusion upon the joiners of
Ireland to get them here, so that it will throw more
expense on us to send them back again: we have
already sent three men back this week ;—and they
likewise think of filling the town by advertising the
country for men. They (the employers) consider our
Olct lost to us; but we don't, nor do we intend such
a thing if we can only get support, for the men are
determined to have what they asked for, and not to
flinch the least under what they proposed: having
stood out for 94 weeks they consider it would be a dia.
grace to give up the contest now, after the sacrifices
they have made and deprived themselves of the real
necessaries of fife, and are ready to sacrifice more I
rather than submit to the wishes of our would-be
tyrannical masters. We still hope you think as* we
do, that it is not for our town alone that we are
engaged in this struggle, but for the country at large
—for you may rest assured that if we lose our object
other towns must follow in the same destructive
stream. Yet we hope that such an occurrence will
never happen to a number of men who are in unison
with a number of thousands, when the same can be
prevented by a further effort on your part. Total in-
come, £834 16s. 6A-d. Total expenditure, £949 16s. 81d.

MR. PRITCHARD'S JOINERS.-The following 'Appeal
to the Public' appeared in the Daily Telegraph :-
'Sir,---In consequence of the disastrous fire at Mr.
Pritchard's, builder, Portpool-lane, Gray's-inn-lane,
on Tuesday night last, when the workshops were
totally destroyed, thirty-six joiners were thrown out
of employment, with the loss of all their tools. Know-
ing that your columns are always open to cases of
distress' we, through your assistance, appeal to the
public to render a little help to enable us to replace
our tools.-THE JOINERS.-The Grapes, Portpool-lane,
Dec. 10.'-[This appeal has not been sent to us for in-
sertion, and we only notice it to ask a question of those
who signed it. How many of theit number belong to
any of the societies connected with their trade, in all of
which there are special funds to remunerate the mem-
bers for loss of tools by fire? It would be unfair, in
these times when there are so many claims on the
Purees of the benevolent, for men thus insured against
loss to ask further aid from the public; but it would
8' be more monstrous for those who do not belong to
any society to expect the public to come to their aid,
when they had neither foresight, prudence, nor prin-
ciple enough to
provide for themselves against a con-
tingency Such
as that which has happened. Having
refused or neglected to help themselves, by what right
do they claim the aid of others ?-R. H.]

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1862.

D_ESTRUCTIVE FIRES.

FIRE IN TIIE ClTY.—Shortly before one o'clock on
Tuesday morning, a fire of an extensive character
broke out in the vicinity of Little Tower-street, East.
cheap, destroying the whole of Mincing-lane Chambers,
occupied by merchants and brokers, and other premises
that adjoined. The chambers in question belonged
to Messrs. Adams and Co., and stood fronting a small
square approached by a gateway in Eastcheap, and
were connected with passages leading into the Colonial
Chambers, and other commercial buildings in Mincing-
lane. The fire originated in one of the ground-floor
offices. As quickly as possible numerous engines were
brought into requsition ; but although the time was short
the entire suite of offices throughout the whole length
and breadth
,of the building was in flames, and the
different floors commenced ?ailing rapidly. The fire
had also extended into the warehouse of Messrs. E.
Carr and Co., linen sack manufacturers, a building
nearly of the same dimensions as the Mincing-lane
Chambers. In the opposite direction the fire travelled
into the premises of Messrs. Adams Brothers, printers
and machine rulers, &c., which quickly shared, along
with Messrs. Carr's warehouses, a similar fate, being
burned to the ground. At one time the conflagration
assumed a most terrible aspect—three other spacious
buildings, including the Colonial. Chambers, had be-
come ignited, and it was fully expected that the whole
of that property would fall a sacrifice, and the fire
sweep its way into Mincing-lane. The engines played
upon all quarters of the fire, but it was a long time
before the firemen succeeded in stopping its career,
and it was not till 9 o'clock on Wednesday morning
that it was finally extinguished.
FIRE IN GRAYB-INN-LANE.—A few minutes after
five o'clock on Monday evening, a destructive fire
broke osit on the extensive premises of Mr. W.
Pritchard, builder and timber merchant, Portpool-
lane, Gray's-inn-lane. The workmen in the car-
penters' shops were on the point of leaving off work for
the day, when they were alarmed by seeing a large
sheet of flame breaking out in that portion ot the shop
immediately over the engine room, in which the
machinery was situated for driving the saw mills.
The shop being full of shavings and light wood, they
bad scarcely time to give the alarm before the whole
shop was in flames, and they were compelled to make
a precipitate retreat, a few only of those nearest the door
being able even to snatch up their hats and coats. The
alarm spread through the neighbourhood with great rapi-
dity, and in less than ten minutes a large body of the men
employed in Messrs. Reid's brewery, in the adjoining
street, came round to the aid of Mr. Pritchard's work-
men, while another body set to work, and having
manned the powerful engine belonging to the brewery,
brought the pipes over the roof of the brewery, and
poured a copious stream of water from the brewery
tanks on to the burning premises. There being a
plentiful supply of water, the firemen succeeded in
preventing to any great extent the fire from spreading
beyond the premises where it originated. These,
however, with the whole of the valuable stock and
plant, were entirely destroyed, amounting in value to
several thousand pounds. The whole of the tools of
the carpenters, 36 in number, were also destroyed. By
nine o'clock all further danger was at an end, at
which time the whole area on which the timber yard
and workshops stood, about an acre in extent, was one
mass of burning ruins, emitting dense volumes of
smoke, blinding all who were within a distance of some
hundred yards. The fire is said to have originated
from the overheating of the shaft of the engine-room,
which caused a quantity of shavings and sawdust
lying close alongside of it to ignite. The rooms and
scanty furniture of the poor people thickly inhabiting
the surrounding houses in Verulam-street were much
damaged by fire and water.

GENERAL GA_RIBALDP S HE .41.771

GARIBADfS Vim ro ENGTANIL—The presence of
this illustrious patriot in this country may shortly be
looked for.

GARIBALDI.—A friend writes from Turin, Dec. 5,
I have received a letter from the General to day. He
says he is going to get on horseback, and that he will
soon return to his blessed solitude in Caprera—which
signifies that he is better.'
lATTEn FROM GARIBILDI.—The following letter has
been received in reply to resolutions forwarded to
General Garibaldi from a public meeting at Norwich:
—' Pisa, Nov. 30.—Sir,--I beg to express to you and
your friends, and to the British public, my sincere
gratification for the sympathy you show to me and to
the Italian cause. Born in a free and glorious country,
you have noble feelings. You give your hearty
support to a people struggling for liberty and inde-
pendence.—Believe me, yours devotedly, G. GARIBA.LDI.
—J. J. Colman, Esq., Norwich, Sheriff, Carrow
House.'

GARIBALDI AND AMERICAN SLAVERY.—Mr. John
M'Adam, of Glasgow, has received a brief letter from
Garibaldi, dated Pisa, 3rd instant, in which the general
says :—‘ You may be sure that had I accepted to draw
my sword for the cause of the United States, it would
have been for the abolition of slavery, full, uncon-
ditional. lam most thankful to your gallant country-
men for the numerous proofs of sympathy they have
given me. I know that no people better than the
Scotch sympathise for those whcise struggle is for civil
or religious liberty.'
GARIBALDI'S SON MORTALLY WOUNDED.—TIIO Turin
correspondent of the Times, writing on the 9th, says:
--‘ A calamitous duel has been fought to. day near
Turin between Menotti Garibaldi, the hero's eldest son,
and that Colonel, no* Brigadier-General, Pallavieino,
who attacked the volunteers at Aspromonte. This
latter had given offence to the officers of Garibaldi's
staff when he said in his report that while the combat
raged these officers were busy sharing the contents of
their chief's military chest among them. Menotti
Garibaldi is said to be mortally wounded in the side;
Pallavicino is also seriously hurt. Other letters from
Turin throw discredit on the statement that serious
injuries were received by the combatants.

articles.title: CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
articles.text:
CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-

GENCE.

THE SHEFFIELD AND lIALLAMSHIRE ANCIENT ORDER
lOF FORSTERS' CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—A petition to
wind up the above society came on for hearing last
Saturday, before the Master of the Rolls, on the ground
of inability to pay its debts. The society was consti-
tuted under the Friendly Societies Act, but not regis-
tered under the Industrial Act, 1862. Mr. Roxburgh,
in support of the petition, contended that the jurisdic-
tion to wind up was under the Companies Act, 1862,
and not under the Industrial Act, inasmuch as the 17th
section of the latter act giving jurisdiction to the
county court applied only to companies registered
under the Industrial Act, which was not the case with
this company. The Master of the Rolls was of opinion
that the jurisdiction of this court was taken away by
the Industrial Act. His Honour, however, gave Mr.
Roxburgh leave to mention it to the Lord Chancellor.
STAINLAND.—On Saturday evening, a large co-opera-
tive meeting was held at Holywell Green, to celebrate
the opening of the stores in this neighbourhood. The
meeting was preceded by a public tea, at which upwards
of 200 sat down. This being over, the chair was occu-
pied by the president of the society (Mr. Hodgson).
Mr. Akroyd, the secretary, read the report, after which
the following bpeakers addressed the meeting, viz.,
Mr. David Eccles and Mr. Whiteley, of Sowerby
Bridge, and Mr. A. Stradling, of Halifax.
KEIGHLEY. CO-OPERATIVE MANUFACTURING COM-
FANY.-The members of this company still go on with
their payments, and on Thursday about five acres of
ground suitable for erecting a mill, &c., was purchased
by them.

articles.title: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FORESTERS.

LONDON.—On Wednesday evening last, the members
of Court Victory, 2,952, held at Bro. Greenwood's,
Myrtle, Ashford-street, Hoxton, had a very large
meeting, on the occasion of presenting a testimonial
(consisting:of a very elegant time piece) to Br. Wm.
Masterson, P.C..R., in appreciation of his services to the
court during the years 1861-62.
BRISTOL.—The first anniversary of Court Bristol
Castle was held on Monday, at the Old Castle Tavern,
Castle-street, when about forty gentlemen sat down to
an excellent supper. After the cloth was removed,
Bro. W. Warman, C.R., was called to the chair; and
the usual loyal toasts having been given and responded
to, the chairman said the most pleasant part of his duty
that evening was to present to Bro. John Snary, on
behalf of Court Bristol Castle, a testimonial, which
consisted of a very handsome silver patent lever watch,
manufactured expressly by Bro. A. Fish, of Clevedon.
litriz.---A° lecture on 'Life's Stern Struggles' was
delivered by Bro. Cornelius Backwell, P.D.C.R., be-
fore the members and visitors of Court Angel, No. 538,
on Tuesday evening last. On the same evening, this
court kindly voted the handsome sum of ten guineas
towards the fund for the relief of the distressed opera-
tives of Hull; and a resolution was passed that sub-
scriptions be solicited from each member of this court
towards the same benevolent object. Although an
appeal had been made for the Lancashire operatives, it
was considered that Hull had great claims on the
benevolence of the public. The courts in Hull
(numbering seventeen) are now making subscriptions
from their funds and individual members towards the
the relief of the Hull distressed operatives.

ODD FELLOWS (M. U.)
HALIFAM.—On Saturday evening last, Mr. W. H.
Emmet, and Mr. S. P. Norris were initiated as honorary
members of the Loyal United Brothers' Lodge, No.
4,912, held at the Stannary Inn. After the ini-
tiatory ceremony, Brother J. R. Ingram was called to
the chair, when the remainder of the evening was spent
in a convivial manner.
ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A SECRETABY OF A
LODGE AT WESTON-SrPER-MARE.—George Wm. Map-
stone, a cabinet-maker, and late a member of, and secre-
tary to, the Star of the West Lodge of Odd Fellows,
appeared at the Town Hall, on Tuesday, before Messrs.
R. A. Kinglake and Rockett, in answer to a summons
charging hint with embezzling 14s. the property of the
lodge. He was committed for trial.
METROPOLITAN BENEFIT SOCIETIES ASYLUM.—This
building, in the Balls-pond-road, Islington, has been
thoroughly repaired and embellished, and a handsome
iron railing erected in front, added to which the com-
mittee has invested £7,000 as an endowment fund, the
income of which is to be paid to the inmates.
