Mn. GEORGE MYERS AND THE IIoUR SYSTEM.—Mr.
Amos, a member of the Amalgamated Carpenters'
Society, No. 1 Lodge, informs :us of an attempt made
by Mr. Myers to reduce the 7d. per hour to his men at
one of his large city jobs. When our correspondent
was paid on Saturday, he found his money short, and,
on applying to the timekeeper, was informed it would
be rectified on the Monday. On asking for the differ-
ence on the Monday he was told the wages had been
reduced to the rate of ss. per day. He summoned
Mr. Myers for the balance and extra for his lost time
on Monday morning, and, sooner than appear in court,
Mr. Myers paid in the money, with the costs.
NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF PLASTERERS AND THE
Bxenrvz.'—Mr. C. Williams, the general secretary
of this body, in his circular to the trade just issued,
says t---‘ I may allude to the BEEHIVE newspaper, which
has for its object the promulgation of those principles
which must of a necessity be the great lever for rais-
ing the hard working sons of toil in the social scale;
and while calling my brethren's attention to the sub-
ject, I assert that, when writing any letter on the
subject of our National Association for its extension,
the editor very kindly admits the article, and surely,
it being the only medium whereby the toiling masses
can express their sentiments, it is worthy of their sup-
port. I would recommend that each district try to
induce their members to support that which will
grant them space to make known their wrongs.'
NORTHUMBERLAND AND DURHAM MINERS' PERMA-
NENT RELIEF FUND.—A meeting of the workmen of
Cramlington Colliery was held on Wednesday night
in the Primitive Methodist Chapel in connection with
the above fund. Mr. Job Robinson occupied the
chair. Mr. Alexander Blyth, the Secretary of the
Association, read the rules and explained the general
working of the society, and the meeting was highly
satisfied, in proof whereof sixty-six members were
enrolled, and a local society was formed. Mr. W.
Lumsden was chosen secretary, and Mr. Thos. Balks
treasurer. The proceedings terminated after arrange-
ments for another meeting to be held on Monday, the
15th inst. _ _ _

LEATHAM, M.P., ON AMERICA..—II 2 a speech to
his constituents at Huddersfield on Tuesday evening,
Mr. E. A. Leatham, M.P., went at some:length into the
American question. With great force he showed the
wickedness of England sympathising with the South,
and contended that Englishmen could have no friend-
ship for men who were fighting to perpetuate slavery.
Mr. Leatham was loudly cheered, and at the close of
his address received a warm vote of confidence.

articles.title: :TEE BARNSLEY COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
articles.text:
:TEE BARNSLEY COLLIERY EXPLO-
SION.

LATEST PARTICUL xiitS.

During the whole of Tuesday night the men were
busily engaged in making the sluice from the Old
Dyke to the mouth of the colliery. On Wednesday,
at noon, the work had proceeded so far that the water
flowed for some distance, but as the fall near the pit
must be at least fifteen feet, it was not expected that it
would be completed before late at night. A number
of men were also engaged in preparing the material
for sealing up the works. From the body of smoke
issuing from the cupola, and the peculiar smell it has,
there can be little doubt that it is caused by the smoul-
dering coal, which, unless shut out from the air, would
soon burst out and rage through the workings. The
agitation amongst the colliers throughout the district
continues. Numbers who went to work this morning
left off at nine and ten o'clock, and proceeded to the
Edmund's Main. Many of them proffered to go down ,
the shaft and endeavour to rescue the bodies. One
man belonging to the colliery said that he knew where
twelve or fifteen bodies at least were huddled together,
and that he could bring them out. The wives of some
of the men entombed also begged hard that an attempt
should be made to reach the bodies, remarking that
anythinc, was preferable to their present state of
doubt and uncertainty; to see the bodies would give
some relief. The attitude and language of many of
the colliers on Tuesday morning was such, that fears
were entertained whether the officials could prevent
the men from going down, and in all probability sacri-
ficing fresh lives in their desire to reach those beking-
ing to or connected with them. Some considerable
time must now elapse before the bodies can be
recovered.

The following is a list of the missing and killed, so
far as can be ascertained :—George Lawton, steward,
wife and one child; Henry Lawton, his son, deputy
steward; George Firth, Worsborough Dale, married;

smith, ditto, wife and eight children; Matthew Bates,

children; William Rigby, Worsborough Common;
George Columbine, do.; Thomas Roe, do.; Henry Pal-
freyman, Barnsley, wife and six children; George Ogley
and William Ogley, brothers, Worsborough Com-
mon;• George Shaw, Barnsley; William Sharrock,
Worsborough Common, wife and two children; Wm.
Parkinson, ditto, wife and two children; Jas. Ratcliffe,
Worsborough Dale, wife and one child; James Tong,
hurrier, Worsborough Dale; Peter Blacker, ditto,
wife; Benjamin Hoyland, ditto, wife and one child; '
Edward Leech and two sons, wife and five children.;
George Baker, Worsborough Dale; John Hitchin,
ditto, wife and one child; John Schofield, ditto, wife
and one child; Joseph Hawley, ditto, wife and two
children; Joseph Walker, Worsborough Common,
wife and two children; Patrick M'Court, Barnsley;
James Wellow, ditto; William Porter and his son, W.
J. Porter, Barnsley, wife and three children; Robert
Farrington, Oxterly Dyke; Richard Cottle and his
son Nicholas, Worsborough Dale, wife and five chil-
dren; Isaac son.in-law of the above; Richard
Watson, Worsborough Dale, wife and three children;
Richard Hough, ditto, wife and two children; John
Parkin; George Ogden; John Hartley and two
sons, one child; Walter Lockwood, James Eastwood,
wife and two children; William Falding, Barnsley;
George Galloway, Worsborough Common; Geo. Row,
Worsborough; James Ellis and his two sons, Wors-
borough Dale; Charles Thrubbershaw, ditto; Rcbert
Osfield, ditto; George Pickering, wife and eight chil-
dren; It. Oldfield, wife and two children; Thomas
Margerson, boy; William Davey.
A correspondent writes :—I have been to the scene
of the explosion to-day ; they are closing up the
pit tops with 67 men and boys in, and digging a deep
grip to let in the water from the canal, though some
people think the fire is not raging to any great extent.

A CASE FOR TEE DIVORCE COURT.

The lovers of gossip in a certain suburban locality
in the vicinity of Liverpool, have during the last few
weeks had ample material for tattle in a case which
will soon occupy the attention of the Divorce Court.
It appears, from what rumour says, that a gentleman
highly connected has for years been married to an
accomplished and beautiful woman from the ranks of
our merchant princes, but no issue has been the result
of their union. Within the last few months,
however, there appeared every evidence that
the lady would not long remain childless. The
husband suspecting from some cause that all
was not right, made inquiries as to what
persons had been visitors during his absence,
and was told that no other than a near rela-
tive ever saw the mistress during the period he was
from home. Feeling, however, still uneasy in mind,
he resolved to test his wife's fidelity, and accordingly
took a house in a not very remote watering-place. In
a few days after they had arrived at this quiet resort
for the wealthy, the husband received a letter upon
urgent business which required that he should be from
home for several days. Every preparation was made
for his immediate departure, and the truthful, loving
wife was foremost in attending to the requirements of
the journey. The departure had all the appearance of
fact about it: but one of the servants was placed in
possession of the secret that this was a ruse to test
the accuracy of certain suspicions. During the
day upon which the gentleman had undertaken his
supposed journey the lady despatched a missive to
a person in Liverpool, who, it is said, is her cousin.
Under the 'shades of evening' the husband entered
his house while his wife and her near relative were in
the drawing-room. By the aid of his servant the
husband reached his bedroom unknown to anyone else,
and at once secreted himself under the bed. At the
usual hour of retiring to rest the servants were told
that they were not igain required that night, and
that she (the mistress) would 'let. out' Mr. -.
About midnight the two participators in crime entered
the bedroom, and the husband emerged from his hid-
ing-place when they had retired together. He at
once aroused the domestics, proved to them. his wife's
infidelity, and turned her and her relation out of doors.
Both parties are said to be highly connected, and no
doubt when the matter is brought before the Divorce
Court it will create a great sensation in Liverpool and
the neighbourhood.

articles.title: MASSACRE OF FIFTEEN OF THE CREW OF THE PENGUIN.
articles.text:
MASSACRE OF FIFTEEN OF THE
CREW OF THE PENGUIN.

News has reached Plymouth by a private letter, of
the massacre of an officer, twelve seamen, and two
marines, of H.M.S. Penguin, 5, screw gun-vessel,
Lieutenant J. G. G. Mg:lardy, employed in the sup-
pression of the slave trade on the east coast of Africa.
It appears that, in September last, while the Penguin
was in the Mozambique Channel four boats were
detached from her for the purpose of watching some
slavers along the coast, after the usual manner of the
British cruisers. It was the intention to pick them up
again at Fort Durnford, about sixty miles south of the
line. The boats were, however, blown so far north by
the trade winds as 1,200 miles from where they started,
and arrived on Oetober 25 at an Arab village called
Bunder Feluk, near the entrance of the Red Sea.
There, on landing to replenish their expended supply
of provisions and water, they were set upon by the
natives, and the whole of the two boats' crews mas-
sacred. The names of the unfortunate deceased are:
Sub-Lieutenant Fountain°, W. Mitchell (quartermas-
ter), J. Carpenter (gunner's mate), J. Kemp, H. Stote,
C. Kennedy, J.. Watson, J. Childs, M. Jolley, R. Heath,
H. Williams, A. Matthews, and J. Pratt, seamen, and
G. Hotton and C. Foley, marines. When the news
left the Penguin had arrived on the spot to make
reprisals, and had secured twenty of the murderers,
whom it was resolved to hang.

LETTER BROM GARIBALDI TO PROFESSOR NELATON.--
11. Nelaton has just received the following letter from
General Garibaldi :—Pisa, Dec: 5. My Very Dear
Friend,—l owe you'a word of love and gratitude. Your
appearance at Spezzia brought happiness to me, and, if
any doubt of my recovery could ever have crossed my
mind, in spite of the fraternal and learned car? of the
surgeons who attended me, a your interview, so
eminently sympathetic, and at your words, so sub-
limely encouraging, it would have disappeared. lam
much better since the extraction of the ball so ably
effected by our corn-patriot Professor Zanetti, and with
the instruments which you had the kindness to send
me. To-morrow a fixed bandage will be applied, and
I hope to be able very soon to move about upon
crutches. God bless you, as well as those virtuous
men whose humane principles have honoured the
eminent man of science and the benefactor.—Your
devoted, G. GARIBALDI.

THE THEATRES are all busy with the work of pre-
paration for the Christmas entertainments. Pantomim
lo to be the order of the day at Drury Lane, Covent
Garden, Haymarket, Princess's, Surrey, Victoria, and
the City and East-end houses. The Adelphi, St.
James's, Olympic, Lyceum, and Strand, will aim at
the more classical burlesque. Mr. Falconer, leaves
the Lyceum for Drury Lane, M. Fechter succeeding
him at the former place. Mr. D. Boucicault also opens
the new theatre in Westminster-road, late Astley's.
Next week we shall give some particulars respecting
the new pieess, and matters theatrical' will in future
receive due attention in these columns.

EGYPTIAN lIALL.—Mr. Edmund Yates, the son of
the late Frederick Yates, and Mr. Harold Power, eon
of the late Tyrone Power, on Monday last opened an
entertainment at the above hall, entitled An Invitation
to an Evening Party and the Seaside.' It is full of
character and was very successful.

I ANOTHER DISTURBANCE AT CHESTERFIELH.—The
murder of Cooper at Chesterfield seems destined to
produce permanent ill-feeling between the English and
Irish of this district. On Tuesday the workmen at
some pits at Sheepbridge, about twe miles north of this
place, rose in a body and ordered all the Irish from the
works. The latter resisted, and a desperate fight en-
sued. Ultimately the Hibernians were vanquished and
forced to take refuge in flight. The English then re-
turned to the works, collected the tools of the defeated ,
Irish, and sent them after them in a cart. A similar
affair also took place at Dronfield on Tuesday, and at
I Clay Cross and Alfreton disturbances have also taken
place, it being the iatention of the Derbyshire colliers
to drive the Irish to seek for work in some other county.
I The exasperation felt by these rough men at the
cowardly murder of Cooper is not easily described, but
the feeling against the Irish is rapidly spreading.
A POLICE CONSTABLE SENTENCED TO PENAL SERVI-
TUDE—AU ex-police officer, named Joseph Scott, was
sentenced to three years' penal servitude, by Mr. Com-
missioner Gurney, at the South Lancashire Assizes, on
Wednesday, for forgery. In connection with the
police force, of which the prisoner was a member, a
sick and burial. society had been established, and having
been appointed its secretary, he broke his trust, and
forged various certificates of death, in order to obtain
SUMS of money belonging to the proprietary.
GROSS INHUMANITY OF A MOTHER.—VERDICT OF
MANSLAUGHTER.—Mr. H. Raffles Walthew resumed
the adjourned inquiry at the Wellington Tavern,
Canon-street, St. George's-in-the-East, respecting the
death of Margaret Jackson, aged fifteen months, who
died from starvation and neglect in the workhouse of
St. George's-in-the-East. The mother of the child
was present by the authority of Sir George Grey, the
Secretary of State, in charge of the police (Inspector
Allison) of the K division. After a deal of evidence,
the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against
Margaret Jackson for calming the death of her off-
spring. The prisoner was then fully committed for
trial at the ensuing sessions of the Central Criminal
Court, Old Bailey.
THE Vicnits OF PALMYRA. —lt is stated that one
of the victims ordered to be executed at Palmyra, Mis-
souri, on the 18th ult., by the Federal General M'lsTeill,
was a man who had a wife and several children de-
pendent altogether upon his daily labour for their sup-
port. A young man, knowing the condition of the
family, offered himself as a substitute for the husband
and father, was accepted, and was one of the ten who
were shot.

articles.title: LAW INTELLIGENCE,
articles.text:
LAW INTELLIGENCE,

COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH.

(Before Lord. Chief Justice Cockburn and a Special
Jury.)

HALL V. TEMPLE.-ALLEGED LUIVACY.

This case was brought to a conclusion on Tuesday,
having occupied the Court for four days. It was an
action brought by Mr. Hall against a physician, Dr.
Semple, for having caused his incarceration in a
lunatic asylum; by signing a certificate of plaintiff's
insanity, at the instance of his wife, and in the absence
of any direct proof. Matrimonial disputes was the
origin of the affair. The jury acquitted the defendant
of any malice, but found him guilty of negligence, and
gave plaintiff damages of £l5O.

articles.title: COURT OF EXCHEQUER. (Before Chief Baron Pollock.)
articles.text:
COURT OF EXCHEQUER.
(Before Chief Baron Pollock.)

RICKETTS V. STONE. -DOE GILT/ V. S TONE. -ACTION

FOR FALSE IMPRISONMENT.

These actions both arose out of the same affair.
Ellen Ricketts, the daughter of a publican at Clerken-
well, accompanied by a young man named John
Doughty, went to the Foresters' Fete at the Crystal
Palace on the 19th of August last. In the evening,
finding great crowding at the station, they walked to
Anerley, and, while waiting for the train, a Mr. Stone,
the defendant in the present actions, charged Doughty
with stealing his watch, and both he and Ricketts
were taken to the police-station at Norwood. Next
morning they were brought up at Lambeth Police-
court, and Mr. Stone swore that he found Ricketts'
hand in his pocket. Mr. Elliott remanded them both
for a week, and they remained in prison during that
time, bail not being admitted by Mr. Norton, to whom
application was subsequently made. On the re-hearing
of the case the two were discharged, and now brought
these actions. The defendant repeated his statement
as to finding Ricketts' hand in his pocket, and also as
to Doughty having said he believed he knew who had
the watch.—The jury, however, found for the plaintiffs
in both actions, giving Miss Ricketts £25 damages, and
Doughty £l5.

articles.title: COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.
articles.text:
COURT OF BANKRUPTCY.

(Before Mr. Registrar Hazat.)
RE EDMUND O'ROURKE.

This was the day appointed by adjournment for
hearing the application on a rule to set aside an order
which had been granted by the late Insolvent Court
to Mr. Edmund O'Rourke, known as Falconer, of the
Lyceum Theatre. Mr. Keene now stated that on the
last occasion the matter was before Mr. Commissioner
Fonblanque, who had suggested that some arrangement
should be made between the parties. That, however,
had not been done, and it was now agreed upon by
all parties that an adjournment should take place until
the return of that learned Commissioner. The
Registrar: I think we had better adjourn the matter
generally, as I wish to spare the parties the trouble of
coming again. Mr. Keene assented to this and left
the court.

SOUTHWARK COUNTY COURT.
(Before Mr. Whitmore.)
AMALGAMATED CARPENTERS' SOCIETY v. J. LEA.—
In accordance with the decision of the Judge pub-
lished since last week, application was made by the
plaintiffs to the defendant for the delivery of the books
to Applegarth, the present secretary of the society.
The defendant kept out of the way, and could not be
seen. Application was therefore made to the Judge
for a.compulsory order, and the case came on before His
Honour on Thursday. Mr. Joyce, the counsel for the
defendant, in showing cause why the order should not
be made upon him, produced no fresh evidence, but
urged that he had the power of appeal. His Honour,
however, assured him he had not. The Court had full
jurisdiction under the Act. He should make an order
on the defendant, Lea, to give up the books to Apple-
garth, the present secretary, on or before the 18th inst.,
and in default of his so doing he should inflict upon
him the penalty of £25.

articles.title: ASSIZE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
ASSIZE INTELLIGENCE.

NORTHERN CIRCUIT.—LIVERPOOL.
(Before Mr. Commissioner Gurney, Q.C.)

CHARGE OF FRAUD AGAINST A MANCHESTER BANKER.

Jonah Andrew, who was formerly in business at
Manchester as a banker, was charged with appropriat-
ing to his own use money for which he was bailee.
Mr. Higgin, in opening the case, said the prisoner
was formerly head of an establishment known in Man-
chester as the City Savings Bank,' but that establish-
ment having been discontinued between two and three
years ago, he opened a place of business in Market-
street, which he called the 'City Bank.' He was the
only person connected with the establishment. Mr.
Samuel Lyons had a bill falling due at the Union
Bank, London, and on the 21st October, in the fore-
noon, he went to the priOner's bank for the purpose
of retiring it. He paid the amount, £37 165., to have
the bill retired. Mr. Lyons made the arrangement
with a clerk named Colson, and his strong impression
was that the prisoner was in the inner office during
the time, but of that there appeared to be some doubt.
The money never reached London, nor was the bill
taken up according to promise, for the prisoner sus-
pended payment the very next day, Oct. 22; and this,
Mr. Higgin contended, was an offence against the Act
of Parliament 24 and 25 Viet., cap 96, sec. 75.
His Lordship remarked that all they seemed to know
was that the money was paid to a clerk, and that the
prisoner was in an inner office talking to somebody
else. Was it to be inferred that the prisoner knew
the purpose for which the money was paid? He cer-
tainly thought it would be a waste of time to proceed
with the cege unless there was further evidence.

Mr. Higgin having acknowledged the difficulty, and
not being in a position to offer further evidence, the
prisoner was discharged.

NORTHERN CIRCUIT.—DURHAM.
(Before Mr. Justice Keating.)
TILE MURDER NEAR CRESTER-LE-STREET.

Joh* Cox, 25, pitman, and Mary Cox, 27, his wife,
were charged with the wilful murder of Ann Halliday,
an old woman, eighty-two years of age, at Broadmires,
near Chester-le-Street, on Sunday morning, the 10th
of August. _ _

The-learned judge having summed up the evidence
with great care, the jury found both prisoners guilty.
Sentence of death was then passed in the usual form ;
the prisoner Mary , Cox being respited, as she is
enceinte.

The Newcastle Chronicle thus describes the scene in
court after sentence of death had been passed :—When
the foreman communicated the result of their delibera-
tion, the female prisoner gave utterance to a loud
hysterical cry, which echoed through the court. From
the return of the verdict till the sentence was pro-
nounced the wretched woman continued moaning and
rocking her body to and fro, under the influence of her
overcharged feelings. When sentence was passed she
cried out hysterically. The scene that ensued baffles
description. Her husband raised his hand in an
appealing manner, and then, turning round, faced
the body of the court, which appeared to be filled
entirely with his fellow-countrymen. Directly he did
so, a rush was made by the latter towards the dock,
most probably for the purpose of bidding the con-
demned farewell; but, whatever the real object was,
the authorities evidently feared that a rescue was
about to be attempted, and a cry of 'Shut the doors ! '
was accordingly raised, while a strong body of officers
formed round the dock. At the same moment the
male prisoner was forced, although violently resisting,
down the steps leading from the docks to the cells, and
was then taken out of sight. Some time elapsed be-
fore order could be restored, but at last this was
effected, and his lordship then inquired: Is the pri-
soner pregnant? The female warder . She says she
is. His lordship: Impanel a jury to try her. A
jury, consisting of twelve matrons, was accordingly
quickly obtained. They retired to a room, to which
the condemned woman was also removed. After being
absent for some time, they returned into court. and the
fore-matron stated that they found the prisoner was
pregnant. His lordship at once ordered execution to
be respited, and the prisoner was then carried out of
court, apparently in a state of insensibility.

articles.title: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

BOW- S TREET.

THE CASE OF STABBING A POLICE CONSTABLE.-It
will be remembered that Francis Bartlett Graham, an
alleged lunatic, who stood charged with stabbing a
policeman at the Lyceum Theatre, had been twice re-
manded on that charge, and should have been brought
before the magistrate for further examination on Wed-
nesday. Mr. Macrae, barrister, waited on Mr. Henry,
and stated that, acting upon the. instructions of Mr.
Lewis, solicitor, he had made certain representations
to the Home Secretary, which representations were
supported by evidence satisfactory to the mind of the
right hon. baronet. It appeared that Mr. Graham was
in an unsound state of mind, and that he was getting
worse in prison. On this representation the prisoner
had been removed to Hanwell. He (Hr. Macrae) had
thought that it was due to the magistrate in courtesy,
to apprise him of these facts. Mr. Henry was quite
satisfied.

articles.title: MARLBOROUGH-STREET.
articles.text:
MARLBOROUGH-STREET.

ATTEMPTED SmanE.—Maria Bastard, about 20, was
charged with the following determined attempt at
suicide: It appears that on the 18th Sept. last while in
service in Princes-,street, Hanover-square, the young

woman attempted to destroy herself by cutting her
throat with a razor, and with such determination had
she acted that the windpipe was found, on her admis-
sion to the Westminster Hosyit-a.l, to be completely
severed. She now appearea in a pitiable condition,
only able to speak i • a whisper, and had inserted in
her throat a silver tube to enable her to breathe. Mr.
Tyrwhitt said it was quite clear from her demeanour
that she was not fit to be at large, and ordered her
to be taken to the House of Detention for a week on
remand.

articles.title: WESTMINS":IIR,
articles.text:
WESTMINS":IIR,

CHARGE OF BIGAMY. —John Ebenezer Weston.
Guymore, a carpenter, was charged with intermarry—
ing with Sarah Packer, his former wife being stilt
alive. On the 25th of December, 1853, prisoner was
married to Caroline Seed, at St. Pancras Church, Eus-
ton-road, in the name of Weston. He deserted her,
leaving her with three small children, three years ago,
and in January last was married to Sarah Packer, who
is entitled to some property in a few days' time. Both
wives were in court. The second had a child in her
arms, and was stated to be also in the family way.
Prisoner was committed for trial.

'A SKELETON IN EVERY HOUSE!—A dirty-looking
. woman, giving the name of Mary Ann Everett, was
charged with being drunk and creating a disturbance..
I Police-constable 329 B, said that at half-past seven in
the evening he heard great screams in Belgrave-place,
and on going there found the defendant, who com-
plained that her daughter had struck her. She had
been previously in the hands of the police and let go.
A gentleman was now present at whose house she
had made a great disturbance. Mr. Craven, of St.
Michael's-terrace, Pimlico, said: On arriving homc
that evening, I found this woman in my house, and
my wife in a dreadful state. I found the defendant.
had been in the habit of coming to the house and, by
intimidation extorting money from my wife. She had
been there before in the course of the day, and had
-
refused to leave. She then had her taken to the sta-
tion, when she threw stones at her and behaved very
ill. She was then permitted to go at large, but
returned, thundered at the door, and disturbed the en-
tire neighbotrhood. To my great surprise I
discovered that this woman is my wife's mother.
And another very extraordinary thing is that my
wife's sister, another of this woman's daughters, has
been living servant with us, and I did not know it.
For fourteen years I have been deceived.—Mr.
Arnold: It is a very odd discovery.—Complainant: It
is. My wife confessed it. This woman has been for
years living upon me. I may say that she has had
hundreds from my wife. She has been constantly
there during my absence threatening her. Mr. Arnold
ordered the defendant to enter into recognisances to
keep the peace for six months.
On Thursday Mrs. Everett was again charged before
the magistrate by her daughter. It appeared that
after her discharge on the previous day she again went
to the residence of her daughter's husband, and created
a great disturbance. By the statement made by the
daughter, it appears that she has three other children
and a husband living but through her drunken habits
and general misconduct had been discarded by them.
She was ordered to find one surety of a, but being -
unable to do so, was sent to prison for seven days.

articles.title: GUILDHALL.
articles.text:
GUILDHALL.

A WIFE KILLED BY HER HUSBAND. - Robert Wil-
Hams, a licensed victualler, of Aston New Town, near
Birmingham, was brought up before Alderman Hum-
phery, on the charge of manslaughter. Inspector
Leonard said the prisoner had been apprehended upon
information received from Birmingham, to the effect
that the coroner's warrant had been issued for his
arrest upon the charge of killing and slaying his wife ;
and, as the prisoner answered the description given
of him in the Gazette, and had also been identified by
a witness present, he was at once taken into custody,
Jeremiah Beach, a licensed victualler, of Wolverhamp-
ton, said he had cause to know the prisoner, as he had
come to London with his (witness's) wife. The
prisoner had kept her while his wife was alive in Bir-
mingham, and was living with'hpr now. He (witness)
was present at the inquest, and never saw such an
awful sight as the body of the prisoner's wife pre-
sented, it being one mass of bruises from head to foot,
where he had kicked her, and in addition to two black
eyes she had three of her ribs broken. The jury re-
turned a verdict of manslaughter against the prisoner,.
who had absconded. Prisoner was han.cled over to a
Warwickshire constable, to be conveyed to Birming-
ham for examination.
CLERKEN WELL.

PICKPOCKETS AT THE CATTLE SHOW.—A large num-
ber of thieves, of both sexes, was brought before Mr.
Barker on charges of picking pockets in the New Agri-
cultural Hall, Islington, and in nearly every instance
his worship sentenced each offender to three months'
imprisonment with hard labour.

articles.title: SOUTHWARK.
articles.text:
SOUTHWARK.

ATTEMPTED SIIICIDE.—James Williams, aged about
22, in a most deplorable state, described as a carpenter,
was charged with attempting to drown himself near
Southwark Bridge. On Saturday afternoon last the
prisoner was seen to jump off Bankside by the inspector
of the floating fire-engine, when he pulled off in a boat,
and, with considerable difficulty, succeeded in dragging
him out in an exhausted state, and delivering him over
to Inspector Roe, of the Thames Police, who took him
into custody. The prisoner said he had no friends in
the world, and he was driven to make the attempt on
his life through starvation. Mr. Burcham remanded
him, so that inquiries might be made.

IDEATH OF A FEMALE IN A POLICE CELL.—Soon after
Mr. Combe had taken his seat in the Southwark Police
Court, on Wednesday, Inspector Mackintosh informed
him that one of the prisoners whose name was on the
charge-sheet had died since she was taken into cus-
tody. Her name was Mary Ann Johns, aged about 25,
supposed to be married, with three children, and de-
serted by her husband. At a quarter past three on
Tuesday afternoon she was brought drunk and incapa-
ble to the station-house. She was placed in the cell,
and looked at every quarter of an hour. At half-past
four, when the turnkey went his usual rounds, he saw
the woman lying on the floor, and on raising her found
that she was dead. A doctor was immediately sent for,
who pronounced life to have been extinct about ten
minutes. The deceased had been heard to vomit, and
the medical man's opinion was that she was suddenly
choked.
DEATH THROUGH AN ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO PROCURE
ABORTION.—Mr. J. Payne resumed an inquiry at the
George Coffee-house, Strand, into the death of Ellen
Saunders, aged 39, who lost her life, as alleged,
through the agency of instruments used, to procure
abortion. The case excited great interest, from the
fact that the female doetress in question had been
stated to be the wife of Dr. Goss. Mr. Dickie said he
attended on behalf of Mrs. Ed ward Goss, who was a
regularly qualified midwife, and he held a diploma in
his hand. Mrs. Goss was in attendance, and was
quite ready to answer any reasonable questions that
might be put to her. At the conclusion of the evidence
the coroner summed up, saying there was nothing to
implicate Mrs. Goss, but considered the inquiry would
have a good effect, and put the public on their guard
in the use of means to procure abortion. The jury
then returned the following verdict :—' That the
deceased woman, Ellen Saunders, came by her death-.
through ulceration of the colon, but how it occurred
there was no evidence to show.' .. .
THE INEQUALITIES OF THE POOR-LAW RATING.—A.
public meeting of the inhabitants of the parish of St.-
George-the-Martyr, Southwark, was held on Tuesday
evening, in the New School-room, Lent -street, for the:
purpose of endeavouring to obtain an alteration in the
mode of raising. the funds for the relief of the poor.
The chair was occupied by Mr. Churchwarden Lock.
Dr. Jones, in opening the proceedings, said the pre-
sent system of raising the rates pressed with undue
severity on those who were just a little above the rank
of paupers, and, therefore, ali alteration was required.
Mr. Robert Archer proposed, 'that the present system
of raising money for the relief of the poor of this.
country is founded on error, and gives rise to the most
unjust and unsatisfactory results; that the poor are a
national burden, and ought to be relieved from a
national fund; and that such fund should be 'Reduced.
from a contribution (in the form of a property tax)
from all realised property in the nation (whether real.
or personal) such as that charged to the present pro—
perty tax under Schedule A.' Mr. Barnes having
seconded the resolution, and after some further discus-
sion, the motion was put and carried unanimously.
THE WORKMEN'S STRIKE IN NEW YORK. The
strike among the labouriug population in New York
is extending. The carmen and others employed by
the street cleaning contractors (there is but one clean
street in the business part of New York, and that is
Broadway, all the side and off streets being models
of filthiness and bad paving), have demanded an
increase of wages of 25 cents. a day. The boat-
builders, who have hitherto received 2 dols. a day,
demand 2 dole. 25 cents. The members of the Ger-
man Cabinetmakers' Association demand an increase
of 25 per cent. on their former wages, which they
allege to be no more than a just equivalent for the.
rise in the price of the necessaries of life under the
financial regime of Mr. Chase. The omnibus and car
drivers have resolved to cease running their vehicles
unless in three days their wages are raised 25 cents. a,
day. The boilermakers have demanded a rise, with-
out specifying its amount. The whole of the labouring
population is in a ferment of excitement. Meetings
are nightly held to debate on the measures to be
adopted to bring the 'bosses' to a proper frame of
mind. It is generally conceded that the masters---that
is to say, the 'bosses '—must yield the point in dis-
pute, and that there must be a general rise in the rate
of wages for all labourers and handicraftsmen, under a.
penalty of a general cessation of labour, if not of riote.
in the street. —American Paper.

THE SHIP BI7ILLING TRADES
DISPUTE.

We arc requested to insert the following in reference
to this subject :
BOILER-MAKERS V. SHIPWRIGHTS.

TO TIIE EDITOR OF THE DETONPORT INDEPENDENT.
once more, and I sup-pose for the last time,
through your kind permission, answer A. J.'s letter,
and feel much obliged to him for another opportunity
having been offered me. I am sure that his letter in
your last week's impression m Ist excite the deepest
gratitude in the heart of every one that reads it; its
statements are quite surprising. They read more like
romance than reality,sbut as the source from whence
they come precludes the possibility even of the least
exaggeration, I should think the public would thank-
fully accept its statements, for he has made everything
as clear as moonlight in a Londonfog.
Th 3 attempted reply of my friend A. J., is full of
superfluity, of honied words, signifying nothing, say-
irlg a vain scholastic display, beneath which
runs a shallow sarcasm, which I pass over as un-
worthy of notice, but come at once to the point at
issue.

Now, Sir, in the first place, I will take the Triton
and the plate to which he makes such special reference.
He charges me with trying to mystify the statements
I male in my former letter, which is false, as I made
it more plain in my last. I said the plate cost six
pounis for labour alone, riveting not included, but in
the first letter the words, • 'riveting not included,'
were omitted: so the, last was much plainer than the
first, but being aware that he knows not what to say
in defence, I forgive him, as he is glad to grasp at a
shadow.

2nd. He charges me with telling a falsehood in
Baying that every attempt has been made to baffle any
one from keeping an account of the cost of the Triton;
he asks me how I discovered that such was the case,
which he says was a mere supposition. I think the
reason was stated quite clear enough in my last letter,
and I would ask any reasonable man if he-would not
have come to the same conclusion as myself, when he
saw one day there would be thirty six men working on
the ship, and the next twenty, and the following day
thirty in the forenoon and eighteen in the afternoon—
if such proceedings were not calculated to baffle any
one from keeping. an account. • I-am at a loss what to
.call it.

3rd. He says there were 88 pates fitted on the Tri-
ton in all. Yes,
they
I say so, but not by shipwrights,
as I am positive they have not put on more than 78,
for any one can go and take the number of the old
ones that came out as they are all lying by the dock.
I am quite certain myself about the number of plates,
as I have been over the ship both inside and out and
have seen the new as well as old.

4th. He says the smallest plates weigh 2 cwt., 1
qr., and the largest 5 cwt., which I can prove to be a
gross falsehood, and any one can see it by the follow-
ing figures, taking the largest plate, not the smallest,
which measures 8 feet by 2 feet 4 inches, thick: one
superficial foot of plate weighs 14 lbs. 14 oz., and in
a plate of
,the above mentioned size there are 18 feet 8
inches superficial, making the total weight 2 cwt. 1
qr. 25 lbs., and not 3 cwt.' I qr., as be says. Then
take the thick plate at his own given size 1,-; inch iron,
7 feet 6 inches by 2- feet 4 inAes, the weight of one
foot being 24 lbs. 14 oz., and there being 17 feet 6 in.
superficial, the total weight is 3 cwt. 3 qrs. 17 lbs,, and
not 5 cwt. as he would have it. Now a man that
would make such- statements as he has done reminds
me of the school-master who asked his pupil how long
he considered a man could live -without brains? The
boy coolly turned to his master and asked him—what
is your age, sir? So I think if I knew the age of A. J.
I could answer the question.
sth. Respecting the painting, which he says is also
, false, I do not know whether he calls red lead and oil
mixed paint or not, but one thing I do know the ship
has been coated four times with red lead and oil, and
- -twice with paint; he can have it that way if it pleases
him better, and one coat of composition. They were
.careful that she should receive the coat of composition
before taken out of dock, or it would have been the
same with her as it was with the Princess Alice; they
would be obliged to dock her again and employ smiths
or boiler-makers to stop the leakages.
6th. I feel rather surprised that A. J. admits the
fact stated by me respecting the rain water going
through the bottom of the Triton; but he says it was
not enough to damp-a lady's pocket handkerchief had
it been used to take it up; but if such was the case
they were not very handy at stopping holes, as they
were there one whole day cutting and putting in rivets
and cutting two plates; but perhaps they resemble the
tinker, who mends one and makes three.
7th. A. J. appears to be very conversant with the
history of past ages, for when he cannot find a way of
escape, being attacked by his opponent, he tries to
draw away the attention of the public from the point
at issue by relating a nice little anecdote, which he
has done with respect to the statements made in my
last letter, about plate levelling, which, he says in his
first letter, was easily effected by the most simple
method, but which I can prove the shipwrights were not
capable of performing at all; as they were there trying
week after week, and spoilt plate after plate, until
strength and patience were exhausted, and they were
compelled to give it up altogether, and convey the
plate from the Dockyard to Keyham, a distance of half-
a-mile, to get them levelled! But he says the public
should know that since the discharge of the two platers
the work has been done by labourers' but he does not
say what part they perform; perhaps it is not con-
venient as it will not suit his purpose, but as he does
not tell the purpose I will,—the labourers lift the
plates from the ground and place them on trucks and
take them to the 'rolling mills, where the plates are
passed through, add then the labourers return them to
the place from whence they took them. But lam
really surprised that he should so far forget himself as
to admit the capability of labourers performing work
-which they could not do themselves but such is the
case. I can get twenty labourers at themselves,
whose
wages do not exceed sixteen shillings per week, capable
of doing any kind of iron work better than either
twenty shipwrights in the dockyard!!
Taking a survey a few days since I felt anxious to
learn what wonders the shipwrights were doing on
board her Majesty's ship Ocean, so I just took a bird's
eye view, and it reminded me of a description I had
read of the days of Noah when he first started ship-
building, for I am sure that he and his co-operators
handled their tools and materials equally as well as
the shipwrights do in putting up the plates to form
the bulkheads; now they had the wrong end of the
plate before, and then it was the wrong side ;in
fact they scarcely knew the right from the wrong side,
or the top from the bottom, when they saw it,—one
poor fellow there amused me more than all the rest,
for he was trying to cut a large plate with his hand
saw ! ! It was, as A. J. says, 'I could scarce believe
my own eyes.' I was once more reminded of the old
saying, that truth is stranger than fiction, to see a
man with a hand saw trying to cut a large iron plate,
when he had all the modern and efficient appliances
in the kingdom but knew not how to use them. I
hope they will take a little good advice, and not allow
any stranger to go on board to see them at work; but
ehould they do so in future, I hope they will let the
strangers understand that they are shipwrights learn-
ing to do their work.
A. J. says that the shipwrights feel anxious that the
work done by theta on the Ocean should be compared
with a similar job performed by boilermakers on the
Liverpool. It would be very bad, indeed, if they could
not make up a little of their deficiency by talk; they
much resemble the schoolboy who has just completed
his first lesson in drawing; he looks on it with de-
light, and considers it the very height of perfection,
the lines are so straight, and the colouring so clear,
that he feels anxious that it should be compared with
the original, for to him it is without fault; but when
it comes under the eye of one capable of judging be-
tween each, he sees at the first glance that the one was
performed by a man of genius, and the other was but
the first leeson.

And respecting my statements about the Princess
Alice, he says the smiths did not refuse to go and re-
pair the defects of the shipwrights. Ido not wonder i
at the smith denying what he said, as the have been
strictly caution“l against giving any Information.
They must see all and say nothing. But A. J. must
have known the very man, or how could he have asked
him about it, as there were more smiths besides him
working on the ship, and, respecting the red lead, he
says by the smith's own statement it was resolved into
a very simple matter, so that anyone can see at a
glance that my statements were correct.
But, air, it is quite immaterial as to the words used
by the smiths; they did not alter the facts stated by
ma, that the shipwrights had the Princess Alice under
repair for two months. and called her finished; that
she was taken out of dock and that they were com-
pelled to dock her again or she would have sunk; that
the shipwrights were not allowed to go on board to
work after, but that the smiths repaired the defects
made by the shipwrights. This he cannot deny.
Neither can he deny the total cost of the Triton,
which I proved so clear to be £6 Is. 3d. per plate,
great and small, for labour alone; but let your readers
see how he tries to get over the difficulties by taking
the area which they cover and comparing it with the
new stern post on the Princess Alice put by boiler
makers. Now every rational man that ever saw a
vessel knows that there is more work on two feet of
the stem or stern of a vessel than there is in six feet
on the sides. This statement of his shows most con-
clusively, that my opponent knows but very little
about the experimental part of work, or he would
never have made such an assertion. Taking that
into consideration I forgive him,

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 18( 2.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 18( 2.

Now, Sir, the boiler makers had to put a new
wrought-iron stern-post ten feet long and six new
plates which he says covers an area of 37 feet, and
the job was so difficult that they were obliged to put
on six plates, when two plates of the Triton would
cover the same space according to his own measure-
ment. So the boiler makers had three times as many
joints to make, and three times as many rivets besides
the stern post, a job they were not capable of perform-
ing at all, but it is a very poor defence when a man is
obliged to tell a falsehood to cover his faults. A. J. in
his first letter says they were a fortnight about the
job, and in his last he says they were nine days.
A. J. says,—Let boiler makers stick to their boilers,
I can tell him that we are workers of plate and angle
iron; it matters not into what shape the materials are
required, whether a boiler, bridge, cylinder or vessel,
and as workers of such materials we are best adapted I
to form iron into any shape. As an illustration, a
gentleman takes a contract to build a battery, the said
battery to be composed of stone and mortar, but in-
stead of his employing masons to perform the work
because they build houses, he employs carpenters,
tailors and shoemakers to build the battery. Now
wh,at would every sane man think of such proceedings ?
he would take the contractor to be a very silly man,
and say that notwithstanding tailors and carpenters
and shoemakers may be intelligent men, one mason
would perform more work and much better, than
either three of the others; the reason is obvious,
the mason has been accustomel to the materials, and
therefore the most fit person to work it, whether in a
house, a bridge, or battery; andthe same by every
branch of profession. 3-17
A few words on his last remarks ; yes, let me re-eche
in the ears of my censor that his 'first impression' was
right—and glad am Ito confirm that impression. I
am a member of that society—his shortsightedness
would tell us to act upon, Discretion being the better
part of valour.' But we have learnt even a wiser and a
noble lesson. We are not actuated by those selfish
principles his disregard of truth would endeavour to
prop up. We can defend the fortrede of our Domain'
by a moral influence that A. J. is evidently a stranger
to. Allow me to tell him that all our powers are united
to promote the downfall of false and pernicious prac
tices and usages of evil, corrupt, and oppressive
institutions. We fear not the cold repulsive look,
or the open rebuke of unscrupulous antagonists.
By the principle of a strong, honest and earnest
union of our fellow workmen we ,can look upon
discouragement—the loss of domestic, social,. or com-
mercial friendships—with the strong steadfast gaze
of men guided by the holy principle of and truth.
Glad am I that I have opened the eyes of your
otherwise blind correspondent, and that he '.rejoices'
at the discovery of our acknowledgment, that we have
'moral and intellectual faculties,' senses which he
evidently once believed belonged only to the select few
it was his privilege to move among. Let me tell him
that passion' with us has ever given place to principle,
that we believe the moral law shall take the place
of universal selfishness, that the age of might and
right will be followed by the age of a true brotherhood,
and that we have done our-duty when we have exposed
the falsehoods by which we have been assailed, know-
ing that rectitude and moral courage will guide us to
do battle in this age of strife.—Adieu,

EXTENSIVE 13U11GL..48Y IN LEEDS.

On Saturday morning a man named James Kirk
was apprehended by Inspector Hunt, of the Leeds de-
tectives, in a publichouse near Bradford, on a charge of
having taken part in the burglary at the Aire and
Calder Navigation Company's offices in Leeds, on the
21st ult., when upwards of £BOO in bank-notes and gold
was stolen. On the morning after the burglary a
youth, aged 17, named Robert Pearson, who on the Bth
of November left the Aire and Calder Company's ser-
vice, was apprehended by Inspector Hunt at his
father's •residence, Eldon-place, Leeds, and he shortly
afterwards, by the advice of Mr. Granger, his solicitor,
made a confession of having participated in this
burglary, being assisted by Kirk and another man
(named James Spence), who is still at large. Mere-
over, he took Mr. Granger, and Hunter,. the detective,
to a hedge near the Archery-ground, in Leeds, and
there produced from under some leaves in the hedge-
bottom £220 in bank notes, which he had received
as his share of the proceeds of the burglary. On Monday
Kirk was examined before the sitting magistrates. at
the Town-hall, Leeds, when Pearson, the accomplice,
was admitted as Queen's evidence. He gave a minutely
circumstantial account of the depredation, and stated
that he first became acquainted with Spence, who is a
publican's son in Leeds, about three weeks before the
burglary. having first met him at a betting house in the
tovvn. They had some conversation about the Aire and
Calder Company's premises, and the night follpwing,
when they met together, Kirk joined their company..
Spence and Kirk, both of whom are much older than,
Pearson, then asked him (Pearson) where the key& of.
the Aire and Calder Company's safes were kept, and he
told them, In the manager's house,' which forms part
of the office premises. It was then agreed that they
should rob the place, and Spence and Kirk went down
to the offices the day before the burglary in order to
reconnoitre- At night they told Pearson they had
got the opportunity to see- how the windows were
fastened by going into the office and inquiring
for a person of whom they pretended to be in
search. On the morning of the 21st Spence and Pear-
son went to the offices before the clerks .arrived, and
Spence got into a dark closet under some stairs, but
within the outer and principal, door of the building,
where nothing was kept but firewood, and there he lay
concealed until a. little before 6 o'clock at night, when
Pearson joined him. They heard the clerks leave and
the offices locked up at 6 o'clock, and soon afterwards
they put dusters on their feet and, with a chisel, screw-
driver, and dark lantern, made their way to a nindow
at the back part of the premises. At 11 o'clock Kirk
came to that window, and they admitted him by it.
They broke open all the office doors and got access to the
manager's drawing-room, where Pearson knew the keys
of the iron safes were kept. Then they had little diffi-
culty in completing their purpose. They found three
bottles-of sherry wine, which they drank, and did not
leave the premises until about 5 o'clock in the morning.
They then went to Kirk's father's house, and Spence
and Kirk directed Pearson to keep watch outside while
they divided the spoil. Though it consisted of a con-
siderable sum in gold, Pearson received only notes.
Spence and Kirk then decamped, but Kirk was appre-
hended,,as before stated, after being at large more than
a fortnight. He had only £lO 16s. in his possession
when taken into custody, and it is said that Spence,
whom the police as yet have not been able to trace, has
jilted him of almost all the money which he received,
as his portion.. Some of the notes found among those ,
recovered from Pearson were on Monday identified by the
Aire and. Calder Company's clerks. Kirk has been
committedior trial.

articles.title: AGRICULTWZAL PROSP_ECTS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTWZAL PROSP_ECTS.

• The weather was tolerably favourable at the begin-
ning of the week, but there was slight rain on the-fore-
noon of Monday, and it was very thick and hazy after-
wards. Tuesday morning was rather inclined to frogt
again, wind south-east; but in the evening it became
softer. In Lincolnshire on that day it was stated :
' The weather since our last has been wet and foggy;
at present the temperature is mild; wind southerly.'
From Northumberland on the same day we hear,.` the
weather continued frosty up to Friday; since then it
has been damp, with east and south-east wind.' There
cannot now be much wheat to plant, excepting in the
very latest districts. The markets do not encourage
farmers to thrash freely; and the short yield, combined
with the low prices, has determined many growers
to hold it over until spring, when the condition
may be materially improved, with some hope of
better prices. The present week's average was
only 475. Bd. on a return of 85,103 qrs.,
against 60s. 3d. on 97,663 qrs. the corresponding week
of last year—a sufficient difference to prevent supplies.
The breadth of land sown this season is to a fair extent,
but it cannot be considered as large as that of last year,
when the plant was acknowledged to be very great, and
of course little or none of that can be appropriated to the
same grain this season. The farmers have found the
yield worse than was anticipated after harvest, and with
the increased breadth, not over a general average of years
can be safely reckoned, in the aggregate quantity; and
had it not been for the overwhelming supplies of fo-
reign, particularly those from the United States and.
Canada, prices of all prime qualities must have been
much higher than at present. The public, therefore, are
enjoying the benefit of a cheap 1., and the farmers have
to put up with a low figure for the raw commodity.
All accounts agree in the plant looking remarkably
well, the sharp frosts frequently experienced in the
month of November having given a seasonable cheek.
Stlll it is feared the mild weather of this week will start
off the growth again, and push them on faster than is
desirable before Christmas. Universally the seed proved
so good that -vegetation commenced quickly when once
the grain had been committed to the ground. The
weather from the middle of the week to the end was
damp and mild, and on Saturday very wet, with the
wind generally prevailing from the south-west. This
appeared to be the state of the weather throughout the
United Kingdom—the barometer being well up,
averaging nearly 30 degs. ; althougb slightly lower
than previously, it did not indicate rain. Nothing
can be worse for thrashing corn than this state
of the atmosphere; and the samples brought for-
ward next week will, no doubt, sufficiently testify this
by their damp condition, much against a good sale, and
rendering the millers shy buyers. The farmers appear
to be more satisfied with the price of barley than of
wheat, for they have delivered this extensively, par-
ticularly in the county of Norfolk, where the demand
has been very,large for the great maltsters in Notting-
hamshire and Yorkshire; choicer qualities have com-
manded higher prices generalin'and those maltsters who
will have such will do well to get into stock whilst
quantity can be supplied. However large the yield, the
great deliveries will tell upon it; and after Christmas
we expect to see a steady falling off up to the end of the
malting season. Intermediate qualities may last out
longer; but more attention is even being turned to the
better sorts, all germinating well this season. There is
only a small portion consisting of grinding quality, but
any deficiency in this will be amply made up by foreign
from the south of Europe.—December 8.

articles.title: SHIPWRECK AND LOSS OF TWENTYFOUR LIV_ES.
articles.text:
SHIPWRECK AND LOSS OF TWENTY-
FOUR LIV_ES.

Two men, survivors of a most disastrous shipwreck,
have been landed at Queemtown, and received into the
Cork Sailors' Rome. On Sunday last the Eliza, a
barque of 760 tons, Captain Smith, left Liverpool for
Monte Video, laden with machinery and coals. Her
crew, inclusive of the officers, consisted of 26 men.
After passing Holyhead the breeze freshened, and it
began to blow strong from the south-east. About two
o'clock next morning the wind grew so strong that
sail was shortened, and at nine o'clock in the forenoon
the three top-gallant masts were carried away. With
the loss of these spars one man was carried overboard,
another had his leg broken, and the third, one of the
two landed at Queenstown, a man named Montgomery,
had his arm dislocated at the shoulder. In an hour after
the ship sprang a leak, and before long she had seven
feet of water in the hold. The ship was then about
midchannel. All hands were employed at the pumps, but
the leak continued to gain at the rate of an inch-and-a-
half every two hours. The mate, an American, named
Burns, urged the captain to bear up for Queenstown, but
the captain refused. For twenty-four hours they con-
tinued in this position, when the captain at last con-
sented, and the vessel's course was changed for this port.
The wind, however, continued in full force, and the
ship laboured heavily. All at once her three top-masts
went by the board, and shortly after the sea began to
make breach over her. One sea swept her fore and aft,
carrying away with resistless ferce• two boats, and no
less than twelve men, not one of whom was ever seen
again. At three o'clock she was completely awash
and sinking. The two seamen who have been saved,
William Lyons, a native of Liverpool, and John
Montgomery, a native of Scotland, got into the life-
boat and cut away the tackle. The boat was driven
clear off the ship, and she had scarcely parted with it
when the vessel went down bodily, with every soul on
board, these two men alone escaping. A small schooner,
named the Aspia, whose captain was also au American
named Smith, and like the lost vessel was bound from
Liverpool to Monte Video, hove in sight to windward,
and picked up the two men. They were received on
board and treated with the greatest humanity. The
schooner getting leaky, she had to bear UD for Queens-
stown to get pumps repaired. At the Cork SAilore'
Home they have been received with that kindness the
institution is intended to show those in their unfortu-
nate position, and every attention has been paid to them
by the hon. secretary, Captain Stuart, R.N., to whom,
that may add, it is owing th there exists such an estab-
lishment. The seafaring inmates of the Home gene-
rously entered into a subscription for the ship wrecked
men, and provided them with a sum of money and
clothes. The survivors were the only two British sub-
jects in the entire crew. All the rest were American,
and all strangers to each other, as they had only been
shipped four days before ler.vi3g Liverpocil.—Cork

articles.title: LOSS OF THE COLOMBO.
articles.text:
LOSS OF THE COLOMBO.

The Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Com-
pany have received the following telegram .
BOMBAY, Nov. 27
•

- -
The Colombo was totally lost on Minicoy, Island (445
miles this side of Galle), on the morning of the 19th
inst. The passengers the crew, and a portion of the
mails were saved. If weather is moderate we hope
to save a part of the cargo. The news was received at
Bombay on the evening of the 26th. The Ottawa, with
two divers, left for the wreck this morning to take the
mails and passengers to Suez. The Colombo was bring-
ing the homeward Calcutta, China, and Australian
mails. The intelligence is brought by the jeddo, which
passed Jubal on Sunday, at 6p.m.

articles.title: GREECE.
articles.text:
GREECE.

The following is the note published by the Journal de
St. Petersbourg on the candidateship of Prince Alfred, a
brief summary of which has been already received by
telegram

Tile question of the choice of. the future Sovereign of
Greece deeply engages the attention of the foreign press.
Even before the National Assembly, which is about to
meet at Athens, has begun to consider the question, can-
didates are put forward, the resolutions of the great
powers prejudged, and a kind of rivalry is even
established between them, as if they were not bound
by common engagements. We think ourselves justified
in affirming that the Russiqn Government has not for a
moment thought of departing from the principle laid
down by the protocol signed at London on February
3, 1830, which excludes from the throne of Greece
the members of the reigning families of three Courts.
The majority of the foreign journals contain contradictory
assertions on this subject. In an article- in a _France,
that journal attributes, for instance, to the Cabinet of
London the initiative of a declaration in that sense to the
two other protecting Powers. We are in a position to
affirm that, as early as the 19th of October, the Imperial
Cabinet formally declared, on its side, that it remained
faithful to the spirit of the protocol of 3rd February,
1830). and that it has not since varied from that attitude.
By a comparison of dates, it will be at once- seen that
this declaration too, closely followed the eventsat Athens
.r it to have been anticipated by any such stepas above
nentioned, and that the Cabinet of St. Petersburg was
zlis first to refer to the principle agreed on in common
and to declare its resolution to observe it faithfully at
:he present conjecture:

anniversary of his career as a musical composer,. the

A NEW Do= FOR THE ThIBER CARRIERS -AT
LivntrooL.—On Monday a m.ew dock for, the use of
the timber carriers in Liverpool was opened at
the north end;of the town. The new dock, in addit:on
to immense quay space, will haveerected on its margin
a large warehouse for the storage of general goods. The

From January 1 to April 2; 1861, the exportE.l, of
-letroleum oil from New York. were 50,004 gallons.
-During the first three months of this year the exportanf
this oil from, New York, Philadelphia, and Boston were
2,398,506 gallons—worth nearly £200,000. In April

- MOUNT'S, BAT.—A French barque DTlnion, Barrett,
from Sierra Leone, with oilnuts, for Dunkirk, was
totally wrecked at Portleven en Saturday. The French
lugger, Eliza, of Bordeaux from Swansea, was totally
wrecked on the same day Off Marazion. Several other

GARIBALDI'S RELIGIOUS BLIP.—It is difficult (says
a Germam religious journal) to ascertain the exact re-
ligious belief of Garibaldi. He has too moral and, noble
a character to acquiesce in cold sober Atheism or Ra-
tionalism. Those who know him, maintain that he is
very regular in saying his morning prayers. In reply
to a letter from an Evangelical Christian who called his
attention to a pamphlet entitled ‘.Dottrina Garibalclina,'
which was a parody of the Lord's Prayer, the Apostolic
Creed, and the Ten Commandments, Garibaldi expressed
his entire disapprobation of the irreligious style and
contents of the pamphlet..
THE MANCHESTER BANK FRAUDS.—On Saturday the
unfortunate shareholders or subscribers to the classes '
in connexion with the City Bank of Mr. aonah An-
drew, held a meeting at Manchester to deliberate on
their position. The meeting was numerously attended,
aid, as might be expected, the revelations by the
depositors were most pitiable. It is reported that the
feeling of the meeting was in favour of quietly winding
up the affairs of the 'classes.' At the South Lancashire
assizes on Monday, the grand jury returned a true bill on
that part of the indictment which charged Andrews with
appropriating the moneys of the bank proprietary to his
own use.

SINGULAR ACCIDENT. —A few minutes before eleven
o'clock on Saturday morning a singular accident oc-
curred at the London-road Railway Station, Manchester.
In order to facilitate the erection of a new station, the
contractors have erected a scaffold about 35 or 40 feet
high, to the top of which a six or eight-horse steam-
engine had been elevated, for the purpose of raising the
stonework. In the absence of the driver the engine
was seen to start along the runners, and before any one
could reach the scaffold to stop it, it fell over the end of
the framework and dropped into Store-street, which is
at this point about 35 feet below the level of the
station-yard, so Ithat the engine fell a distance of not
less than 70 feet. It was broken to pieces. Fortunately
no one was injured, though several passengers in the
street had narrow escapes. - -

AUGMENTATION OF THE METROPOLITAN POLICE
FORCE.—In consequence of the numerous garotte rob-
beries and burglaries which of late have occurred in the
suburban:districts of the metropolis, the Commissioners
of Police have decided upon immediately augmenting
the police force by 300 men, and also to attach a corps
of the A reserve to the S and K divisions. It is also
:ntended to increase the number of police doing duty in
the principal thoroughfares of the metropolis and
crowded parts. The men of the X division—a division
temporarily assigned for the International Exhibition,
and many of whom have bad considerable experience—
will be drafted to the different divisions.

FORTUNATE CAPTURE OF A SMASHER' N THE
COUNTRY.-At the Rc-ading borough Police-court on
the Bth a middle-agfd man named Richard Bonner, a
licensed hawker, was placed in the dock, charged with
uttering counterfeit coin on Saturday evening. The
accused succeeded in passing off a base shilling at a
shop in the town, and walked away towards the police
station, but was watched by a m,in named Barnard,
who gave information to an officer, and he was at once
apprehended, and on his being searched in the office no
less than sixty-eight counterfeit shillings and thirteen
counterfeit florins were found upon him. lie was also
in possession of some good money, and had with him a
hawker's licence issued to Richard Bonner, Old Brent-
ford.' The man, who is a perfect stranger in Reading,
was remanded for the purpose of communication being
made with the authorities in London.

LIFEBOAT SERVICE.—PLYMOUTH, SUNDAY NIGHT.—
During a heavy gale from the south-west on Monday, it
was reported to Captain Aylen, R.N., the Queen's
harbour-master, that a foreign vessel was in distress not
far from the Ramo Head. He at once signalled for a
government steam-tug, and ordered the lifeboat of the
National Lifeboat Institution to be launched, which was
directly done. The steamer then took the lifeboat in
tow, and with Captain Aylen went to the ship, which
was at anchor a mile and a-half to the north-west of
the Rame Head, and which proved to be the Dutch
galliot Aromana, bound from Saffer to Falmouth. She
had overshot her port, and being embayed had let go
her anchor, but was fast driving towards the shore. The
lifeboat was found to be of essential service on the occa-
sion, in effecting through the surf a communication with
the vessel. The lifeboat is most highly spoken of by
the crew. The vessel, after some difficulty, was taken
in tow by the steam tug, and safely brought in here
about B'p.m., accompanied by the lifeboat. This is the
first service performed by this fine lifeboat, which was
stationed here by the National Lifeboat Institution in
February last, through the liberality of Miss Burdett
Coutts. The crew of the lifeboat, after this severe trial,
have the greatest confidence in her, both in respect to
her sea-going and rowing qualities.

Lord Feversham (says the Yorkshire Gazette) pre-
sented his celebrated bull Skyrocket to the Leeds
Lancashire Committee. The bull will at once be sold,
and the proceeds added to the fund for the relief of the
distressed.

The funeral of Professor Shaw, teacher of English
literature at the St. Petersburg University, who died a
few days since, has just taken place. A large concourse
of persons were present (and amongst them several
graLd dukes) to pay the last AOfIOUFa to the professor.

articles.title: TICKET-OF-LEAVE SYSTEM:
articles.text:
THE TICKET-OF-LEAVE SYSTEM:

The Nottingham Assizes were opened on the 6th by
Mr. Baron Bramwell, and after the labours of the grand
jury were completed they m•ide a presentment on the
t:eatmelit of criminals by their foreman, the Right Hon.
J. E. Denison, M.P., Speaker of the House of Commons,
who said

'MyLord,—l have been desired by my brethren of
the grand jury to make a representation to your Lord-
ship on an important point connected with the admin-
istiation of justice. I mean the system now pursued
in granting tickets-of leave to convicted criminals.
We nave conferred with the chief constable of the
county and with the Governor of the House
of Correction, and we are by them confirmed in the
opinion that the system of granting tickets-of-
leave to the extent now practised is a failure in the
essential points for which it was established, both as
regards the reformation of criminals and the protection
of society. It ha e rendered the sentences of the law
quite uncertain, and in so rendering them uncertain has
deprived them !of their chief deterring effect. It is our
opinion, also, that the discipline ot our gaols
and penal stations is not effective in its cha-
racter. We do not trouble . your Lordship ivith
details, but cases have been placed before us
of criminals sentenced to a term of penal servitude,
soon after at large, again convicted and sentenced to a
longer term of penal servitude, again speedily at large,
and again convicted. These early remissions of penal
sentences do not appear to us to be reconcilable with.
any principle which ought to guide the administration
of justice. Daring and hardened criminals thus let
loose upon society become the leaders in the worst
cases of violence and outrage. We respectfully submit
this representation to your Lordship, and request that
you will be so good as to place it before the proper
authorities. We are aware how meeh weight will be
added to it if it should receive the sanction of your
Lordship's approval.'
The Learned Judge NM sure the presentment would
receive the attention which the weight of the subject
and the intelligence of those by whom it was presented
demanded. He thought that much might be said both
for and against the ticket-of-leave system, the true
theory of which was a conditional remission of punish-
ment. A prisoner sentenced to seven years? penal servi-
tude, with hope of a remission if he behaved well,
suffered lese.than one sentenced. to five years without
such hope;. but it was desirable to get the prisoner into
a good habit of conduct, even although that habit might
not outlast his imprisonment. Although himself offer-
ine° no opinion on the merits of the system, he desired
ti direct the attention of the grand jury to what had
been done under it in Ireland. As to the effects of the sys-
tern here in England, he entirely concurred with the views
they had expressed. He had tried men who had had, if
he might use the term, one sentence overlapping.another,
V4e men being convicted, let outrand convicted again.
He did not think that the ticket-of-leave system short-
ened the terms of imprisonment, and the fixing, for
instance, of 10 years for a certain offence—with the ad-
dition of five years—if the prisoner behaved ill, would be
found practically to have the same effect, a conditional
lengthening, instead of a conditional shortening ofpunish-
meat. The jury had adverted to another matter of still
more importance and that was the character of our
punishments. da man was to be punished, he must be
hurt—pained. Punishment, without pain, was a con-
tradiction in terms. A man could not be punished
without something being done to pain him, and the
punishment ordinarily inflicted might be sufficient to
deter certain peesons who commit offences hurriedly.
But habitual offenders—people who made a trade of
crime, were not to be deterred, either by imprisonment
or by penal servitude. He had occasion to make that
remark recently in London when passing sentence
upon the prisoners who were convicted of garotte
robberies. Some of those men had been offen-
ders against the law from their childhood.. To
send such men to penal servitude was, to send them
among persons of their own class,, of their own
habits. They were not cramped for room; they were
in a clean abode ;.they were well clad and sufficiently
fed; their labour was light. If those who heard him
had any doubt on. the subject, they could go and do as
he had done—they could converse with these men.
The men would readily answer, and: would confirm
what he now said. Their punishment was not painful; it
was only tedious. They were deprived of spirits, tobacco,
and other luxuries; but their condition was not one of
suffering. Once free they soon forgot their tedium. If
their punishment wa,s to be painful, they must be pinched
in food, or subjected to painful labours, and their
behaviour would be different from what it was now.
That he was certain of, not only from a priori reasoning
on the subject, but from actual conversations he had had
with them. Certain persons were engaged ha carrying
out an impossible proposition of punishment without
penalty, and exclaimed against what they called brutal
punishments. He should be sorry to encourage brutal
punishments;. indeed they were impossible—public
opinion would not permit them; but offenders must be
mule to feel, or there could be no effectual punishment.
He would take care that what the grand jury had said
should be made known to the proper quarters, and was
glad to see among them many who could take very
effective steps elsewhere towards carrying out their
views.

articles.title: POSITION OF THE TiIEPINGS.
articles.text:
POSITION OF THE TiIEPINGS.

The following Taeping letter was intercepted by the
Imperialists near Ningpo, and there is no doubt of its
authenticity. It is from one of the rebel leaders in the
province of Ningpo to a subordinate chief, and is inter-
esting, as furnishing information with regard to the
position and views of that party :
Le-she-heen, the Attendant Prince, to the worthy Duke
Chin (General Commanding) at Tungyang.
Gracious younger brother, know that last year we.
committed two great errors in our military tactics: the
first was, abandoning the province of Ganhwing to,
invade Chekiang; the second was, neglecting to pro-
vide for a retreat into Keang-se by holding the two
cities of Changshan and Yushan. At this present
time, a great Chief of the Imps, a Prince of the first
rank, is leading against Nanking an army of Mani-
choos, Hankenns, and Mongolians, to the number of
600 000 men; we have already lost nine-tenths of the
ground we held there. The road (through Ganhwing)
being closed, my army is unable to go to the rescue, so
that the danger awaiting our Royal House is imminent.
Tsang, a Chief of the Imps, is holding Kinchowfoo and
Yenchowfoo, with an army of 400,000 men so that
there is no road open through those parts; whilst Le,
another Impish Chief, is garrisoning Changshan and
Yushan with 400,000 men, assisted by 200,000 local
bandits (i.e. country people, men of the soil). Half of
his army has now gone to garrison Lan-chi, a strong
position from which they mean to attack me at Kinhwa.
The minds of my soldiers are unsettled, and they
will not exert themselves in the fight, so that
things look very threatening. I further hear that
the people are rising in all parts of the
country, and Chowmow (in command at) Shinghieu,
writes to say that the Cisaffected throughout the North-
West parts (of Shaouingfoo) are most numerous, and
that it will require a force of 100,000 disciplined troops
to put them down. Now I am of opinion that these
risings are owing to the excesses of the brethren (our
sildiery) who force the people to rebel by their acts of
murder and rapine and that they cannot be attributed
entirely to the bad disposition of the people. I have now
heard, gracious brother, that your government has been
such as to keep Tuogyang free from disaffection; this
good work of yours merits the highest approbation. I
would counsel you to use your hest efforts, from this time
forth, to show love to the people, so as to prevent them
looking upon us in the light of enemies. Then, should
we meet with any unlucky chance; we shall still have
places of retreat and concealment left open to us;
whereas (if we ill-treat the people)—one revere,—and
we shall find no spot of earth for our dead bodies to rest
in. You must inform all our officers of my ideas on
this subject. This letter is intended for your edification '
solely; it must not be made common, lest it disturb the
minds of our soldiery. When you have perused it,
consign it to the flames.
Given on the 12th day of the 7 Moon (7 Aug. 1862,
Chinese calendar).
Intercepted by the Public Committee of E- woo, and
forwarded to Taontai of Ningpo, on 21 Aug., 18 62
