articles.title: VIE MURDER IN WALES
articles.text:
VIE MURDER IN WALES

On the- 7th the examination of Thomas Edmunds,
aged 24, charged with the murder of his fellow servant,
Jane Lewis, aged 21, in a wood at Tyntalla Farm, in
the parish of Ystradyfodvrg,in the Rhondda Valley, in
the county. of Cardiff, on Sunday evening, the 2nd of
November,.on her way to chapel, was resumed, at the
New Inn, Pontypridd, before William Perkins, Esq.
The leading facts in connection with the alleged murder
have been already given in the notice of the in-
quest held, on the body of the deceased girl. At the
examination, on Friday, the constable who appre-
hended the prisoner was called, and Mr. Davis, the
surgeon who examined the body, repeated the• evi-
dence he had given before- the coroner, expressing his
opinion that the wounds found on the body were not
self-inflicted. No man or woman could have inflicted
the three mortal cuts. Dr. Edwards' of Cardiff, con-
curred in- this opinion,. and said he believed the case
to be one of murder, and not of suicide. The inquiry
was then adjourned till Saturday morning, when evi-
dence was given showing that the prisoner had a strong.
attachment for the deceased, and was courting her
shortly before her death. Two witnesses deposed that
the prisoner was in chapel on the evening of the death
of the deceased, when he spoke of his intended marriage
with 'lane.' Thomas Williams, deceased's"sweetheart,
a collier, was examined, and said they had been keeping
company together for a year and a half, and they were
engaged to be married. On the Sunday morning before
her death she appeared well and contented as usual, and
they proposed to meet at chapel in the evening. The
deceased had told him that the prisoner wanted to court
her. He saw the prisoner as he came from chapel on the
night of the deceased's death; the prisoner did not speak.
Upon one occasion the prisbner was caught listening to
the courtship of witness and deceased in the cow-house
in the dark. In cross-examination he said he had heard
that one John Thomas had been courting the deceased.
She never turned him off for one John Thomas. Mrs.
Williams was recalled, and said that deceased was
right-handed, and the prisoner also to the best of her
knowledge. On the case for the prosecution being
closed it was five o'clock, and the court had sat for ten
hours without rising for refreshment. As it was antici-
pated that Mr. Verity's address and the conclusion of
the examination wauld take some hours longer, after a
consultation between the professional gentlemen and
Mr. Perkins, it was decided that the examination should
stand adjourned, and the prisoner was remanded to
gaol.

articles.title: NEW- ITALIAN MINISTER.
articles.text:
THE NEW- ITALIAN MINISTER.

The Turin correspondent of the Times gives some
account, in a letter published on Monday, of the statesmen
composing the new Italian Ministry. He writes, how-
ever, before the Ministry was formed, as though assum-
ing that it would be headed by Count Pasolixi with-
out knowing who would be his colleagues :
Cowat fe.solini is a native of Ravenna, who joined
the Liberal movement in the Papal States at a very
early period of his life. In 1818 he was a member of
the first Consulta or Constitutional Cabinet of Pius
whose personal friend. he was, and has always
shared the fortunes as well as the political opinions of
his then colleagues in the Ministry, Minghetti,
and. Audinot, both of whom are, therefore, ex-
pected to join him in the present combination.
Pasolini left, rather from, choice than compulsion, his
native city and the Roman States after the Pope's resto-
ration in 1849, and lived in an honourable and genial
exile, chiefly at Florence, and in a pleasant villa in its
neighbourhood. Soon after the annexations of 186.0 he
was included in the very first batch of Senators chosen
from the lEmilian provinces. Baron Ricasoli appointed
him Governor, then Prefect of Milan, an office which he
filled with great credit to himself, and to the great satis-
faction of the Milanese. He is a man .of considerable
wealth, and, unlike most other Italian statesmen, he is
not only married, but rejoicing in a helpmate (a charm-
ing Milanese lady who went among her townspeople by
the name of 'La Perfetta), who shares his greatness with
him, and whose salon is one of the most popular centres
of political reunion wherever she resides. At Milan
Pasolini's ball or balls of last. Carnival, at which the
Prefect had the honour to entertain his Sove-
reign, were something unexampled either for splen-
dour or taste even in the annals of the Lombard capital,
so renowned as it is for the wealth of its nobles and. for
the magnificence and liberality with which they are
ever ready to lavish it. On the accession of the Ratazzi
Cabinet, Pasolini resigned the Milan Prefecture, less,
perhaps, from any irreconcileable antipathy to the new
advisers of the Crown, than out of regard to the fallen
Premier, and also out of some consideration for his pri-
vate finances, which, in the exercise of that profuse
hospitality, had been perhaps somewhat overstrained.
He soon afterwards accepted the more modest position
of Prefect of Turin, a place which he still occupies at
the present day. He has, by reason of his adPiillis-
trative employment, and also in consequence of his
mild, innate disposition, kept aloof, of late, from the
turmoil of party strife. He has none but friends in
either House, and the confidence of the whole country
in his good intentions, high honour, and integrity is
unbounded.'

NEW YORK CUSTOMHOVSE FRityps.—Some of the
boldest fraudulent transartions that have come to light
for a long time have just been discovered in the New
York Customhouse, involving a number of clerks in
the employ of the Government and some importers.
The means employed were the entry of goods far below
their value, and the selection for examination (where
examination was unavoidable) of particular bales with a
certain mark. Eleven clerks have been already sus-
pended. The New York Tribune mentions as in some
sort accounting for the affair, that all the clerks in
volved in this wholesale fraud, covering a sum amount-
ing to between 700,000 dols. and 800,000 dols.' are old
Democratic employes whom Collector Barney has re.
tamed in the Customhouse.'

_REMARKABLE WINTER WEATHER:

The temperature of the past month of November hats
been considerably below the average of many years. On
five former occasions only has the temperature fallen so

though varied by many days of sunshine 'wind, and rain,

changes. The occurrence of severe weather in Novem-
ber, such as werhave now recorded, generally indicates a
mild winter, and an illustration of this statement may
be remembered to have occurred last year.

articles.title: WILLS AND BEQUESTS.
articles.text:
WILLS AND BEQUESTS.

The will of the Right Hon. Leicester Fitzgerald
Charles Stanhope, Earl of Harrington, C. 8., of Elvaston
Castle, Derby; Gawsworth, Chester, and Kensington
Palace Gardens, was proved in London on the 24th ult.
The personalty was sworn under £250,0'00. The
executors and trustees are the testator's nephew, the
Marquis of Kildare; her Majesty's Attorney. General,
Sir Willipm Atherton; William Lloyd Birkbeck, Esq.,
Inner Temple; and James Boyd, Esq., Furnival's Inn.
The will is of considerable length, bearing date NOT.
IEI6I, and is entirely of a family nature. The Earl has
bequeathed to his relict, the Countess, a life interest in
the estates over which his lordship had a power of dis-
position, which he has charged with annuities to his
two daughters. To the Countess is also bequeathed an
immediate legacy of £3,000, together with a disposition
over £lO,OOO, and to each of his daughters he has given
a like disposition over sums of £lO,OOO each. The re-
mainder of the estates, real and personal, are left to his
lordship's only son and successor, the present Earl of
Harrington (now in his-17th year), who is appointed the
residuary legatee. The late earl, who attained the age
of 7.8, was a colonel in the army, and a Knight Com-
mander of the Order of the Redeemer, of Greece.—The
will of James Walker, Esq., C.E., President of the
Institute of Civil Engineers, who died at his. residence
Great George-street, Westminster, on the Bth of Oct.,
aged 81, was proved in the London Court on the 15th
ult., the executors nominated being his son in-law,
Alexander Boyle and William Smythe, Esqs., together
with the Rev. J. bole, M.A., and G. K. Ricards,
Counsel to the Speaker of the House of Commons. The
personalty was sworn under £300,000. The will was exe-
uted in March, 1860, and there are appended six codicils,
which, by revocations, involve much complexity. These
instruments are of very ample dimensions, extending
over upwards of 300 folios. The bequests are also ex-
ceedingly numerous. There is a singular item in the
will with reference to wine, in which the testator men-
tions one stock alone as consisting of 5,500 dozen and
upwards, a number almost unprecedented in the cellars
of a private gentlemen. A large portion of these wines
is bequeathed, conditionally, amongst his sons-in-law
and some personal friends. His estates, subject to the
payment of annuities and legacies, he directs to be
divided into ten parts, and shared in certain specified
proportions, chiefly amongst his daughters and their
husbands and children. Legacies are left to servants,
and to the London and Westminster Hospitals £5OO
each, and £5O to the Westmioster Dispensary.
Illustrated News.

Letters from Nice speak of the weather as not one bit
better than we have here. They complain of cold, rain,
and severe storms. The latter have done great damage
to the new railroad,.which was promised to be completed
as far as Cagnes, a small place seven miles from Nice, in
January; but now, on the principle of going two steps
backward to one forward, it is only open as far as
Vidauba.n, the storms having torn up the road between
that place and Lee Ares, to which place it was com-
pleted. Moreover, they have felt three shocks of earth-
quake during the fast week, so that the sunny South is
not one whit more enjoyable than the foggy North.
Notwithstanding this dismal account, the hotels are all
as full as they can hold, and, in consequence, house rent
is exorbitant, se that many have wended their way
onwards to Rome and Naples.
ARMY ESTIMATES.—The Committee of the Cabinet.,
together with his Royal Highness the General Com-
manding-in-Chief, have had two meetings within the
last week for the purpose of seeing what room there is
for reduction in the next Army Estimates. Large as is
the cost of our military establishments, we fear that
there is but little room for the judicious use of the
pruning knife. Some saving may no doubt be effected.
in the barrack and recruiting departments, but nothing
deserving the name of reduction, unless there be a
diminution of the number of men, and this is. a question
to be decided on political considerations far beyond the
ken of War-office administrators. It is at present alto-
gether premature to state what reductions are likely to-
be carried out; but them- appears to be a feeling in
official quarters that the recruiting staff may be.
diminished, and the depots of regiments at home amal-
gamated with their service companies without any loss
of efficiency. We do not expect, however, to see any
reduction of the combatant part of the army.—Army
and Navy Gazette.
MARITIME CASUALTIES.—The late storms have pro-
duced several casualties. Three crews of vessels foun-
dered at sea, or abandoned in a sinking state, have been
brought into port daring the past week, and we fear that
news of further losses will reach us. On the 22nd inst.
the Peninsular and Oriental Company's steamer Ceylon
brought in Captain Pearson, and the crew, nine in all„
of the English bark Eva, of Scarborough, which foun-
dered about 150 miles to the south-east of Malta, at
8 a.m. of the 21st. The Eva was from Taganrog to
Falmouth, with a cargo of wheat, and her captain and
crew were pieked up in their boat an hour after she had
gone down. Her Majesty's ship Gannet, which arrived
on the 23rd inst. from Constantinople, had on board Capt.
Wooldridge and crew of the English bark Jane Strong,
of Shields, with grain, bound from Odessa to Great
Britain, which was abandoned on the 20th inst. in lat.
26.32 N.,, long. 18.48 E., and soon afterwards foundered
in sight of the officers and crew of the Gannet. The
third instance is that of the English brio. Satellite, of
Stockton, which was abandoned in a sinking state on
the 11th inst., in lat. 37.3 N., long 18.19, on her voyage
from Salina to Cork or Falmouth,, with a cargo of grain.
Captain J. Trowsdale, of this vessel, and nine persons,
forming her crew, arrived here by the Austrian brig

LATER FROlf AMERICA,

NEW YORK, Nov. 29 (Morning.)—No movement
has taken place at Fredericksburg. The rail way is
completed from Acquia Creek to the head-quarters of
the Federal army. The Confederates have driven in
the Federal pickets at Newbern, North Carolina. They
endeavoured to capture three companies of Federals,
but were repulsed. The Confederate force. is said to
number 4,000. The Confederates have abandoned
Iblly Springs. Hudsonville (Mississippi) has been oc-
cupied by the Federals. The Confederates are massed
at Tullahoma (Tennessee) in order to resist the advance
of Rosencranz from Nashville.
The New Yeili Tribune asserts that it is reported on
high authority from Washington that the British Admiral
Milne is in pursuit of the Confederate steamer Alabama.
A large Democratic meeting has been held at New York.
Speeches were made urging the unfaltering prosecution
of the war to re-establish the constitution throughout
the Union. Hopes were expressed that the North atid
South would again be united in order to attack Eng-
land. M'Clellan's removal was denounced. Denuncia-
\ tions against England continue to be poured forth from
. the press and the pulpit, and by public speakers on all
Noccasions which seem to elicit popular approba-
tiO. 'Numerous attempts to burn Memphis
haiT been made by incendiaries. Another forag-
ing expedition by a Federal coloured regiment
has been made from Beaufort, South Carolina.
The Nassau Guardian asserts that Admiral Wilkes had
threatened to enter Nassau without the permission of the
Gover, or, but that he afterwards bore away and lay at
the di nce of a marine league from the shore. The
Guar 'an expresses fears that Admiral Wilkes' hasty
con ct may embroil America and England in war.
Th same journal likewise states that the captain of the
Fqderal steamer Octovora had infringed the Queen's
pioclamation in capturing a schooner within the Abaco
aeef, near Allen's Cay. The steamers Herald and
'Leopard have arrived at Nassau from Charleston.

NEW YORK, -Nov. 29.—General Burnside's army con-
tinues on the Rappahannock, opposite Fredericksburg.
)1\ General Lee is in command of tffe Confederates with a
krce estimated at 80,000 men. General Burnside will
/ in '-all probability attempt a flank movement, and order
Gene‘ral,Sumuer to pass the river at another point. The
President-skisited General Burnside's headquarters at
'Acquia Creek on Wednesday to investigate matters per-
smally, and 'returned to Washington the same day.
Thkl.csgivi9g-day was celebrated throughout the North
on the 27-th. The Government took the opportunity to
release all the political prisoners in Forts Warren and
Lafayette ; among tbe number set at liberty are Mr.
W. H. Winder, of Philadelphia, and Mr. Pierre Soule,
of New Orleans. No oath of allegiance was exacted of
them. nor were they required to make any promises
whatever: The Democrats claim the result as a direct
consequence of their recent triumph at the poll. Gen.
Banks is fitting out his expedition to the South. Great
secresy is maintained as td its destination. It was at
first believed to be Texas. It is now believed to be for
the James River, to co-operate with General Burnside
in an attack upon Richmond.

articles.title: DO THE SLA.VES WANT FREEDOM-.
articles.text:
DO THE SLA.VES WANT FREEDOM-.

The Richmond correspondent of the Times has taxed
the credulity of the readers of that misleading journal
by the following extraordinary statement :--‘ Again and
again,' he writes, the slaves have fled from the Yankee
army into the swamp to escape from compulsory free-
dom and there is abundant evidence that if a being so
morally weak and nerveless as the African could be
made to fight for anything, he would fight for slavery
much rather than liberty.' It is difficult to understand
how any man, even the most violent of partisans, could
put on paper such lying trash as the foregoing, unless,
indeed, considerations of personal safety make him
desire to give to the citizeßs of Richmond the most
ample assurance that he is pro-slavery to the backbone.
The negroes, we are told, reject the offer of freedom
with scorn, and seek a refuge in the swamp rather than
have it thrust upon them! It is true we have heard of
negroes escaping to the swamp, but then they were pur-
sued by bloodhounds arid by human demons, whose
object it was to drag them back to slavery and the lash.
There is, for example, the dismal swamp, an impene-
trable morass, which is marked with the footprints of
many a:fugitive who preferred freedom there to a life of
bondage. But we have to do with the present, not with
the past. Will the Times endeavour to account for this
paradox—that, despite the manner in which the slaves,
according to its Special Correspondent's letter, fondly
hug their chains—more than two hundred thousand of
these contented beings have availed themselves of the
opportunity which the war has afforded of becoming
freemen? The truth is, that the South, by its maintenance
Of slavery, has so cut itself off from human sympathy
that it is obliged to coin falsehoods for the European mar-
ket. Slavery is the weak place in the rebel armour—
it is the one vulnerable point which can only be hidden
by cunning and .artifice. Wherever the Union flag
makes its appearance it is hailed by the slaves as the
symbol of deliverance—wherever the Federal armies
go their camps are crowded with jubilant contrabands.
In the Border States whole districts have been denuded
of their former slave inhabitants. It is difficult to obtain
reliable statistics on this subject, but one fact, for the
truth of which we can vouch, speaks for itself :—The
eensts of 1860 shows that in the State of Missouri there
were at that period 115,000 slaves, while at the present
moment there are not more than 40,000, and the num-
ber is daily diminishing. It will thus be seen that
although the war has entailed great sacrifices it has not
been without its compensating element. Tens of thou-
sands of negroes are free, who but for the Fedetals
would have been doomed (and their children after them)
to all the misery of life-long and unrequited toil.—The

THE HIGHER LAW:--Stidge Swayne, in his charge
‘-) the grand jury at Memphis, maintained the laws of
he State in relation to slaves, and laid it down that
the general Government has no power to disturb those
laws, and stated that in his belief .the result to the
slaves of a change will be want and poverty, idleness
and vice, all the shapes of depravity and wretchedness
from which, as a race, they have been materially re-
claimed in the South; in short, a relapse into their
original abyss of degradation, and to the State a burden
of taxation, thefts, insurrection, human butcheries, and
all the forms of crime and immorality that break the
peace and blacken the face of society. The Provost-
Marshal made short work of this charge, and on the
next day, the 11th ult., issusd a proclamation that any
attempt to execute State laws at variance with the
orders of the President and military commanders will
be summarily punished; adding, however, that 'so far
as the Court confines its business to punishing murder,
arson, burglary, and climes male; in se, the Provost
Guard is to co-operate.'

A FATAL WAR-CRY.—The alfonde expresses the
belief that there is something fatal in the attempt to
make Rome the capital of Italy, since ill fortune attends
every one who strives to arrive at such a result. It
says:—' Rome, capital of Italy! Those words bear
misfortunes with them. The first who pronounced
them, Cavour, disappeared suddenly. Ricasoli repeated
them, and fell. "Rome or Death!' cried Garibaldi, and
a ball sent him to within an inch of his grave. 'Rome
Pa capital V repeats Ratazzi, and Ratazzi falls.'

articles.title: FATAL AFFRAY WITH NAVVILS.
articles.text:
FATAL AFFRAY WITH NAVVILS.

A fatal encounter is reported to have taken place on
Saturday night last, about two miles from Hillsborough,
at a placed called The Galt,' on the way between
Hillsborough and Dromore, Ireland. Two men, named
Robinson and Irvine, gatdeuers, were on their way
home from Dromore near to Hillsborough, when at
The Gulf' they encountered a number of navvies, who
were fighting with each other in the middle of the road.
Some of them asked the two young men where they were
' heading ' to, to which they replied that they were going
to catch the train at Lisburn, and that they belonged to
Belfast. The railway labourers apparently knew the
parties, and disbelieved the statement, retorting that it
was false, and adding, We know you well enough.'
What their object in interfering with these men might
have been is not known, but the navvies, it would
seem, molested them in a most brutal manner. One
party attacked Robinson. They beat him unmercifully,
and kicked him with their shoes until lie was quite
unconscious, and believed to be dead, after which they
threw him over the hedge or fence into a field on the
road-side. Irvine received no better treatment at the
hands of the assailants, for another party of the navvies
abused him in even a worse manner than his comrade.
First, having beaten him about the face,le was after-
wards attacked by one 'of the men with a crowbar, which
was used with great violence on his body, in conse-
quence of which he was also rendered insensible. A
woman, it is stated, having interfered to save the two
men frombeing naurdered, the navvies, not d esiring herpre-
Bence, inflicted such injuries upon her as, it is said, have
terminated fatally, but this part of the story is not
authenticated. The navvies then left their victims on
the road, where they were subsequently discovered and
removed to the heipital in a hopeless state. Irvine died
on Monday evening, but Robinson, according to the
latest accounts, is expected to survive. Irvine,
before his death, made a deposition, and identified three
men, who have been apprehended, as his assailants.

HOT/ TA TICKET-OF-LEAVE 314.07 HAD

A FAIR START IN LIFE.

An Old Soldier' writes the following letter to the
Times: The advocates of the " ticket-of-leave "
system urge that the reason of the failure of their bant-
ling is that no one will employ the licensed convict.
Allow me to state my humble experience. We all
know how our army is recruited. The sergeant goes
into the market-place, or the bars of inns, or the pits of
theatres, and for a shilling purchases the soldier. If he
passes the surgeon's inspection, no further inquiries
are made, his antecedents are utterly unknown, and,
though he makes a statement of his name,
parish, and profession, in two-thirds of these
cases they are purely fictions. The returned con-
vict has once again a start in life. He is in an
honourable profession, his antecedents are unknown,
and he is as much respected as the honest clerk or the
fair-famed yokel; his conduct alone regulates the
opinions of his officers, yet in every case that came under
my notice a very few months showed that the escaped
convict was as bad as the day he garotted the honest
burgher in the city of London. One of many instances
I will give.:—G— enlisted and joined at Canterbury.
Before he had been there two months he went out on a
marauding expedition, and doubtless, attempted a high-
way robbery. His victim being intoxicated the
magistrate only convicted him of a common assault.
He was in a few weeks Afterwards tried and con-
Ticted, and punished with six months' hard labour
for picking a prostitute's pocket. On leaving gaol he
brought a most exemplary character with him from
the governor and chaplain. Soon after one of his com-
rades confessed to me of having met G— 'abroad,' and
when taxed with it, G---- told me that he had been a
lawyer's clerk in Birmingham, and had five years from
Warwick Assizes for forgery; he was then convicted on
his return at Chester and Liverpool for pocket-picking,
and at Leeds for housebreaking, in the last case sentenced
to penal servitude, and was now on his ticket-of-leave.
His religious views were uncertain. I observed he at-
tended church, or the Roman Catholic chapel alternately,
.as suited best his escape from midday btables. As G—
committed military crime upon crime, and as punishment
followed on punishment, his life became irksome, and,
taking "French leave" one morning, he deserted, and I
have never heard of him since.'

DEATH AND TRADE. The American Government
advertises for 2,000 head-boards for graves. They are
to be of black walnut, clear of knots, 4ft. long, and 10in.
wide. D. W. Kolbe, of Philadelphia, advertises to fur-
nish artificial limbs at 50 dollars for each limb ampu-
tated above the knee-joint, or 35 dollars if amputated
below the knee-joint—Mechanics' Magazine.
TILE REMAINS OF THE LATE PRINCE CONSORT.—It
is expected that the remains of his late Royal Highness
the Prince Consort will loe removed from the Royal
vault in St. George's Chapel, Windsor, before the 14th
Inst. to their last resting-place, which has been pre-
pared in the new Royal mausoleum now in the course
of erection in Frogmore gardens. This beautiful build-
ing, a description of which has already appeared in the
colums of the Times, is gradually advancing towards
completion.
INFALLIBILITY OF THE FEMALE SEX.—The Ladies
have a belief that Parisian corsets wear much longer
than any other ones, and the dear creatures are right,
as they always are, for we beg leave to point to the
occupation of Rome by Louis Napoleon's army as an
incontestable proof of how exceedingly lasting French
Stays are.—Pnnch.
EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPE OF Two MEN. The
Fraserburgh correspondent of the Northern ~Ensign gives
an account of a marvellous escape made there by two
men on Sabbath morning. About seven o'clock, a
small boat, with two men on beard, was observed at the
back of a dangerous ridge of rocks known as the
Bushes,' near the harbour. There was a heavy sea
running at the time, and no hopes were entertained of
the men being able to reach the shore. A. pilot-boat
crew, at great risk, ventured out and succeeded in
bringing them safe to the harbour. They proved to be
the crew of the small sloop Happy Return, of Dundee,
-Captain George Henderson, from Newcastle to Spey
.coals. When about seven miles off Fraserburgh the
vessel sprang a leak and became unmanageable. The
two men then betook themselves to the small boat, with
nothing but their wearing clothes, and had little more
than reached the punt when the sloop foundered. They
laboured to reach the land under a heavy sea for several
hours, and at last succeeded, making an escape which
is truly wonderful. They were sent home on Monday
by Mr. Couper, agent for the Shipwrecked Mariners'
Society.

DFATII OF LIETJTENANT-COLONEL WILLIAM DONALD
MACDONALD.—We observe by our advices from India
that the above gallant and distinguished officer of the
93rd (Sutherland Highlanders) Regiment of Foot had
died of cholera. This officer entered the army as ensign
June 4, 1847, and became lieutenant Oct. 1 1850. He
embarked with the 93rd Regiment in Feb., 1854, and
served in the Eastern campaign that year as provost-
marshal, and for his services was rewarded with the
medal and clasps for Alma, Balaklava, Inkerman, and
Sebastopol, together with the sth class order of the
Medjidie. He was made a captain October 10, 1854,
and was appointed deputy-assistant adjutant general and
deputy-assistant quartermaster-general January 8, 1855,
and remained at Scutari until August 13, 1856. He
was promoted to brevet-major Dec. 26, 1856, appointed
deputy. assistant adjutant general to the fore( s in China
from March 23 to Nov. 19, 1857, and served with the
above regiment in the campaign of 1857-58 in the Doab,
ande, and Rohilcund, including the capture of Lucknow,
Bareilly and Furrakabad.

NEW COMETS.—M. Bruhns, Director of the Observa-
tory of Leipsic, has just discovered two new comets, one
on the Ist inst. and the other on the following day. On
the 3rd, about four o'clock after midnight, mean time of
Paris, the first comet was in right ascension 159 deg.
38 min., and south declination 2 deg. 11 mm.; the
second, being the fourth, of the present year, was at the
same time in right ascension 209 deg. 9 rain., and south
declination 14 deg. 45 min. Judging from their respec-
tive motions of the 2nd and 3rd inst., they must now be
more or less in the vicinity of Spica Virginis, which
rises about three o'clock after midnight. The second
comet is brilliant enough to be observable during moon-
night, but the first is fainter, and the moon may prevent
its being seen. The moon is now on the decline since.
the 6th, and crosses the meridian at midnight.

neighbour. As the poor fellow groaned and moved-ii;
easily on his couch, a ready hand was near him to assist
and give a cheerful word of encouragement. 'I can't
lie; I can't sit; I can't stand; what shall I do!' ex-
claimed the sufferer. Pray God to help you through,'
said his daughter. Thou'll weather it yet, George,'
said one of his fellow-workmen; but the moaning of
Pickering mingled with the sighs and tears of the
women as he feebly urged his friends if they wished to
see him, to come at once. This is only a faint picture of
what must have happened in many a house last night.
Towards four o'clock the state of the mine was such
that no farther chance remained to get men out.
Exploring parties who went down were unable to
penetrate more than a few yards from the foot of
the shaft, the hot air and after-damp compelling them
to retreat. Reluctant as they were to come to this
conclusion, it was evident to all that further efforts to
save he would only result in a greater sacrifice, and
orders were given that no more men should be allowed
to descend. During the drawing out much confusion
had of course prevailed, and no complete list of those
recovered could be made out. One thing, however,
was certain—a great number must be still in the pit,
and they must be dead. 'Chose whom the blaze had
spared, the after-damp had choked. The ventilation
was entirely gone, the only current of air being from
the down cast to the up-ca3t shaft, and in that space, it
was known no one was. The list of names of those
who are gin in the pit is not complete, but still it in-
cludes 39 names. There may be 12 or 14 morein the
pit whose names are not known.
The revattions of the last body of explorers who
descended the mine convinced the managers of the
colliery of the hopelessness of further efforts, and they
immediately turned their attention_ to other means of

extinguishing the fire, which was still raging belo-v-C-7lt
was also known that the destruction of the ventilation

of the pit permitted the accumulation of gas, and if this
•ahould reach the flames another explosion, more fearful
in violence than any of the others, would result. The

THE FATAL COLLIERY EXPLOSION! list discharge had effectually cleared every obstruction
.NEAR BARiVSLEY. in the mine, and another would range unchecked
through the workings, and in all probability destroy the
gearing in the shaft. The occurrence of such an ex-
plosion was hourly dreaded, but meanwhile *bands of
men had been set to work to cut a trench from the canal,
which runs within about a hundred yaris of the colliery,
to the nearest shaft. When this was completed a large
stream of water could be thrown into the pit, and the
fire by that means extinguished.
The full extent ot the calamity will not be known
until a roll-call has been gone through of the whole of
the men employed at the mine. Many of the men lived
at Barnsley and at Worsborough-common, and on leav-
ing the mine they at once hurried off to their respective
homes, without waiting to report themselves to the
owners of the colliery.
We ought to state that the general testimony of
several of the rescued workmen was that the ventila-
tion of the mine was extremely good. One of them
said that the current of air constantly travelling through
the working was almost always so strong that a candle
could not be used.

WORSBOROUGII, Dec. 9.—The following is a detailed
account of the dreadful explosion at Edmunds Main
Colliery
The colliery is the property of Messrs. Mitchell,
Bartholomew, and Ty as, is 180 feet deep, and is one of
the most extensive collieries that are worked in the
Barnsley seam. The bed of coal is the nine-feet Barns-
ley seam. The w. rkings extend for more than a mile
from north to south, and there are three shafts, two
downcast, and one over the cupola furnace, by which the
ventilation is obtained.
The primary cause of the accident was the ignition of
a 'blower' of gas by the blasting of the coal at the ex-
treme dip point' at the southern-most extremity of the
workings. It seems that the mine was being connected
with a new shaft which had been sunk to the southward,
and a straight heading was being driven through the
coal in the direction of this shaft. About 7 o'clock yester-
day morning the men engaged in the operation found it
necessary to 'blast' the c al, and a charge of powder
('a shot') was accordingly fired. The coal in the new
workings gave out a great quantity of gas, and the men
were obliged to use Davy lamps to ward off danger.
The shot ignited a blower' of gas, which exploded, set
fire to the coal, and blew down a portion of the air
course. At this time there were about 260 men and
boys in the mine, and when so alarming an occurrence
in one part of the workings had taken place, the reason-
able inference seems to be that the persons in charge of
the mine should have sent word to all the men warning
them that there was danger of an explosion. Some of
the men, however, say that this was not done. George
Laughton, the bottom steward, endeavoured to put out
the fire without ailowing the miners to become cog.
nizant of its existence and the danger. it entailed. He
went with a party of the men and commenced building
a solid brick stopping' to restore the ventilation.
The work was carried on vigorously, and an attempt
made concurrently to put out the fire. But neither
seems to have been successful. The foul air accumulated
in the mine until at about half 11 o'clock, a fearful
explosion tool place, the gas having fired where the
coal was burning. The effect of the explosion was
most disastrous, many of the air: courses being blown
down, and the miners began to flock to the bottom of
the main shaft. Many of them received their first
warning of danger by the presence of the deadly after-
damp in their workings. One young man, named
James M'Quillan, states -that he was employed in No. 2
board, in the south workings, a considerable distance
from any other working place. He 'felt' the gas and
became alarmed, and left his place to seek some of the
other miners. He saw one of them named Peter Blacker,
and told
.him there was something the matter in
the mine,, and suggested an immediate retreat, but
Blacker told him he was too soon frightened, and
that if he wanted to go he might, but he (Blacker)
should stay where he was. Fortunately for himself;
M'Quillan went on towards the shaft, and on the wa.y
the gas became so powerful that ,he was in extreme
danger, and had to -make a circuit round the workings
half a ;nile out of the direct path, in order to get into a
purer air. On the way he met a man named Edward
Hunt, who asked him to go with him and seek for his
brother. They went to the bottom of the board where
young Hunt had been working, but the place was so
full of gass that they found it impossible to go up.
M'Quillan struggled on until he came to the shaft,
where a great number of men and boys were waiting
to take their turns to ascend. By this time the alarm
had become general, but notwithstanding the excitement
the shaft was worked With quickness and order, and
a great number of the men were rescued. Hopes were
entertained that the whole would be brought out before
any serious calamity took place, an event which was
dreaded every moment, in consequence of the rapid
accumulation of gas. The communication between some
parts of the mine and the shaft had been destroyed by
the second explosion, and a number of men and boys,
variously estimated at from 50 to 70, were still in the
mine. The hope of rescue appeared every moment
growing fainter. A number of noble fellows volunteered
to go down into the mine and search for those who had
been cut off from succour by the progress of the suffoca-
ting vapour. Five men, named George Laughton, the
bottom steward; Henry Laughton, his eldest son;
Charles Frobisher, John Parkin, and Benjamin Hoy-
land, were the volunteers, and it is one of the most
melancholy facts connected with the calamity, that
these noble men became involved in the fate of those
whom they were endeavouring to rescue. They had
been for some time in the mine, and a number of
i
the injured men—some of them n such a eondition
that death would have been welcomed as a release
from intolerable agony—had been sent to the pit
bank, when suddenly a third explosion took place,
about one o'clock, and sealed the fate of all who were
then in the mine. The effect of the repeated ex-
plosions had been, of -course, almost wholly to destroy
the means of ventilating the mine. The doors and
stoppings in nearly every part of the mine had been
demolished, and the current of air, no longer com-
pelled to pass through the whole of the mine, on
its way to the upcast shaft, was felt only in the direct
level from one shaft to the other. The headings and
board-gates were totally without ventilation, and became
magazines of explosive gas. An • overthrow,' or bricked
archway, which was built on the incline, about 160
yards from the cupola, to carry the air over the work-
ings, was blown down, and the ventilation was neces-
sarily destroyed in that part of the mine. In other parts
of the workings the force of the blast produced the same
effects. When the third explosion took place, a consul-
tation was held at the pit-bank, and as the shaft-gear
was not injured, several persons volunteered to go down
and rescue the poor fellows who remained in the mine.
The attempt to enter the workings was, however fruitless.
The men found they could pass with comparative ease
along the main road between the upcast and down cast
shafts, a short time after the third blast, in consequence of
the current of air which was travelling over the level;
but in a short time this path became impassable by the
advance of the fire and after-damp, and about 4 o'clock
orders were issued to allow no more men to descend the
shaft: When the last party returned they reported
that the place was so full of foul vapour that they
found it impossible to proceed more than ten or
twelve yards from the bottom of the shaft. Most
of the men got out after the explosion were un-
injured; others were nearly suffocated with the
after-damp, but a few minutes in the fresh air re-
vived them; others, again, were burnt or bruised more
or less seriously. One poor fellow, William Davy, of
Worsborough Common, was so burnt that he only sur-
vived a few minutes, and was removed by the police to
the nearest public house. As far as we were able to ascer-
tain, in the confusion that prevaied at the pit last
night, and in the face of an order from one of the pro-
prietors not to give any information to any reporters,'
the injured were as follows :—George Pickering (fire-
man), Hollingsworth, Samuel Tyas, Joseph Walton,
John Bellerby, Samuel Soresby, Hewitt, Swift, Morri-
son, William Davy, and Edward Hunt. In addition to
these, there were several other wounded men who had
been removed to Barnsley.
George Picketing, the fireman, is most seriously in-
jured. He had gone down the pit in the forenoon,
after hearing of the accident and the firing of the coal,
and when the last explosion took place was in one of
the headings. The 'blast passed over him, licking up
with its tongue of flame his clothes and hair and leaving
him almost dead. By some means he managed to
crawl to the pit bottom, and was brought out and re-
moved to his house in Worsborough, about half a mile
distant from the colliery. There he lay on a tem-
porary bed in the house-place in an agony of pain,
carefully tended by his wife and daughters, who
were administering such remedies as they were able.
Around the bed stood a group of grimy colliers, some
of whom had been in the pit when the accident hap-
pened and others who had come to assist their afflicted
_

articles.title: BLASTED HOPES.
articles.text:
BLASTED HOPES.

(From the New York Times.)
We are pained to see that the London Times has been
again exposing itself to disappointment. The amount
of hope deferred, of confident expectation never realised,
and of prophecy never to be verified, which that journal
has been afflicted with since the rebellion broke out, .are
beyond estimation, and yet, like the Bourbons, it learns
nothing by experience. The Union men still refuse to
give up the existence of the nation; the 4 mob' quietly
acquiesce in the determinations of the constituted
authorities.; the financial bubble' obstinately refuses
to burst; and the danger which the Times ob-
viously fears more than any other result of the war,
viz., the suppression of the rebellion, is still gathering
on its horizon. These Yankees obstinately decline to
gauge their conduct by what the English organ lays
down to he established laws, and it has been BO often
astounded by a result which was in its opinion simply
impossible that it would be only reasonable to think it
would give up expecting anything.. But the ruin of the
Union lies too near its heart to allow it to do so; and
we find that it has fallen again into the same old ditch.
In a recent article it rejoices that it has cause to
hope that reason and humanity are dawning again in
America, after a long obscurity.' We catcnot accept this
praise. In our opinion, reason,' by which the Times
means judging of our affairs according to the interests
of England, instead of our own—and humanity,' by
which it means giving over our country to a never-end-
ing warfare, instead of fighting the matter through now,
are as far from dawning among us as ever.
The ground of this hope on the part of the Times is
not only that General M'Clellan's army is unable to take
the field, and that the men of whom it is composed are
quarrelling, plundering, and deserting in presence of a
victorious enemy, but it is that men dare to speak out
and tell us that all this is going on, and that there is
little hope of its amendment.' And the conclusion to
which it comes on the whole matter-is, that evidently
the reaction from the frenzy-of the past eighteen months
has begun, and we may cherish some hope that the
worst is past.' _

We cannot but feel some little sympathy with the
Times when it learns that, by the. day its exultation
reached our shores, that army which it declared to be
'unable to take the field, and to be occupied in
'quarrelling, plundering, and deserting,' is again ,ori its
way toward Richmond, under a new leader, and with
higher hopes and sterner determination than even We
trust that a few short weeks may suffice to show our
funny critic that what it deems the worst' is not past,
but is rushing forward steadily and inexorably to be-
come an established fact. In the meantime we 2,ecom-
mend to the Times to moralise upon the singular uncer-
tainty of all things in this world, and particularly in
America.

The Prussian Ambassador at the Court of Austria,

Times of Nov. 23:—' Mrs. Edwin James has filed her
complaint for a divorce from her husband, charginc,
adultery. It is understood that Mr. James denies the

THE SACKVILLE-STREET CLUB OP DUBLIN.— An an-
nouncement is made in the Daily .Express,' writes a
Dublin correspondent, 'which must be in the highest
degree gratifying to Sir Robert Peel and his friends.
The Sackville-street 'Club, one of the principal Con.
servative clubs in this ,city, if not the principal, at the
fullest meeting of members ever held, have elected Sir
Robert unanimously; there was not a single black bean.
This is an honour which, I believe, no Liberal Chief
Secretary ever received before in Ireland.'
TEMPERANCE MEETINGS IN CITY WAREHOUSES.—
Samuel Bowly, Esq., President of the National Temper-
ance League, delivered an address on Temperance to the
young men at Messrs. 'George Hitchcock and Co.'s
warehouse; St. Paul's Churchyard, on IV ednesdayeven-
ing, under the presidency of George Williams, Esq-, one
of the partners. There were upwards of 100 Persons
present, including a few ladies, and at the close of the
proceedings eleven signed the pledge. A similar meet-
ing was held a few days ago within the business pre-
mises of Messrs. Copestake, Moore Crampton, and Co.,
Bow Churchyard, which was addressed by Mr. Bowly
and Mr. Samuel Morley, and thirty of the audience

AN Ex-Pansumir.—The will of ex-President Van
Buren has been admitted to probate at Hudson. It is
dated Jan. 18, 1860, and commences as follows :--` I,
Martin Van Buren, of the town of Kinderhook, county
of Columbia and State of New York, heretbfore governor
•of the state, and more recently President of the United
States, but for the last and happiest year of my life a,
farmer in my native town, do make and declare the fol-
lowing to be my last will and testament,' &c.
Certain persons, belonging to that political party
which has lately lifted up its head so much in Prussia,
propose, it is said, to present to the ex-King of Naples a
silver shield, commemorative of his exploits and misfor-
tunes, and for which the design is already sketched. It
represents Francis 11. on a rock, defending himself
against the attacks of a troop of demons, two among
which are considered unmistakeably to resemble Victor
Emmanuel and Garibaldi.
A Cassel letter in the Hamburg News says The
Princess Hohenlohe, daughter of the Prince Elector,
whose husband has gone to America without paying his
debts, which amount to very considerable sums, has
been summoned to appear before the tribunal of the
free city of Frankfort; as well as her brother, the
second son of the Elector. The princess signed bills for
800,000 florins which her husband put in circulation,
and the princess's brother gave his guarantee by
attaching his signature to 80,000 florins' worth of those
bills.'

A singular charge of -stealing £lOO was heard by the
Bradford magistrates on Monday. Two manufacturers
belonging to Shipley were the prisoners, the prosecutor
belonging to Bradford. An inquiry narrowed the charge
considerably, but it is still a serious one for the defen-
dants. They hud given a bill for £5OO to the prosecutor
for a heap of wool, but fearing that the wool would not
be delivered, they called upon the prosecutor, offering
to bet £lOO that the wool would not be delivered, and
afterwards snatching two £5O notes from the hands of
the prosecutor's daughter, where they had been placed.
The case was remanded.

ATTEMPT TO POISON A SHIP CAPTAIN.—At the Liver-
pool Assizes on the 9th, Wm. Peck, a coloured seaman
formerly of the ship Palatino, was sentenced to three
years' penal servitude, for mixing vitriol and blue stone
with some tea, which the steward of the Palatino had
prepared for the captain. The prisoner had become in-
subordinate, and had formed a spite against the captain
in consequence of his having been compelled to do a
proper share of work.

- SIBERIAN EXPLORATION.—A letter from Archangel,
in the No; them Post, gives some account of the expedi-
tion which was organised, with the co-operation of the
Russian Government, by Captain Kruscnstern, of the
Imperial navy, for the purpose of exploring the Icy Sea
and the coasts of Siberia as far as the mouth ofthe Yenissey.
According to the plan decided on, the Yermak, com-
manded by Captain Krusenstern, left on the Ist of
August the town of Kouiski, on the river of that name,
accompanied by a small yacht, with four men on board,
under the orders of sub-officer Korotki. The yacht
returned some time after alone to Kouiski, and gave
the following account :—The two vessels safely crossed
the Strait of Yongorski-Schar, and entered what is
called the Red Sea. They had always kept within
sigi, of edch other up to that time, but on Sept. 10 the
schooner became surrounded by such compact masses of
iee that the yacht was obliged to keep at about a mile
distance. The fog afterwards became so thick as to
completely prevent the position of the Yermak froAxt
being seen. Three days after the weather cleared up,
but nothing could be seen of her, and Koroti considered
it prudent to return and wait in the Strait of Yongorski-
Schar for tie return of the schooner. The yacht re-
mained there for a fortnight, but nothing was seen of
her, nor could any intelligence be obtained from the
inhabitants on the coast. Since that time no intelli-
gence has been received of the Yermak.

articles.title: SILK DISSOLVED.
articles.text:
SILK DISSOLVED.

A curious communication has been received by the
Academy of Sciences from M. Persoz, jun., on a pro-
perty possessed by chloride of zinc' which, when con-
centrated, will dissolve zinc rapidly by the aid of heat,
and slowly at the ordinary temperature, or when the
solution is weak. But this property of chloride of zinc
is confined to silk; it does not dissolve either wool or
vegetable fibres, so that a means is now at our disposal
of determining with scientific precision the exact
quantity of silk in a given stuff, a discovery which
the fair must be thankful for. Let them take a piece
of stuff alleged to be pure silk, and put it into a boiling
solution of chloride oi zinc; if pure, it will dissolve en-
tirtly, if not, filaments of wool or cotton will remain.
If it he required to find the quantity of cotton mixed with
wool in a certain stuff, the latter may be treated in a
similar way with soda, when the wool will be dissolved and
the cotton alone remain. The chloride of zinc should be
neutralised by boiling it with an excess of oxide of zinc,
otherwise it might act as an acid. By contact with
this chloride, silk is converted into a gummy mass,
which, if the quantity is considerable, will become
quite viscous, like a dense syrup or a solution of gum
arabic. Ammonia produces a white precipitate in the
diluted solution of silk. To separate the silk from its
solution, M. Paso; after various ineffectual trials, at
length resolved to proceed according to Mr. Graham's
method of dialysis, with which our readers are already
acquainted. By this method, the chloride of zinc, in
a few hours, passed through the dialyger ; the viscous
consistence of the solution increased, and, after swelling
up a little, at length became an opaline jelly, like that
obtained by starch, and having nearly the same taste.
It had not, however, the same chemical properties; it
did not swell under the action of ,caustic potash, nor
become liquid by sulphuric acid. But it evaporated
to dryness in an open basin, it produces a substance
of a bright currant-red colour resembling murexine.
This colour, however, has no stability. It requires
a dull red heat to decompose the jelly of silk, which
then emits the disagreeable odour of burnt silk.—Gal-
saint.

articles.title: CONVICTS AND PRISONS.
articles.text:
CONVICTS AND PRISONS.

Several letters on the treatment of convicts, prison
discipline, and tickets of leave, appeared in the Tunes of
Tuesday. A Justice' disbelieves in the efficacy of soli-
tude and separate confinement :—_ _

The •mail who garottes A to-night took his mid. day
meal with men and women who nave taken the gaol
degree and came out with its testaanur ; neither he nor
his companions suffered so much, or were imprisoned so
much, that they are afraid or ashamed of felony. They
were good prisoners—will be so again; they are utterly
bad men because they love crime, and the love of it
outweighs all they have learnt of the suffering which
follows on detection.

I believe you could not manage Chatham Portland,
Dartmoor, or even Pentonville, except you had a greater
:force of officers, unless OR this plan of buying obedience
by
,payment in abridged confinement. I say, go to any
'expense for staff. Let the sentence of the judge be
carried out to the day. Avoid long sentences, but in
diet and discipline be severe. Transport without mercy
those on whom it is clear that home penal treatment has
failed. If, however, you will persist in giving tickets-
of-leave, let every ticket-holder be directly under the
supervision of the police. Let him be known as a felon,
allowed to try and be honest, content to be watched in
the effort.

It would be far better to flog twice in a three years'
sentence than to degrade a man by keeping him as a
pampered wild beast for five years, pretending all the
time that you are reforming him by making his patient
submission a merit. I own I think the separation from
the other sex, the iron repression of all intercourse but
what is called 'guarded' with those of his class for a
long period of years, fatal to all that is valuable in
humanity. You make the hard harder.
W. 11. S. describes the diet provided for the garotters
recently sentenced by Baron .Bramwell, and for other
.convicts tnidergoing penal servitude :
'Breakfast—.oz. of flaked cocoa or cocoa nibs, made
with 2oz. of milk and six drams of molasses into of a
Tint of liquid coca. Dinner-4oz of meat, weighed
when cooked without bone; and pint of soup, and Ilb.
of potatoes, weighed when boiled. Supper—one pint
of gruel, sweetened with six drams of molasses. Bread,
.20oz. per diem; a liberal allowance of salt. Soup made
:with liquor of meat of the same day, strengthened by
legs and shins to 100 pints. Barley, peppers, and car-
rots added, and a seasoning of onions. Gruel, lioz. of
oatmeal to one pint.'
Uriah Lleep, at Mr. Creakle's model prison, found the
beef 'rather tougher than he could wish,' and Mr. Litti-
mer complained that the milk with which the cocoa was
boiled was not qttite genuine. 1 believe neither of these
gentlemen would have the least reason to find fault with
the chef of the present establishment; but, should they
do so, their suggestions would instantly be attended to
by the obliging officials who watch over the comfort of
the prisoners._

The most singular letter of the series is one ignod A
Ticket-of-Leave Man,' which gives us a picture of Dart-
moor Prison regarded from the interior. The writer
sus it was his misfortune to be there for several years
as one, who, having broken the laws of his country,
fully deserved the punishment inflicted on him
When I reached Dartmoor from Millbank Peniten-
tiary I was put into an association ward, containing
upwards of 90 prisoners. In the evenings the noise of
this place resembled that of a low taproom; and though
without drinkable stimulants, they had stimulants of
another kind having very dangerous tendencies. In one
corner might have been seen an old hand' instructing
a youngster how to excel in pugilistic encounter; in
another quiet recess 'greenhorn' was trying his hand
at a 'light-fingered' experiment; while a third was
being instructed in the latest and most approved mode
of garotting. In various parts of the ward loquacious
old lags' were t' spinning yarns' to admiring groupes,
who were drinking in the information the others were
so well able to communicate in regard to their expe-
rience and adventures in housebreaking, lock and pocket
picking, and the scientific use of the bludgeon or life-
preserver on their victims or the police. In every
direction might have been heard in common conversation
such oaths, curses, and imprecations as I never heard
before. I assure you, Sir, my blood has run cold when,
having no other place to go to, I have been compelled to
sit and overhear things which would have shocked
all but the most abandoned villains. At fist I
bodly reproved their wickedness, and argued with
those who seemed most open to conviction in re-
gard to the sin of rapine and wrong; but I was soon
voted a nuisance,' and accordingly was compelled
to refrain from interference. In writing to my rela-
tives at this time I stated what sort of a place I was
located in, and the result was, I received a severe
rebuke from the Governor, who told me he did not
believe my statement, for he was surethe officers would
put an end to this state of things if they existed. But,
as regards the power of the warders in the circum-
stances described, I conceive it to be impossible that,
with only one in a large ward, and he often occu-
pied in an adjoining room serving out clothes, &c., to
the men, there can be the requisite supervision. The
chief remedy is to put an end to the associa-
tion wards; and: of late, owing to there being a
reduction in the number of convicts at that station,
these wards have been partially given up. When I
sacceeded, after a few weeks, in getting removed to a
separate confinement prison, the relief I experienced in
having a cell to myself was great indeed.

SINGULAR IMPRISONMENT.—In 1301, King Edward I.
Caused the Countess of Buchan to be placed in a wooden
cage in the shape of a crown, and shut up in one of the
towers of Berwick Castle for crowning Robert Bruce at
Scone. She was attended by two Englishwomen, and
remained six years in this confinement.
Pennant very justly observes, that 'the pursuit of
natural history would become no order of men better
than our clergy, as they are (or ought to be) the best
qualified, and the most stationary part of the community ;
and as this is a mixed species of study (when considered
as physicotheology), it is therefore particularly pertinent
to their profession. _

THE FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF
LEIPZIO.—Next year being the fiftieth anniversary of
the battle of Leipzig, a project has been put forward for
the erection of a great national German monument, a,
sort of Temple of Victory, with statues, busts, and por-
traits of conspicuous military characters, and basreliefs
and pictures of the most important episodes of the great
fight. Contributions, it is Proposed, should be exten-
sively invited. The project s on a grand scale, and
includes that of a complete museum of the battle, to
contain relics and memorials of the most various kinds,
specimens of all the weapons used and suits of all the
uniforms worn by the various regiments, copies of all
the pictures of the battle already existing, and a library
of the literature relating to it. In short, to carry out
the plan as sketched by its originators a very large sum
would be required, and is is no detraction from the
patriotic and national spirit of Germany to doubt if it
would easily be raised for such a commemoration of a
battle the magnitude and results of which fully suffice
to secure it against oblivion.—Letter front Berlin.
A FEDERAL CORVETTE AT FALMOUTH.—The Federal
corvette Onward, Captain Nickels, put into Falmouth
on Saturday last from Fayal, to r pair some slight
damages and to re-victual. She is about 900 tons, has
nine guns and 114 hands, and is one of the ships on the
look out for the Alabama. Her crew appeared to be in i
a very unsatisfactory state of discipline, as her officers
cannot come on shore in the ship's boats from fear of the
men deserting.

THE WATERS OF COMFORT.
When did ever land beside
Show the sight that England's showing—.
All these streams of bounty flowing
Swift and steady, far and wide?
From cottagers' and children's hands
Many a tiny rillet springing,
Many a new Pactolus bringing
From rich purses golden sands.
Silver streams and streams of gold,
Meagre rill and mighty river,
In their flow converging ever,
•
As one tide at length are rolled.
All the desert on its brink
Gathers green from those glad waters: -
Far-off warfare's guiltless martyrs,
Fainting stoop them down to drink.
Of the myriads that throng
Te those waters none shall perish:
England's charity will cherish
Needs not bred of England's wrong.

MODERATE CHAR GS.—Mr. Punch, who, after his
labours in the sphere of absurdity, seeks recreation in
serious reading, was much diverted with the Bishop of
London's Charge. For tolerance, good sense, charity, and
freedom from cant, it is quite a curiosity of its kind. Mr.

Tait's Charge is as moderate as the charge of 3d., or 4d.

cal, and is all that Mr. Punch will ask for his magnifi-
cent forthcoming Almanac.

number of years that he has had his hand in, did he ever
draw a winning number.

mill between Mace and King was a 'demoralising ex-

The attraction of a prize -fight does not consist in the
chance that it may terminate fatally; but how many

certain that he could not possibly break his neck?

THE Rev. G. C. (" Boatswain ")
SMITH, now in his 81st year, has become greatly
enfeebled, and is in straightened circumstances. He
needs an attendant, but cannot pay one. Mr. Smith has
been labouring as a Christian Minister about fifty-eight
years. It will be remembered that he commenced
Destitute Sailors' Asylums and the first Sailors' Home,
from whence sprang all the other Sr ilors' Homes. He
gave great blows to the crimping system, revived open-
air preaching, and commenced and carried on for many
years all the efforts for the religious instruction of
sailors. Besides which he originated the first Temper-
ance Society in Britain. and established the London
Mission (1814) and Sailors' Orphan and Magdalen
Homes, and commenced the efforts for the religions
instruction of soldiers. For all this Mr. Smith has
passed unrewarded by his countrymen. Now that he is
aged and poor, a friend pleads that public gratitude and
sympathy might be manifested.
Donations may be sent for Mr. Smith to Mr. Daniel
Pratt, the Publisher of THE BRITISH STANDARD, 10, Bolt
Court.
